text: I don't either. I think it was the low voltage; it just fell off. Maybe it got hit.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Stand by for shutdown.

speaker: Gordon
text: Stand by. 31, 32 [garble].

speaker: Conrad
text: There it is...

speaker: Conrad
text: Shutdown.

speaker: Conrad
text: Shutdown. 11 plus 33, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Flight Dynamics reported it looks like a good orbit. Showing velocity 25,561 feet per second [7,791 m/s]. Down range 1,450 [nautical miles, 2,685 km]. FIDO. FIDO says we are Go.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. Before you get down there to work on that switch, try pulling on panel 5, your IMU main A and main B breakers.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. That did it. They're both out. Now what do you want us to do?

speaker: Carr
text: Your S-IVB safe now. Stand by.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Carr
text: You've got a go orbit. You're looking good. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That's CapCom Jerry Carr talking to Pete Conrad. The backup crew commander Dave Scott is also at the CapCom console here.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, be advised that I am resetting on the stabilization and control system logic bus A 3 dash 4 Baker, which was out, for some reason.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. We copy. Also on your IMU main A and B breakers, let's leave them out for at least 3 minutes.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. And then what do you want us to do, reset them and then come up with a P51 when we get in the darkness?

speaker: Carr
text: That looks like the right plan, Pete. We are still talking; we'll give you a final on it.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. What do you all figure? - I think we got hit by lightning. [Pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. We are about 45 seconds from LOS; we'll pick you up Canaries about 16.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Roger. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. Can you go to P00?

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: P51 is a computer program for orientation

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. We'll go to P00.

speaker: Carr
text: Thank you.

speaker: Conrad
text: We were going into P00 and P00. Now, can we reset the breakers?

speaker: Carr
text: That's affirmative. Go ahead. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: P00 is program zero zero, the idleing position for the computer. We've had loss of signal from the tracking ship Vanguard. We'll pick up Apollo 12 at the Canaries very shortly. We're showing an orbit of 102.5 by 100 nautical miles, a good orbit. Showing weight in orbit 300,253 pounds and an orbital period of 1 hour 28 minutes 14 seconds. Canaries have acquired now.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston through Canaries, How do you read, babe? [Pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston through Canaries. How do you read?

speaker: Conrad
text: I read you loud and clear.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. You are pretty garbled.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. How's that?

speaker: Carr
text: Much better, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Alrighty. I've got a little note for you. I've got a lot of ice on the outside of my number 1 window. I think there was a fair amount of water underneath the BPC that hasn't sublimated yet.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: And we're working on the REG check, and we have the IMU breakers back in, and we're looking at a 000 on the IMU.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. We've looked at your REFSMMAT; it's looking good, Pete. You can press with P51 and 2.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: P52 is the realignment for the inertial platform.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. When you do your P51, you're going to wipe out your REFSMMAT. If you'll go P00 and Accept, we've got 4 minutes left; we'd like to get you a new up-link of your REFSMMAT.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. There's P00 and accept right there.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay, Pete. It's on its way.

speaker: Carr
text: Pete, your P52 should be in Option 1; just a reminder.

speaker: Conrad
text: P52 should be in Option 1. Roger. You're going to give us a - the PAD REFSMMAT back, is that right?

speaker: Carr
text: That's affirmative, Pete. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: REFSMMAT is a reference matrix for the platform. The flight dynamics says the Canary Station confirms a good orbit with its tracking.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. The load's coming up now.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We're standing by. There's a helmet over here. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, I may have screwed you up there. I hit the Reset button.

speaker: Carr
text: No, it's okay, Pete. We're still going.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okey-dokey. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Hey, Houston. The LMP is no longer a rookie, and you can tell SimSup he gave him a heck of a one to break in on. We're still laughing. [Pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. We'll tell him. Pete, we're about due to lose you; LOS here. AOS at Carnarvon will be at 52:15, and we hope to have some word for you by then on what the plan is. [Pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We got a - We'll try and have you a good platform by then.

speaker: Carr
text: Computer's yours, 12.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. The computer's yours. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. We'll see you at 52.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. See you at 52, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 24 minutes into the mission. We have had loss of signals at the Canary Island station now. Next station to acquire will be Carnarvon. Tananarive station is no longer in the network. Carnarvon is due to acquire at 52:15 seconds. During this launch, Apollo 12 lost its electrical distribution system, that's AC Bus 1 and 2, - speculated due to lightning. We don't have a reason - a definite reason, however, right now. That loss - loss of that threw the fuel cells off the line and this system also powers the inertial measuring unit, the platform. That was lost. We still had the backup guidance system, the stablization control system, which is powered by batteries and not by the fuel cells. The electrical distribution system is now back in operation. The fuel cells are back on the line and on the dark side of this orbit the crew will realign the platform, using the sextant to take star measurement and get the platform back in the proper shape as a reference point.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 26 minutes, 31 seconds. We have a voice operated relay recording of the lift-off air to ground. It will not be in real time, but we will play that for you now.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 33 minutes, 59 seconds. That's the end of the tape on the liftoff. We'll stand by now on this line for remarks from President Nixon, who is in the firing room at the Kennedy Space Center [garble].

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Launch Control. We're here in firing room 2. The President of the United States and Mrs. Nixon have arrived in the firing room. The President has come right down the middle line, basically right in the middle of firing room 2 mostly at the consoles where the first and second stage personnel are located. The President is walking slowly across the main isle of the firing room shaking hands with all the console operators as he comes by. He has now covered the course of firing room 2. As expected shortly, he'll come up to the rear of the firing room where a microphone is waiting. Accompanying the President and Mrs. Nixon is the Administrator of NASA Thomas Paine. Miss Julie Nixon is in the firing room watching from an observation area to the rear. The President now coming up the steps going to the rear of the firing room. We expect he will be back up on the back row here shortly. We have most of the pilots for the Apollo 13 and 14 missions here. The commanders of those two flights, the Apollo 13 Astronaut Jim Lovell, and Apollo 14 Astronaut Alan Shepard are here in the firing room. The President now coming back up to the rear on management row with Dr. Paine. We expect shortly he will be coming up to the mike. We'll stand by here in the control center. The President is now up on the back row and meeting some of the project officials here. This is Launch Control.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Mission Control, Houston at 51 minutes, 5 seconds. We're just about to acquire at Garnarvon. Acquisition there at 52 minutes, 15 seconds. We'll stand by for conversation through that site. And data is coming through on Apollo 12 from Carnarvon now. No voice contact yet, but we are getting telemetry data Jerry Carr getting ready to put in a call now.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Houston. Do you read Apollo 12 through Carnarvon?

speaker: Carr
text: Hello, Stormy. We're reading you loud and clear.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Read you the same. We just finished a P51 with a four balls 1 star angle difference. Dick just did a P52 on stars 14 and 15 with another star angle difference of 1. The torquing angles were plus 00755, plus 00941, minus 00366; the time 52 plus 29; and things are back to normal.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. We copy your data. Your torquing angles : plus 00755, plus 00941, minus 00366 at 52:29.

speaker: Conrad
text: That's affirmative. And we're getting on with our TLI checks.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. Would you turn your tape recorder off and set your bit rate at High. We don't have a command - computer at Carnarvon. So you'll have to do it for us.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We just got a Program Alarm 20430, whatever that is?

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. We'll check it out. 12, Houston. Can you give us a Verb 96, Enter, to stop your integration? And we'd like you to do an E-MOD dump. Give us a 3, 2, 1, Mark when you do your Verb 74; and if we get it done now, we should have an answer for you on your Erasable Memory by the time you get to Guaymas.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Verb 74 coming at you. 1...

speaker: Carr
text: Do a Verb 96 first. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. Your Program Alarm was an integration problem.

speaker: Conrad
text: I saw some illumination out the window; I'd almost be positive that we got hit by lightning some place.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. I don't think we got all of that transmission.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. I'm just saying - in thinking back to when we had our big glitch, I remember seeing it get light outside the window. We were in the clouds; I'm pretty sure we got hit by lightning.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Copy. Pete, here's our plan. When you finish your E-Mod dump, then we want to get you up on Honeysuckle - and make sure, by the way, that you get your S-band volume up for Honeysuckle - We want to up-link you a state vector at Honeysuckle, and then the next dark pass, we want you to do a P52 Option 3.Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We'll do a P52 Option 3 on the next dark pass, and that'll give you a drift check. Is that right?

speaker: Carr
text: That's affirmative, Pete. All the memory we can see so far looks okay, and we should have a real verdict for you at Guaymas after this E-MOD dump.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. [Pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: We're going to be passing you up some data later on in your checklist, little pieces that you can take out and go through in order to exercise some of your electrical system to give us a chance to see how it all looks.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Of course, we - we're on the time line, and we've exercised fuel cell purges and things like that, and all that seems to be functioning okay.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay, Pete. It looks down here like the reason for your IMU problem was strictly a power supply problem.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes. We understand that. The voltage on the main buses went down to 24 volts.

speaker: Carr
text: Yes.

speaker: Conrad
text: And when we got the fuel cells back on the line, then - all three fuel cells just flat fell off the line.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Pete. We're going to lose you here in about 30 seconds; we'll pick you up on Honeysuckle, S-band only, at 59:33.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We got the - we got the S-band up for Honeysuckle and - I was wrong. We're completing the fuel cell purges at this time; you can see some Master Alarms.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. We got your E-Mod dump.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger.

speaker: Carr
text: Pete, when you hit Honeysuckle, give us P00 and Accept.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 58 minutes, Carnarvon has had LOS. The Honeysuckle Station in Australia will acquire within a couple of minutes. During the Carnarvon pass, Apollo 12 did dump their Erasable Memory in the computer to the ground; it will be checked here and verified, and we should know by the time Apollo 12 is in acquisition at the Guaymas, Mexico station whether that computer memory is good or not. Over Honeysuckle we will pass them up a new state vector: their position and velocity. We should be picking up at Honeysuckle within a few seconds now. We'll continue to stand by.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: The Honeysuckle has acquired Apollo12.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston through Honeysuckle. How do you read?

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Houston. Read you loud and clear on the S-band. The computer is P00 and Accept, and I see another Program Alarm. I guess it went back into P00 again.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: He just gave it a Verb 96; let me look at the alarm. Yes, it's 20430 again. I just - you're - in P00 and Accept right now, and you can go ahead and take it.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. We got it.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. I had just recalled P00, and I started integration again. My fault.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. After we get the state vector up, we'll give you your 66 and your 45. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger-Roger. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. Go.

speaker: Conrad
text: We had a normal Docking-Probe Extension.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. We're about 20 seconds from LOS on Honeysuckle. You're going to have to put your bit rate back down to Low and tape recorder to Forward, and we'll be picking you up on Guaymas at 01:20, correction 01:28:21.

speaker: Conrad
text: 01:28:21. Roger-Roger. And is the computer mine?

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. The computer is yours.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 1 hour, 5 minutes into the mission. Apollo 12 has moved out of range of the Honeysuckle station now, passing out over the Pacific Ocean. Next station to acquire will be Guaymas, Mexico at an elapsed time of 1 hour, 28 minutes, 21 seconds. Here in the Mission Control Center flight controllers are planning extra checks of the Electrical system on Apollo 12. We'll be conducting those over the United States to make sure there has been no damage to the electrical system. We have also examining the erasable memory of the computer. Should have word on that for the crew by the time they get to the States. The Apollo 12 orbit changing slightly now as the third stage of the booster, the S-IVB, vents and as the auxiliary propulsion system of that stage provides attitude control. Showing an orbit now of 106 by 102 nautical miles, an orbital period of 1 hour, 28 minutes, 22 seconds, and our weight in orbit is down to 298,999 pounds. At 1 hour, 7 minutes, this is Mission Control Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 1 hour 10 minutes. We have the crew's heart rates now from Dr. Charles Berry. At lift-off all three crewmen had heart rates of 120. Prior to liftoff they had been running between 80 and 90. Peak heart rates during the powered phase of the flight occurred during that high period of activity and ran between 130 and 140 for all three crewmen. This is Mission Control Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 1 hour, 27 minutes. We're about 30 seconds away from acquisition at the Guaymas, Mexico station. Preliminary review of data indicates that problem occurred about 45 seconds after lift-off. Two of the Apollo 11 astronauts were in the Mission Control Center viewing room during lift-off, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin. We'll stand by now. We have data on the booster coming in from Guaymas. We'll stand by for a call.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. How do you read?

speaker: Conrad
text: Loud and clear. How me?

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Read you loud and clear. We've got a few words for you if you'll stand by for a minute.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. I imagine you have. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Are you guys going to be ready for the Service Module RCS hot fire down there, Houston?

speaker: Carr
text: We sure will, Pete. We've got some words for you now. Your E-Mod dump is still in work. We'll have some answers for you shortly on that. Got a couple of tests we'd like you to run while you're here over the States. Are you ready to copy? [Pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. Are you ready to copy?

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes. We're ready to copy. Fire away.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. First thing we'd like to have you do, Pete, is a CMC self-check. Go into your operations checklist at page Foxtrot 2-2 and run that little dude, which is a four-stepper, and on step number 3, do a Verb 21 Noun 27 Enter, and then do a 10 Enter rather than a 4 or a 5 Enter. Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: A CMC self-check on page F-20 - 2-2; step 3, Verb 21, Noun 27, and do a 10 Enter.

speaker: Carr
text: That's affirmative, Pete, and when you finish that one, then we thought we ought to take a look at MTVC check. And your best bet for that is to follow your checklist, page Foxtrot 5-3, and begin where it says TVC check and Prep.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We just decided that was a good idea ourselves.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. And then go through that until you get to page 5-4 and terminate your test at Rot Control Power Norm, two, AC/DC. Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Copy.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. And then, to turn your motors off and clean it up, you want to skip to Foxtrot 5-6; and, on step number 18 there, go down to gimbal motors, four, Off, and finish off the checklist there.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We copied that, and it's all in work right now. While they're getting those books out and getting ready to do that, let me give you the Service Module RCS hot fire; and just - let me ask you a question, Jerry. The Service Module thrusters wouldn't show up with water and, even if they did, it would be long gone; and I've still got a big block of ice sitting outside my window here, so I hope they all fire right.

speaker: Carr
text: So do we, Pete.

speaker: Carr
text: Pete, I also have a TLI plus 90 maneuver PAD. Whenever you're ready to copy, give me a holler. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston.? [Pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Houston, you ready for the fire down there?

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, 12. Also, your Verb 96 flag is still set. If you will re-select P00, we can reset that dude.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We're coming at you with the hot fire.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Standing by. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: I don't think they're firing, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Apollo 12, Houston. We saw all the events on telemetry. Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: You say they're firing? We didn't hear a thing.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Apollo 12, Houston. Affirmative. We saw the events go; but, of course, we didn't hear anything either.

speaker: Conrad
text: Are you telling me they fired?

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Apollo 12, Houston. Best try it again, Pete. We have no telemetry on your TCP's. All we have is the electrical indication. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. That worked out pretty good.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Apollo 12, Houston. Roger. We saw your manifold pressures change a little bit, so it does look like they fired. Also, Neil's here, and he says he didn't hear his go on Min Impulse either.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. But we can see them firing. We're getting some flashes now.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. [Pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Apollo 12, Houston. Are you ready for the TLI plus 90 PAD?

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Ready to copy. Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. TLI plus 90 PAD follows. SPS/G&N: Noun 47 is 63573; Noun 48, minus 1.55, plus 1.29; Noun 33, 004:16:35.77; Noun 81, minus 0438.1, plus 0000.1, plus 5046.7. Roll, Pitch, and Yaw is 179, 182, 359. Noun 44 is NA. The Delta-V T : 5065.6, 6:16, 5043.9. Sextant: 12, 078.2, 24.1; Boresight, 021; up, 09.1; right, 3.3. Noun 61, plus 03.50, minus 027.81. EMS, 1142.4, 34409. GET of 0.05g is 016:46:09. The ullage is none - negative. You are undocked. P37 for lift-off plus 8. GET is 008:00, 6243, plus 166, 025.43. Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, we're doing a self-check on the CMC, and we'll soon complete that; and our 2 is 4, our 3 is 2. Can we terminate that Noun? Do you need a Noun 8? [Pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, 12. Over.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, 12. Houston. Stand by on that a sec.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. And while you're at it, I would to like to bring on the SECS logics for you to get a Go for Pyro Arm, please, sir.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. You're Go.

speaker: Conrad
text: And SECS logics 1 and 2 are up and on.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. And you don't need a Noun 8; just terminate Verb 27, Noun - correction, Verb 21, Noun 27 Enter, Zero Enter.

speaker: Bean
text: Are you ready for a read-back, Houston?

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. We sent you a wrong one on the P37 for lift-off plus 8. Your longitude should be minus 166 rather than plus. [Pause.]

speaker: Bean
text: Roger. Copied minus 166 on the longitude.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, 12. And if you'll give us P00 and Accept, we'll run your state vector up.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. You got it, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.?

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That was Al Bean with that read-back.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, this is 12. We're going to run through this gimbal check if you want to look at it right now.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: And that's Dick Gordon.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. Let us get the state vector in first.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. You want us to wait for you?

speaker: Conrad
text: All right, we'll hold it, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay, thanks. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. You can run that TVC check. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. Did you read my last?

speaker: Conrad
text: No. What was that?

speaker: Carr
text: You're go on the MTVC check.

speaker: Conrad
text: We're in process right now.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay.

speaker: Conrad
text: Here come your gimbal motors, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Apollo 12 now checking the thrust vector control, the system for steering during engine burns. They have also done a self check on the Command Module computer, and have hot fired the service module reaction control systems.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: The erasable memory in the Command Module computer has been verified and it is good.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: The TLI plus 90 minutes pad ...

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. The computer's yours.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. We've checked your E-Mod; it's go.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. The gimbal motor check looked pretty good; we're coming back to AC/DC, and going over to step 18 on F5-6.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. I've got your TLI PAD, if you're ready to copy.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hey, just - let's - let us get the gimbal motors off. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. The bus ties are off, Houston, and we are ready to copy the TLI PAD.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. We're about 2 minutes from LOS, so I'm going to copy - or read up the TLI PAD, and you can read it back when we get to AOS at Canaries. TLI PAD follows. Timebase 6, 2:37:43; TLI, 179, 059, 001; burn time, 5:44, 10515.4, 35420; separation attitude, 356, 092, 332; extraction, 300, 272, 028. Over. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. Your read-back's correct. You're about 1 minute from LOS, and you're go for Pyro Arm.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Understand. Go for Pyro Arm, and we're waiting for those golden words Go for TLI.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. We'll give them to you at Carnarvon. You can expect to pick up the Canaries at 01:50:11.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 1 hour, 49 minutes. Vanguard has had loss of signal. Canary will acquire within a minute or so. The TLI plus 90 pad that was passed up a short while ago is abort information should an abort of this mission become necessary after the Translunar Injection burn. We've also passed up the information for the Translunar Injection burn. The second burn of the S-IVB, the third stage of the booster, ignition time 2 hours, 37 minutes, 43 seconds. Duration of the burn 5 minutes, 44 seconds and a Delta V or added velocity of 1,515 feet per second. We've had acquisition at Canary now. We'll continue to standby.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston through Canaries. how do you read?

speaker: Conrad
text: Loud and clear.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Your PIPA Bias and IRIG drift down here look real good based on the data that we have right now. Also, the - your theory and your idea that it was probably lightning that did it, that looks like about the best - best theory right now. With that in mind, the sequence of events is real explainable. We've got a pretty good idea why it happened. Everything is looking good here, and we see no reason why you can't just press.

speaker: Conrad
text: We concur. I guess the other thing that we were thinking about, maybe not lightning so much, as just unstable air. We were a pretty big piece of static electricity 'buildering-upper' going through there. We might have just discharged ourselves.

speaker: Carr
text: Pete, that - that's exactly the theory that people are thinking here.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes. We sort of glowed all over there when all the lights came on, I think. I just - I'm still trying to search my memory because, of course, when all the lights came on I kept my attention in the cockpit.

speaker: Carr
text: Pete, Dave wants to know why you're not watching what's going on outside.

speaker: Conrad
text: I - I had a pair of eyeballs that were moving pretty fast about then, in and out.

speaker: Carr
text: You had your scan in high bit rate, huh?

speaker: Conrad
text: You better believe it.

speaker: Gordon
text: Jerry, you could have come over and said that booster was right down the pike a little faster, boy.

speaker: Carr

text: TVC Servo Power, two of them, Off.

speaker: Gordon
text: Off.

speaker: Conrad
text: EMS Mode to Standby.

speaker: Gordon
text: Standby.

speaker: Conrad
text: Tape Recorder, Off.

speaker: Gordon
text: Tape Recorder's Off.

speaker: Conrad
text: PCM Bit Rate, Low.

speaker: Gordon
text: Low, okay.

speaker: Conrad
text: Now, Verb 49.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. We're copying television now and soon as you've finished with your ejection and you're clear, we'll go ahead and enable the S-IVB evasive maneuver. [Long Pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: We do have the lines back up and we are getting a picture now.

speaker: Gordon
text: Can you see those flashes, Houston? that's the RCS thrusters reflecting off the quads on the LM.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: We're getting a black and white picture but we have not yet gotten color conversion.

speaker: Carr
text: Haven't seen any flashes yet, 12.

speaker: Gordon
text: They may be a little dim for you to see. [Pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Oh, there's the S-IVB, and I can see it venting.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, 12. When you're well clear and you're ready for us, let us know and we'll start the maneuver to the evasive attitude.

speaker: Conrad
text: Boy, is that thing venting. What's it keep venting, anyhow, Houston? Keeps throwing out big clouds of...

speaker: Carr
text: We're not...

speaker: Conrad
text: ...of something.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. We're not supposed to be venting anything.

speaker: Conrad
text: Boy, it's throwing stuff off the sides and out the back like crazy.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Can you get us a picture?

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, we'll get you some on the TV if we can; it just looks like it's venting something out of the rear end - big radial clouds of it coming out the back.

speaker: Carr
text: That's really something. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: As a matter of fact, Houston, I suspect that maybe you ought to enable that maneuver right now. It sure...

speaker: Carr
text: We'll do it, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: ...it sure is throwing a lot of stuff out of the back of it; I ain't got any idea what it is, but it sure is throwing it out of there.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Maneuver's initiated, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. I can see it firing thrusters, and I can see it starting to yaw. [Long pause.]

speaker: Bean
text: Try to get it out of the center hatch window now, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. Give us Omni Delta, please.

speaker: Carr
text: We're copying your TV real clear now, and the jerking has stopped. It's looking good. [Long pause.]

speaker: Bean
text: Earth is about one and a half times the size of a basketball right now.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston. 12. Let us know when that maneuver is over, please.

speaker: Carr
text: Wilco.

speaker: Gordon
text: Say again, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: We'll let you know when that maneuver's complete. Al, how big's that - how far away is that basketball.

speaker: Bean
text: You probably got a better idea than I do about that one.

speaker: Conrad
text: Could you see that thing throwing stuff out the back, Houston?

speaker: Carr
text: We could awhile ago, and it looks like it's got a halo around it now. Is it still there?

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, that's the Sun shining in the front end. But from the angle that we have on it, there's something venting out the - The aft engines are on either side and the upper aft engine, the engine that's away from the Earth...

speaker: SC
text: [Garble.]

speaker: Conrad
text: No, I'm not talking about that; I'm trying to reference it to whatever it is that's venting back there; it's a line; see that line coming out of the engine, over on the left-hand side?

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. We got a hunch that what happened is, when that Lox valve failed open and we tried to close it ourselves, it probably burned out that burner.

speaker: Carr
text: Maneuver's complete, 12.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay and when are you going to brake the APS? Oh, hey, it just vented something tremendously; can you see that, Houston?

speaker: Carr
text: Yes. We can see it now, Pete. Okay, try it again.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, are you going to make that maneuver on time at 11:40? [Pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. We're looking at 426 plus 18 for that burn.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. 426 plus 18. And Houston, that's, I assume, is 11:40 after our Sep; is that correct? [Pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: We're checking, 12. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, we're changing the scenery on you; we'll come back to that S-IVB just before it goes.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, 12. And that maneuver will be done at 13 minutes past Sep.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. I've got 09:52 right now.

speaker: Gordon
text: How does the homeland look to you?

speaker: Carr
text: Beginning to look kind of small.

speaker: Conrad
text: It's really weird, Houston. There's something that's venting radially. And then there's something that's venting along the axial axis, and it's sort of taking turns. And right now, it reminds me of some guy standing back there with a water hose just spraying it in any old direction; it's just - it keeps venting, whatever it is, and it just keeps blowing away in different directions.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: I'm trying to get all this on film for you.

speaker: Carr
text: Good deal. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. On your event timer; that maneuver will be 12:48.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, understand, 12:48.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston, we're going back to the S-IVB now for the burn.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, 12.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Distance is 14,252 nautical miles [26,395 km] from Earth. Velocity, 15,552 feet per second [4,740 m/s].

speaker: Carr
text: We've got the S-IV now, 12.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. Are you starting the maneu - starting the Sep maneuver?

speaker: Carr
text: That's affirmative. We're ready now.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, we're ready. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Ullage motors are on. [Pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes, we can see it starting to move now, Houston. Hear the motors firing?

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. When you get a chance, turn off your O 2 fans.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. They're coming off. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. The APS maneuver is complete.

speaker: Gordon
text: How much you figure you got out of that, Houston?

speaker: Carr
text: About 10 feet per second, Dick.

speaker: Gordon
text: That's pre-planned, did you really get that? [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. The burn was nominal. If the vehicle is a shade lighter, we might have gotten just a little bit more Delta-V out of it.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. Well, that thing did a fantastic job for us today.

speaker: Carr
text: Sure did. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: The sunlight is starting to come in the window and we're a little concerned about the TV, so I guess you've seen the show for today on the S-IVB and we'll look at the Earth for a little bit for you.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Dick, and we'd sure like to see what you guys look like.

speaker: Gordon
text: Well, we look just like we did this morning when we got out of bed.

speaker: Conrad
text: Now, there's a real reasonable guy for you.

speaker: Gordon
text: [Garble] we'll be glad to show you, and give me an attitude to go to; I'm not going to track that S-IVB any more.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, 12. Good attitude is Roll 58, Pitch 240, Yaw 39.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. The reason I'll leave that S-IVB, it's starting to get in line with the Sun and I can still have it but it's a little tough.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Dick. This attitude we just fired to you is your P52 attitude for 05 plus 30. And the stars that you can use at this attitude are number 12, Rigel; number 16, Procyon. And the reason why we had this one in our hip pocket is that this is the same attitude that you can use for the sextant calibration after you've realigned your platform.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. Give it to me again, 58 - Would you?

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. 58, 240, and 39.

speaker: Conrad
text: And we've just turned off our TV; we've maneuvered where we no longer have the Earth or the S-IVB.

speaker: Gordon
text: Now, that was 390 in yaw, is that right, 039?

speaker: Carr
text: That's 39 - 039 in yaw.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Carr
text: This will save you one maneuver down the pike a ways. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. Give us Omni Alfa. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. If you can give us an interior shot, I'd like to have a rough idea of when you can do it; and if you can't do it, we'll go ahead and release our TV lines.

speaker: Conrad
text: It's coming to you right now; you should have something there.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. Great, Dick.

speaker: Conrad
text: There's Dick Gordon with his sunglasses on. Boy oh boy. I'll tell you, these guys weren't kidding when they said this thing shakes, rattles, and rolls when you fire the thrusters; it's like being on a jerky train.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, we're at 58 degrees in roll, 240 pitch, and 39 degrees in yaw.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, 12. We're not getting your TV.

speaker: Carr
text: We got a good picture here on our monitor.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. On the high gain, give us pitch minus 50 and yaw plus 60 and that should lock us up. Okay, we got your TV. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Picture coming in.

speaker: Carr
text: Dr. Gordon, I presume.

speaker: Conrad
text: Better known to his friends as Shicky Dicky.

speaker: Carr
text: Hey, Red Baron, where's your scarf?

speaker: Gordon
text: Well, I tell you. I think I forgot it during that boost phase. We ought to talk to you about all that good happening. That's a terrible way to break Al Bean into space flight, I'll tell you,

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Say, what time is the Lox blowdown on the S-IVB?

speaker: Carr
text: Stand by, 12. 12, Houston. Cris says he doesn't think you guys are the same age as when you got up this morning either.

speaker: Gordon
text: He is absolutely correct. In fact, I wish you guys would play us that DSE tape back tonight. All Al Bean kept saying was there's power on the buses, there's power on the buses, and every light brightly inside was lit. And I kept thinking, why is he saying that to me?

speaker: Carr
text: That's beautiful.

speaker: Gordon
text: I was saying, Al, there's so many lights on, I can't read them all to you. He's totally recovered from launch, see that?

speaker: Carr
text: Oh, it looks beautiful. That's a nice-looking hat you're wearing, Al.

speaker: Bean
text: We have three of them just alike in here. We got something else for you too.

speaker: Conrad
text: I tell you, this Command Module's a good deal. Dick and I, being use to the Gemini, just hand everything to Al and say hold it. And he's got 25 things in his hands.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Gordon
text: I'm sorry I couldn't follow that S-IVB anymore, but it was really getting into the Sun, and I guess we aren't going to see much of it anyway, any more.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Dick. We'd like to have you guys start a Battery charge now.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. We are going to secure the TV too in just a minute now [garble.]

speaker: Bean
text: I think we're on Battery B in the flight plan, huh?

speaker: Carr
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, we're going to stow the TV, and we'll come back at you later with something.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. We've lost the TV now.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. We just - shut it down. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. Slingshot burn time is 4 plus 48 and it's in attitude.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, 4 plus 48. Well - have you got some gimbal angles for us - that are - well, let me ask you. Is it going to be in our window in the attitude we're in now or not?

speaker: Carr
text: I kind of doubt it, Pete; do you want to watch it go?

speaker: Conrad
text: No, no, we'll just stay put. We're getting hungry, and I think we're going to start getting out of these suits and eat in a little bit here.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hey, Jerry, I'm still not too happy with the way this mission event timer is performing even though we do have the tuning fork intermittently in the window.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Dick.

speaker: Gordon
text: I guess we'll just have to keep an eye on it. Right now, it seems to be performing okay, but we'll watch it. I'm not so sure that that doesn't get a glitch in it every now and then.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay, Dick. And if you are going to lean a lot more heavily on your event timer, you might give us time hacks every once in a while when you're using it, and we'll set ours up and follow you down here and try to keep giving you the right kind of times.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Looks like the mission event timer in the LEB is keeping good time. Now, let me ask you - it also - if it was central timing problem, it would also show up with the pitch fork, right?

speaker: Carr
text: That's affirmative.?

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We've never seen a pitch fork in the LEB timer, and it stayed right in Sync all the way along, so we just periodically call it 1665 and update the - the Mission Timer. What happened is, when a pitch fork comes on, it begins to gain time on us; it keeps getting 5 or 6 seconds ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: The LEB is the lower equipment bay. The mission timer - event timer in that area is working all right - the event timer on the main display panel is not.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: The S-IVB sling shot maneuver was scheduled for 4 hours, 48 minutes Elapsed Time. The present Elapsed Time is 4 hours, 39 minutes. During this maneuver, the remaining liquid oxygen in the propellant tanks of the S-IVB is dumped. Though the engine bell does provide small amount of energy, it will cause the S-IVB to go around the trailing edge of the Moon and then into a solar orbit. This maneuver ensures that the S-IVB does not impact on the Moon or have re-contact with the Apollo 12 spacecraft.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Apollo 12's distance now at 4 hours, 40 minutes is 16,273 nautical miles [30,138 km]. Velocity, 14,664 feet per second [4,470 m/s]. Total vehicle weight now, 97,157 pounds [44,070 kg].

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, Houston. We've started Bat B charge.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, 12. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: EECOM, the flight controller monitoring the electrical system, reports that the battery charge does look good. Astronaut Buzz Aldrin has joined Jerry Carr and Dave Scott at the CapCom console. We're about 30 seconds away from the liquid oxygen dump on the S-IVB.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. We've initiated the LOX dump. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. We'll look for her to go by.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead, Jerry.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Dick. We've been kind of thinking here a little bit, and we'd like for you to consider a proposal here. It's the idea of getting into the LM tonight before bedtime and going through the housekeeping portion of your checklist, short of the communications, and powering up the CMC and giving us a check and an E-Mod dump.

speaker: Gordon
text: Yes, that sounds like a good idea. We've been up here talking about what that launch may have done to the LM, and I think we can do that between the two P23's. What do you think of that?

speaker: Carr
text: We're not going to do MCC 1, Dick. It looks like you won't need it, so you can do that during that time when you would normally be doing MCC 1.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. It sounds good. We really don't have any place to, go tonight, so we don't mind working late.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. It looks like about 11 hours, and we'll work up a good solid plan for you and come up with it later

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay and if that was a proposal, you'd better watch the use of that language. We won't accept those sort of things.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Should I have said this was a proposition for you?

speaker: Gordon
text: No, you said proposal, sir.

speaker: Bean
text: Say, Houston, 12.

speaker: Carr
text: Go ahead, 12.

speaker: Bean
text: I snickered at those ham sandwiches this morning, but I take it all back. They're delicious.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Bean
text: Our compliments to the chef.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. He'll be glad to hear that. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Did you break out the jelly beans yet?

speaker: Conrad
text: No, we're still reminiscing about that launch. We was wondering why we were supposed to try SCE to Aux. We haven't figured that one out yet.

speaker: Carr
text: Well, the reason why is because we lost all of our telemetry.

speaker: Conrad
text: Lost all your what?

speaker: Carr
text: Telemetry.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. When you went under voltage there, you lost the SCE, and we had to go Aux in order to see what happened.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: SCE is the signal conditioning equipment. At 5 hours, 1 minute; Apollo 12 is 16,827 nautical miles [31,164 km] from Earth. Velocity, 13,706 nautical miles [means feet per second, 4,178 m/s]. And the crew is having its meal. Eating some ham sandwiches. We'll take this release circuit down now for a while and come back up if there's further air-ground. This is Mission Control, Houston; 5 hours, 1 minute.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Houston, 12.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Can you explain what is going on with our Comm? We just lost you there. We had a little trouble.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. We just handed it over Goldstone to Ascension.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Now I understand. What did you say about the SCE to Aux this morning on that launch?

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. The reason - what happened here is we lost that dude when we went low on that Bus, so we had to have you go to Aux in order to pick it up again. [Pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. The words are - almost all of your electrical parameters come down on that SCE, and so when you go low on the Bus like that and dump it, about the only thing we can do is go to Aux and try to pick it up again.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. I understand. Thank you, Jerry.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 5 hours and 7 minutes. We're back live now with air/ground. Apollo 12 is 19,645 nautical miles [36,383 km] from Earth. Velocity, 13,443 feet per second [4,097 m/s].

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control. The word 'Aux' that you've heard in the last few transmissions is A-U-X, stands for Auxiliary.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. If you'll give us P00 and Accept, we'll fire up some - a new REFSMMAT, a zero trunnion bias, and a CMC clock update. Over.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. It's all yours.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 5 hours, 23 minutes. Apollo 12's distance from Earth is 21,475 nautical miles [39,772 km]. Velocity, 12,883 feet per second [3,927 m/s].

speaker: Gordon
text: Hey, Houston, 12.

speaker: Carr
text: Go ahead, 12.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. Doing the P23 at 6 hours. You gave me this attitude after we left that S-IVB, but the Flight Plan has star 15 for the optics cal, 204, 262, 0. Are you going to change that?

speaker: Carr
text: Dick, you'll have a new REFSMMAT at that time, and your inertial attitude ought to be - be that now. Once you put in your new REFSMMAT, you ought to be in good shape.

speaker: Gordon
text: Oh, very good, very good. I understand. I was just behind you, I guess.

speaker: Carr
text: That's the maneuver we were trying to save you.

speaker: Gordon
text: Thank you.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. The computer is yours.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Carr
text: And if you can find the time in your busy social schedule, I got a P37 PAD for you.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, just stand by. We'll find the book.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay, this an LO plus 15, lift-off plus 15.

speaker: Bean
text: Go ahead with that P37, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, 12. This is just a four liner. Lift-off plus 15, GET is 015:00, 4714, minus 168, 050:06. Over.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Al.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That was information that would be needed by the crew for an abort at 15 hours after lift-off.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Jer.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. What do you say we break the simulation down and debrief it now, and the backup crew's ready to get in.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes, I imagine they are ready to get in now. [Pause.] You can tell SimSup that's a new one to work on.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Bean
text: It's a good thing we've never seen it before because we sure didn't know what to do about it.

speaker: Carr
text: Oh, you did pretty good.

speaker: Bean
text: That's right, absolutely nothing.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: SimSup is the simulation supervisor.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Carr
text: Go ahead, 12.

speaker: Gordon
text: Rog. You do have the PTC REFSMMAT in now. Is that correct?

speaker: Carr
text: That's affirmative. On that last one, Dick, we sent you a PTC REFSMMAT, a zero trunnion bias, and a CMC clock update.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hey, Houston, this is 12.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger, Jerry. The reason I'm having trouble with this alignment - first star was Canopus. I got that okay in the sextant. The second star in Picapar is Procyon, and I don't have anything in the sextant.

speaker: Carr
text: Right. Stand by, Dick.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Astronaut Ed Gibson is the CapCom now.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, CDR. How do you read?

speaker: Gibson
text: We read you loud and clear, 12. Go ahead.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. No, this is CDR. I'm on the lightweight headset now. Just checking.

speaker: Bean
text: He just couldn't see it.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Gibson
text: We're observing a weak signal down here. We'd like you to go ahead and track - check the position of the track mode switch and also the beam width.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. We've been operating on Omni's. Do you want us to go to high gain now?

speaker: Gibson
text: That is negative, 12.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. We are presently in Omni A.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: At 5 hours, 50 minutes Elapsed Time, Apollo 12's distance from Earth is 24,561 nautical miles [45,487 km], velocity is 12,062 feet per second [3,676 m/s].

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Gibson
text: We recommend that you use star 12 or star 15 for your second star.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, are you looking at the DSKY?

speaker: Gibson
text: Affirmative, 12.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, you are looking at the torquing angles?

speaker: Gibson
text: We have them, 12.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Torquing at this time.

speaker: Conrad
text: Mark.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hello, Houston, 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, go ahead.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. How does the Flight Plan look for this first set of P23s? Okay?

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by, Dick.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, go ahead. There are no changes so far.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. We are going to do the Verb - first maneuver Verb 49 to get the boresight star.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 5 hours, 58 minutes. We are having a shift change in the Mission Control Center at this time. We are estimating the Change of Shift News Conference to begin in approximately 15 minute. Change of Shift News Conference in approximately 15 minutes.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 6 hours, 8 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. In Mission Control Center, Houston, we have just completed a hand-over, change of shift. At this time, Flight Director Pete Frank and his Orange Team of flight controllers now aboard. As we sit here surveying the room, the Apollo 12 spacecraft, the Command Module Yankee Clipper , the Lunar Module Intrepid , currently 26,534 nautical miles [49,141 km] above the Earth. We now read a velocity of 11,602 feet per second [3,536 m/s]. Spacecraft weight at this time, 97,157 pounds [44,070 kg]. The atmosphere of the control center somewhat quieter than perhaps it was earlier in the day. Flight Director Pete Frank at this time talking specifically to his EECOM who has just come aboard. And as was recorded earlier, Ed Gibson has replaced Jerry Carr in our CapCom position. No conversation from the spacecraft for the past few minutes but we'll standby and continue to monitor. At 6 hours and 9 minutes into the flight; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 6 hours, 13 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. The Apollo 12 spacecraft's altitude at this time, 27,043.8 nautical miles [50,085.1 km] above the Earth. Current velocity now reading 11,485 feet per second [3,501 m/s]. We understand the Change of Shift News Conference will start momentarily in the News Center, therefore we will take down the release line from Mission Control for the duration of that conference. At 6 hours, 14 minutes into the flight; this is Apollo Control, Houston signing off for now.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, go ahead.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. Are you copying this P23 data?

speaker: Gibson
text: That's affirmative, Dick.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. I was just wondering. You haven't been hollering at me, yet.

speaker: Gibson
text: It's looking good.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, we've been thinking about the LM check-out procedures. We'd like your thoughts on whether you want to go in there as soon as you finish up with the P23.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We can do that. We could get into PTC and then go on in there. What do you got in mind?

speaker: Conrad
text: I guess what I'm asking is what do you people think may have happened? Do you think we might have blown some breakers out or something?

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, that's affirmative. We'd like to go ahead and check the position of several breakers just to make sure that we are getting the heaters coming off and on on all of the systems as we should be.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. If you think that's a good idea, and we'll get ready to do that now. I think, what we'd like to do here is - Al is - I've gotten all the way out of my suit, but I still have to stow it. Al is working his way out of his right now while Dick's doing the P23, so we want to get Dick unsuited. We want to get everybody cleaned up here and get this spacecraft stowed. And then we'd like to go in the LM, I think; we've got plenty of time. Do you agree with that?

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, that's affirmative. It sounds good. We would like to get into the LM before 8 hours GET.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Well, we'll give her a go. What's your reason for wanting to get in so quick?

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Old curious Pete. You got to give me a reason. [Pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go.

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, one of the reasons we want to get in there early is there is a possibility that the ASA heater is not cycling the way it should be. In which case, 8 hours is the limit, and we ought to get a look at it before that time.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston. Standing by.

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, I repeat. The reason we'd like to get in there before 8 hours GET is that the ASA heater may not be cycling, and the thermal limit then is about 8 hours, so we'd like to get in there before 8 hours and check the position of that circuit breaker to make sure it hasn't pooped and look at the status of the system.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We'll - we'll - we - we'll - we'll hustle.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay, and Pete, we also have the LM check-out procedure that you'll be following for the - going through the activation checklist, and we're ready to read that up to you any time.

speaker: SC
text: [Garble.]

speaker: Conrad
text: You're going to have to hold it for a minute, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hey, Houston. This is 12, and I'd like to continue this last set of 23's without doing another trunnion bias. Just a half hour, right now.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Dick.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 6 hours 37 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. The Apollo 12 spacecraft at the present time has a velocity reading of 10,980 feet per second [3,347 m/s]. We currently register now an altitude of 29,549 nautical miles [54,725 km]...

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. We are done with the P23's - and - I guess we're going to get ready to maneuver to PTC attitude then.

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, repeat after I've finished with the P23. You're breaking up.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, we're getting ready to go into a PTC, or do you want us to hold the attitude we have right now as we go into the LM?

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by on that, Pete. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, if you'll hold your present attitude, we'll get an answer up to you in about 3 or 4 minutes.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We're not going anywhere. [Pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. Would you go over and try Omni Bravo?

speaker: Bean
text: Going to Omni Bravo.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. As you heard in that exchange between CapCom Ed Gibson and Commander Pete Conrad, we are considering having commander Conrad and Alan Bean, the Lunar Module pilot, go into the Lunar Module some time prior to 8 hours Ground Elapsed Time. The ASA or ASA heater referred to there - ASA is an acronym for Abort Sensor Assembly - a part of the Abort Guidance System of the gyros. So this would be the heaters associated with that system. At 6 hours, 43 minutes into the flight; we'll continue to monitor the air-to-ground between capsule communicator Ed Gibson and the Apollo 12 crew. Standing by; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hello, Houston; Apollo 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. Are you going to fix up our state vector?

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by, Dick. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, we'll have one ready for you at about 10 hours.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, you can go ahead and hold off on the PTC and enter the LM with your present attitude. We would like you to first, before you go in, check the Delta-P, LM/CM Delta-P, give us a reading on that and then we have a series of switch and circuit breaker configuration checks, then check the TM and the LGC. We have an abbreviation, or abbreviated procedures taken out of the activation checklist, and we're ready to read that up to you when you're ready to copy.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Did you get our last transmission, and would you give us a call when you're ready to copy the LM check-out steps?

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. You're going to have to give us a few minutes. We're still reconfiguring getting out of suits up here yet.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. Thanks, Dick.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That was Dick Gordon, identifying to Capsule Communicator Ed Gibson that the 12 crew is now getting out of their spacesuits. At the present time we read a velocity of 10,701 feet per second [3,262 m/s], an altitude of 31,013.4 nautical miles [57,436.8 km]. At 6 hours, 52 minutes into the mission of Apollo 12, we will continue to monitor the air-to-ground loop.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. We're ready to copy those instructions you've got about the activities you want us to perform in the LM.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. I only follow. First, before you go in we'd like you to read us down the Delta-P from the LM Command Module, and then the abbreviated procedures to go through on the Activation Checklist are as follows: the activation l, steps l, 2, 3; activation 2, step 2. And activation 3 through activation 9, perform all. On activation 10, steps through 18, activation 11, steps l, 2, 3; activation 12, through step 4. The comm configuration is as follows: PM, Prime, Prime, Off; PCM, Off/Reset, Off, High.

speaker: MS
text: [Garble]...

speaker: Gibson
text: ...on 11, - circuit breaker Panel 11, LGC/DSKY Closed. On activation 27, perform CDR steps 3 through 6; activation 28, through step 7. Then if you'll give us a Verb 74 Enter; take a look at the E-Mod. Verb 37, Enter; 06, Enter; and a Pro; you'll get a Standby light on. Panel 11, circuit breaker LGC/DSKY, Open. And then continue shutting it down with activation 15, steps 2, 3, 4, 5; and activation 16, perform all. That completes it.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. Let me see if I got it right. First thing you want us to do is read CM/LM Delta-P before we go in. Then we start with activation l, steps l, 2, 3. Activation 2, step 2. Activation 3, all. And that's activation 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, all of those. Step - correction - activation 10, steps 1 through 18. Activation 11, 1 through 3. 12, 1 through 4. Comm configuration should be - and I may have missed one here -PM Prime, Prime, Off, Prime - correction - PCM, Off/Reset, and High.

speaker: Gibson
text: Al, Houston. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Yes, Pete. Go ahead.

speaker: Gibson
text: We just had a brief cut-out while we handed over to Goldstone. You did miss one on the Comm configuration. The - after Off/Reset, it's Off, and then High. And then continue with your read-back.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. That'd be Off/Reset, and then Off, and then High. Then CB[11] LGC/DSKY, Close that, and then perform activation 27, commander steps 3 through 6. Then activation 28, steps 1 through 7 to a Verb 7, Enter, and a Verb 37, Enter, 06 Enter, Pro, Standby. Light will come on, of course. Panel 11; then LGC/DSKY, Open, and then do activation15, steps 2, 3, 4, and 5, and all of activation 16.

speaker: Gibson
text: That's correct, Al.

speaker: Bean
text: Okey-doke.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That was Al Bean going through the Lunar Module check-out procedures with the ground. At 7 hours, 1 minute Ground Elapsed Time; we'll continue to monitor. We presently show the spacecraft velocity reading at 10,537 feet per second [3,212 m/s]. Our current altitude reading, 31,966 nautical miles [59,201 km]. This is Apollo Control, Houston; standing by.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Houston; 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, go ahead.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Our Delta-P has fallen off to plus 0.4, and the zero reading is actually 0.1, so it ought to be - It's fallen off about 0.3. And I'm getting ready to Repress the LM now.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. We copy. 0.4 and 0.1, fall off of 0.3.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Gibson
text: We'd like to precede that LM check-out step with one step from TLC 1. That is, on TLC 1, step 4, carry out the last two lines. Suit Isolation, both to Suit Flow. Suit Isolation, both to Actuate Overdrive.

speaker: Bean
text: All right. We understand; we'll do it.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 7 hours, 15 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. We've had no conversation with the Apollo 12 crew in recent minutes but we thought we would update our altitude and velocity reading from our digital displays. Currently we show an altitude of 33,282 nautical miles [61,638 km]; velocity reading in feet per second, that's 10,309.4 feet per second [3,142.3 m/s]. At 7 hours, 15 minutes of continuing to monitor of; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Houston. We've got the hatch out and the probe out, and we're in the process of stowing that, and I'm going into the Drogue right now.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. We copy.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That report from Pete Conrad. The hatch is out and the probe is out. We'll stand by continuing to monitor at 7 hours, 18 minutes into the flight.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. The CDR's in the LM.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, 12. We copy.

speaker: Gibson
text: And Pete, if you find any circuit breakers which are out of configuration, would you hold up until we get TM before you change them?

speaker: Conrad
text: Sure will. I'm not going to touch anything. I'm going to let Al come in here and do the activation - portion. He's got the checklist here, and he's tying the probe and the drogue down now.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That report, commander Pete Conrad now in the Lunar Module. We're at 7 hours, 21 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. We're now showing an altitude of 33,836 nautical miles [62,664 km]. A velocity of 10,215 feet per second [3,114 m/s]. This is Apollo Control, Houston; standing by.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. Al and I are both in the LM now, and we are getting ready to do your checklist.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We put both Suit Isolations to Suit Flow, and now we are going to turn them to Suit Disconnect.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. We are checking the breakers now. The ASA Stab/Control panel 16 CB is in.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. We copy.

speaker: Bean
text: Things 1ook real tidy - things look real tidy up here, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Al. Are you home?

speaker: Bean
text: Pretty nice.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hey, he's not going to be at home for at least 2 days.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. I found in Row 3 one circuit breaker that's out of configuration. Under lighting, utility is out and, according to my book, it should be in.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We copy that, Pete. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. That one circuit breaker out of Panel 11 and all circuit breakers on Panel 16 are in the proper configuration.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control in Houston. Al Bean is also in the Lunar Module at this time. That was Al who reported things look real tidy.

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, would you hold up on activating the S-band until we can get the IU turned off down here?

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, Houston. An explanation on that utility circuit breaker: at lift-off that circuit breaker was out, and that is the way it was configured at the Cape. The change did not get into the checklist, so there was no change during flight, and we'd like you to go ahead and leave that circuit breaker out until we can get power on the LM.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Very good. And we're in the middle of step 11 on act 7 right now.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 7 hours, and 31 minutes into the flight of Apollo 12. Commander Pete Conrad and Alan Bean continuing with their check-out procedures in the Lunar Module. Presently, we show a velocity of 10,055 feet per second [3,065 m/s] for spacecraft Apollo 12 and an altitude of 34,855 nautical miles [64,551 km] above the Earth. At 7 hours, and 32 minutes continuing to monitor, this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hey [garble] Okay, Houston, we're going over on LM power at whatever GET it is right now. [Pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. Copy. You're going over. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: We presently read a GET of 7 hours, 36 minutes. That was Commander Conrad identifying he's going over on LM power.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: TELMU confirms that we're presently on LM power.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, go ahead.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hi. Roger. Are you people looking at quad B? It's up there - a pretty good temperature, 170 degrees now.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Dick. We'll look at it...

speaker: Gordon
text: ...And - Okay. And if there's no reason why we can't start PTC, unless you want to get this Comm stuff, I'll just hold here.

speaker: Gibson
text: Right. Stand by on that, Dick. [Long pause.]

speaker: Bean
text: Okay, Houston. We're checking the voltages on the batteries now. We got - on Battery 1, we got 34 Volts; Battery 2, 34.2; Battery 3, 34.2; Battery 4, 30 - 34.2; Battery 5 is 37; Battery 6 is 37.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Al. We copy. 34, 34.2, 34.2, 34.2, and 37 on 5 and 6.

speaker: Bean
text: Roger. You probably ought give 34.2 to that first one, too.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That was Al Bean reading off battery voltages to Capsule Communicator Ed Gibson. We're at 7 hours, and 39 minutes now Ground Elapsed Time. We presently show velocity of 9,948 feet per second [3,032 m/s]. Altitude now reads 35,564 nautical miles [65,865 km]. This Apollo Control, Houston; continuing to monitor.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, do you now want us to put ourselves in the Comm configuration you requested?

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, that's affirmative.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Going on now. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We're set.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: Do you want us to put in the LGC/DSKY circuit breaker now, Houston? Or do you want to wait until you get some good Comm, with us?

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, let's hold up on that right until we see what we have. And when you put the LGC to sleep, we'd like you to skip Program 06 and just pull the LGC circuit breaker. That way you'll be in the same configuration you were at launch, and the activation that you'll take up subsequently should work out.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, then. We'll just sit tight right now; and for your information, we're on VHF antenna Aft and S-band Aft.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Bean
text: We're looking out our AOT, Houston, and it really looks nice.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, are you getting any data from Intrepid, yet?

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, that's negative. We're still reconfiguring to pick up that data.

speaker: Gibson
text: Oh, okay. We're standing by to come up with the DSKY. And we'll hold until you get our data.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hey, Houston. I was going to report that I had another person in sight, - but it - looking out the AOT - but it turns out that the left rear descent looks right in Dick's rendezvous window, and he's looking right back at us.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. We copy.

speaker: Conrad
text: Say, Houston. How soon you going to be reconfigured? We hate to use these batteries up.

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, we've got about another minute or two, and if we can't make it by then, we'll not go on with it.

speaker: Gordon
text: What seems to be the problem, Houston?

speaker: Gibson
text: We're reconfiguring in order to get that data.

speaker: Gordon
text: Yes. We've been planning to do this for quite a while.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. We're picking up some data from the LM now. Stand by. We're looking at it.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. Very good; and say, we've got a special [laughter] - We've got a favor to ask you for our entertainment tonight.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. Go ahead.

speaker: Conrad
text: You get the DSE tapes, don't you, of the launch?

speaker: Gibson
text: That's affirmative. We have it.

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, [laughter] we want you to play it for us tonight before we go to bed. We're still up here laughing over it, trying to remember all the things that we said and did. So we want to hear it tonight before we go to bed.

speaker: Gibson
text: You want to relive that twice in one day?

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes [laughter]. You better believe it.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That was Pete Conrad asking the ground if they could replay the tape from this morning's launch to relive that moment. 7 hours, 50 minutes continuing to monitor; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hey, Houston. Are you ready for us for the LC - LGC/DSKY breaker?

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, that's affirmative. We're ready to go. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Houston, you want us to bring up the IMU also, huh?

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, that's negative. We've...

speaker: Conrad
text: That's step 2 on page Activation 27.

speaker: Gibson
text: That's affirm. That was - On Activation 27, we had steps 3 through 6.?

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: And, Houston, there's self-test coming at you.

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, we're not copying any computer data yet.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Well, it's doing self-check just fine, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. Copy your self-check looked good.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. It's not complete yet, but it's - it's in the self-check. We've got a two and a one, and we've been running for about 50 seconds.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. We've just completed the self-test satisfactorily. We're going to terminate the self-test.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We've picked up and been copying your DSKY. And, Al, we've been showing a high quad 4 temperature. We would like for you to go ahead and check the position of two circuit breakers on panel 11. Heaters RCS System A/B.1, Quad 4; and on panel 16, Heaters RCS System A/B.2, Quad 4.

speaker: Bean
text: Roger. All the circuit breakers are out. I guess it's because we haven't gone to PTC yet.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Al.

speaker: Bean
text: You ready for Verb 74?

speaker: Gibson
text: Al, could you hold off on Verb 74? We're trying to pick it up on another site.

speaker: Bean
text: Roger. We're standing by ready to give you Verb 74.

speaker: Gibson
text: Al, go ahead with the Verb 74.

speaker: Bean
text: Coming at you.

speaker: Gibson
text: Al, we've got the E-Mod.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. Understand you got that. And that's the end. We are going to pull the DSKY breaker now and power down.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Al. [Long pause.]

speaker: Bean
text: Okay, Houston, we're powering her back down now.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We copy. You're powering down.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That is Al Bean reporting they are powering down now. Every indication from the check are Lunar Module, Intrepid, looks good. Eight hours into the flight. Standing by, this is...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 8 hours, and 2 minutes into the flight. We currently show Apollo 12 with a velocity of 9,634 feet per second [2,936 m/s], an altitude of 37,666 nautical miles [69,757 km]. 8 hours and 2 minutes into the flight, this is Apollo Control, Houston; standing by.

speaker: Bean
text: Houston, we're getting ready to transfer to CSM power right now.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Al.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, have you got anything else for us before we close up the LM?

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by on that, Pete.

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, go ahead and button it up.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, just checked the index angle on the docking here, and it's minus 0.3. Dick's COAS must have been in error.

speaker: Gibson
text: Copy minus 0.3. Well done.

speaker: Conrad
text: Come on, Ed. Smile. You sound too serious down there today.

speaker: Gibson
text: Still thinking about your morning.

speaker: Conrad
text: We're doing our best to forget it [laughter].

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. 8 hours and nine minutes now into the flight. Apollo 12 now shows an altitude reading of 38,311 nautical miles [70,952 km] and a velocity reading of 9,541.6 feet per second [2,908.3 m/s]. Continuing to monitor, this is Apollo Control Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. The LM hatch is closed.

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, copy you got it closed. And we've got a few things for you to pick up on the time line when you're ready.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Give us about 10 here until we - we're still getting Dick out of his gear, and we've got to reconfigure - Let's get the Probe and Drogue back in.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. Will do.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: You heard that report from Commander Pete Conrad reporting that the LM hatch is closed. Conrad and Bean have returned to the Command Module at this time. 8 hours, 12 minutes continuing to monitor; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. We got the drogue in and probe's on its way up this time. We'll be done in about 5 minutes.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. We have the tunnel all in, and everything's taken care of.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. Copy. You got it all buttoned up.

speaker: Bean
text: Hey, we're looking at you down there, Houston, and now you're about the size of a volleyball.

speaker: Gibson
text: Al, how far away is that volleyball?

speaker: Bean
text: I'd say that volleyball's about 2 feet away.

speaker: Gibson
text: Good eye, Al.

speaker: Bean
text: I can't see any landmass at all. All I can see is water with lots of clouds, and I can see sort of a glare point on the Earth. I think that must be the zero phase point to us. Other than that, it's very, very bright. And another interesting thing is, on the dark side, you cannot see where the Earth stops and space begins. It's unlike the Moon at night on in the daytime where you can see it in earthshine. You just can't see anything.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Al. How come the old heads aren't giving us the same description?

speaker: Bean
text: They're still worried about this morning.

speaker: Gordon
text: He won't let us near the window.

speaker: Conrad
text: We've got a couple of interesting things here, too, Houston. I've now started picking up ice on my inner - inside portion of the outside panel on window 1. Don't ask me why.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay, Pete. Let's hear that one again. The - You're picking up ice on the inside of the out-side of the panel.

speaker: Conrad
text: No, on the window number 1, the outside window has ice trickles on the inside of it. In other words, between it and the inner window.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. We got it.

speaker: Conrad
text: And they weren't there earlier. I don't know when they arrived, but I just noticed them a little while ago. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
