text: That was Pete Conrad reporting the ice between the window panes. Window number 1. Earlier you heard a description from Al Bean as he viewed the Earth from Apollo 12's present altitude of 39,687 nautical miles [73,500 km]. We now show a velocity of...

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, would you verify that you left the circuit breakers in the LM according to the configuration on activation 3 and 4 except - for that utility circuit breaker?

speaker: Conrad
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: Bean
text: Does the systems test-meter look okay to you? Why'd you ask, Houston? [Pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: 8 hours, 26 minutes into the flight at this time. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by, Al [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, we show that the current going over to the LM is oscillating as before, but it's about 1 Amp higher on me.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. What's that mean?

speaker: Gibson
text: Give us another long pause, Pete, and we'll be back up to you.

speaker: Gibson
text: Hello, Houston; 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. It - I think it's about time I went to PTC, don't you?

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. That's affirmative, Dick. And now that you're back in out of the LM and ready to pick up, why don't I give you some of the things we've been thinking about as far as the time line. You'll be back on that nominal time line when you take the Primary Evap and deactivate it after PTC. And also for PTC, we'd like you to disable Quads Alpha and Bravo.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. Understand disable Alpha and Bravo. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: PTC referred to their - Passive Thermal Control or the slow barbeque mode that the command and Service Module and Lunar Module go into in route to the Moon and from the Moon to stabilize the thermal conditions outside the spacecraft. We're at 8 hours, 30 minutes now into the flight. We show an altitude on Apollo 12 of 40,159 nautical miles, and a velocity of 9,294.5 feet per second. This is Apollo control, Houston, continuing to monitor.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Would you go ahead and turn off Hydrogen tank 1 heater to get us to do some Cryo balancing? And secondly, give us a readout of the Service Module RCS propellant quantity for all quads?

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Hydrogen tank 1 heater is Off, and 2 is remaining in Auto.

speaker: Gordon
text: Quad A propellant, Full Scale High and a percent. Quad B, Full Scale High; Quad C, Full Scale High; Quad D, Full Scale High.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. Copy all Full Scale High.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, we're going to go ahead and maneuver to 090 and set up PTC.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Dick.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That was Dick Gordon reporting that they would maneuver to PTC attitude or Passive Thermal Control attitude. 8 hours, 32 minutes now into the flight. This is Apollo control, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hello, Houston. We have a Cryo Press, O 2 Tank 2 pressure's a little low. It's about 800.

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, Roger. Copy 800.

speaker: Gordon
text: And is that normal for that particular Tank, or is that one we've - we expected to have trouble with? Like a warning coming on before the heater?

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by on that, Dick.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. Had you gone ahead and stirred both tanks? They both look low at the present time.

speaker: Gordon
text: We haven't done anything to them except leave the heaters on. We can give them both a fan cycle if you like.

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by on that.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. You can go ahead and turn the fans on and bring the pressure up.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. We're bringing them both on now, and understand you're going to watch them for us.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We're looking.

speaker: Bean
text: Hello, Houston; 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Bean
text: What's that tank doing? You give us a [garble] Tank 2 O 2 .

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. We are showing on Tank 1, 737; Tank 2, 755; and they appear to be holding.

speaker: Bean
text: Say that again, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, we show on Tank 1, 737; Tank 2, 755.

speaker: Bean
text: Roger. We are trying to figure out ourselves why they [garble ] normal [garble] [Pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, give us Omni Alpha, Omni Alpha. [Pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, go to Omni Alpha, Omni Alpha. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 8 hours and 40 minutes into the flight of Apollo 12. That earlier report or exchange that power going into the LM was oscillating as before but showing 1 amp higher.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: We are standing by for this.

speaker: Bean
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Bean
text: Houston, this is 12. I just stated that I have quads Alpha and Bravo disabled with the Auto RCS.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. [Pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: And, 12, would you go ahead and verify that the O 2 Heaters are in Auto?

speaker: Bean
text: Both O 2 Heaters are in Auto.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Al. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Retracing our earlier statement with regard to the 1 amp higher, this is not viewed with significance in the Mission Control Center at this time. It's possibly a change in calibration, but we can't really tell. At 8 hours, 41 minutes into t,he flight; we show Apollo 12 with an altitude of 41,129 nautical miles [76,171 km].

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. We're looking at the O 2 again and reading Tank 1, 758; and 777, Tank 2. It's coming up slow.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. We're going to leave our H - I mean our O 2 fans on until you give us a call, then.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. That's a good idea. Looks as though you just have some stratification, and it's going to take a little while to mix it up.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12. Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Ed.

speaker: Gibson
text: Your pitch and yaw rates are - look low. You can go ahead and start the roll.

speaker: Conrad
text: You say our pitch and yaw looks pretty good, huh?

speaker: Gibson
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hey, we've only been waiting about 10 minutes.

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, looks good down here. We're ready to go.

speaker: Gordon
text: Oh, I'm with you. I was just saying that it only took 10 minutes.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hello, Houston; 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. We are still venting this cabin overboard. We think we should have terminated that about 8 hours. Can we go ahead and terminate the cabin purge?

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, we show that we ought to go on with that until about 12 hours.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay [Garble.]

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, we'd like you to take the S-band antenna to the Omni and go to the Bravo position.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. S-band Omni to Bravo.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. Let us know when you think we can deactivate the evaporator.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Dick. Will do.

speaker: Gordon
text: Thank you.

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, you can go ahead and deactivate that now.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Hello, Houston. This is 12, and we're about to change Lithium Hydroxide canister number 1.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Dick. We copy. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, Houston. The evaporator's secured.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, 12. Copy the evaporator secured.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 9 hours, 1 minute now into the flight of Apollo 12. We currently show an altitude of 42,763.7 nautical miles [79,198.4 km] and a velocity now reading 8,966 feet per second [2,733 m/s]. Since the conversational pace has slowed considerably in this phase of the mission, we do plan to take the live release line down and tape, if for a periodic playback. However, if conversation does pick up, we will bring the line back up again. At 9 hours, 2 minutes into the flight, as you heard reported from the spacecraft by Dick Gordon, the first canister change has been made and it's expected that the crew will take some time for an eat period. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: We have some folks back here interested in your comments about the vibration during the S-II burn. Could you quickly give us a few clarifying remarks on that?

speaker: Conrad
text: It just seemed to me it vibrated all the way through the whole S-II burn, that I could feel, and let me ask the other guys. Yes, it just...

speaker: Gordon
text: Had a small low amplitude.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes, a very small low amplitude vibration, you know, just a little shaking, all the time through-out the whole burn.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. Do you have any feel for the direction and the frequency?

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, it wasn't longitudinal, and - I don't know, a couple of CPSs really, I guess, or less.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, can you see it on the records down there or anything?

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, we don't have the - the folks here - the booster folks here are looking at the records right now.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Understand.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 9 hours and 6 minutes into the flight. You heard Pete Conrad reflecting on the powered phase of flight, specifically the second stage of part of the boost phase with Ed Gibson on the ground. At 9 hours and 6 minutes, continuing to stand by in Mission Control Center; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hey, Houston. It might be interesting to note we haven't used the little separator on our water gun and we're working off the sip hydrogen separator; you know, the one that's down in the lower right-hand side of the LEB, and it's very good water so far. It's got a few bubbles in it.

speaker: Gibson
text: Real good, Pete. Nothing but the best for you.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Gibson
text: The folks down here have been looking over the LM E-Mod, and it looks very good to us. See no problem, would you also take the O 2 fans and put them to Off. We're - look pretty high on the tank pressure. It's 883 and 893.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. They're both off. And thanks for the information on the LM.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control Houston at 9 hours, 36 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. We've had no further conversations with the spacecraft since our last report; however, we thought we would provide you an update of our current altitude and velocity. Presently, we show the Apollo 12 spacecraft at 45,708 nautical miles [84,651 km] above the Earth; velocity now reads 8,623 feet per second [2,628 m/s]. At 9 hours, 37 minutes into the flight and continuing to monitor; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, if you'll go to P00 and Accept, we'll give you a new state vector. Negative on the P00; just Accept.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay, 12. It's coming up. We're looking for a midcourse 2 tomorrow at 31 hours for about 61 feet per second, and also we have here an update to an erasable load in your alternate and contingency checklist on page 1-32 when you're ready to copy.

speaker: Bean
text: Go ahead, Ed. We'll get it on the Flight Plan and transfer it later. Is it T Ephem .

speaker: Gibson
text: That's affirmative. And that update is just two lines. Column B, line 4, 14616; line 5, 13744.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay, Houston. What page was that? We got column B, line 4 as 14616 and line 5, 13744.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Al. Numbers are good, and that's on page 1-32.

speaker: Gibson
text: It's in your alternate...

speaker: Bean
text: We got it.

speaker: Gibson
text: ...contingency checklist.

speaker: Bean
text: We got it. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, the uplink is complete. You can go back to Block.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. What did you give me?

speaker: Gibson
text: Gave you a good state vector.

speaker: Gordon
text: You mean I ruined it, huh?

speaker: Gordon
text: Ed, are you telling me that I ruined it with my P23?

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, stand by on that and we'll see what your P23 did do. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, it looks as though your P23 did improve your state vector. However, we had a little longer time to work on it, about 6 hours worth of MSFN, and so we gave you one a tad more accurate.

speaker: Gordon
text: Thank you.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at l0 hours Ground Elapsed Time now in the flight of Apollo 12. The Apollo 12 spacecraft now at 47,619 nautical miles [88,190 km] above the Earth. Currently traveling at a speed of 8,418 feet per second [2,566 m/s]...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. As you heard, Ed Gibson passed up our forecast Midcourse Correction 2. This is the midcourse correction that takes the spacecraft out of a free return and places it into it's - what is known as a hybrid trajectory. This time identified as 31 hours, which would be tomorrow, and Delta-V of sixty - a velocity change of 61 feet per second [19 m/s]. Chatting with Ed Gibson, during this conversational phase, were both Al Bean and Dick Gordon. The P23 referred to Program 23, is one of the computer programs which is cislunar navigation where Command Module Pilot Dick Gordon has been taking star sightings and updating his own state vector. So at 10 hours, 4 minutes into the flight; continuing to monitor, this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Conrad
text: You want that P52 at 10 - about 10:45?

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by on that, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, that P52 is really your option. We don't need it. You can go ahead and do it if you like. You have one coming up at around 15 hours and that would suffice.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We'll wait.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Gibson
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, we're still looking at a current going over to the LM which is about 1 amp higher than before it was manned. It still fluctuates, but the mean is still about 1 amp higher. So we're faced with the question of whether we have it out of configuration in the LM, and we'd like to suggest that you go on back over to the LM and check the circuit-breaker configuration. The possibility here is that you've got a system on line which is not called out for and doesn't have proper cooling. I'd like to have your thoughts on that.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We're going to go back over if you want. Now, we left those two panels, as far as I know, in the proper configuration, but we'll go back over. The other thought that I had, I noticed when I closed the Hatch that I tried to get the Hatch all the way up to the very corner, watch the lights go out - I know the light switch worked on the Hatch, because I tried that, but that would be about the only other thing that I can think of that didn't work.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. So those floodlights did go out when the hatch was closed.

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, no. I don't know that they went out. I'm saying that if you push the switch it went out.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. That indicates at least that you didn't have the switch out of position.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 10 hours and 30 minutes into the flight of Apollo 12. We currently show the Apollo 12 spacecraft at 49,972 nautical miles [92,548 km] above the Earth. Its velocity now reads 8,175.7 feet per second [2,492.0 m/s]...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. As you heard that discussion between Capsule Communicator Ed Gibson in Mission Control and spacecraft commander Pete Conrad. There is a very distinct possibility the crew will make a second trip into the Lunar Module this evening, principally to explore or check the position of circuit breakers aboard the LM. The discussion dealt with a consistent number we been seeing, one in which there has been a reading of 1 amp higher since - 1 amp difference since the two crew members had gone over earlier, a reading higher than had been reflected previously. Because of this possibility that Conrad and Bean will return to the Lunar Module, we propose to leave the release circuit up and live at least for a while and at 10 hours and 34 minutes into the flight, continuing to monitor; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, we're on our way back in now.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: We'll get the world's record for ingress/egressing out of this baby in a couple of more.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. Give us a mark. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, we assume that you powered down the circuit breaker Panel as - on activation 3 and 4. Two circuit breakers there that should be out which are shown in: one is utility light which we discussed and the other under ECS panel 16, the cabin Repress, should also be out. That was closed in a previous step.

speaker: Conrad
text: We'll check them.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. We presently show Apollo 12 50,526 nautical miles [93,574 km] above the Earth. Velocity now is 8,122 feet per second [2,476 m/s]. Standing by; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. You got any more bets? The utility circuit - utility light circuit breaker on Panel 11 is out and the cabin Repress circuit breaker on Panel 16 is out.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. We copy that. Stand by and we'll see if there's anything else we can do while we're in there.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We're going to go through the whole phase 3 here again. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. We've got a question for you. We - When we left last time, we put our exterior lighting switch from Dock to Off, since we'd already docked, and it may be that when it's in Off it doesn't turn out the cabin lights when you close the Hatch. Could you check that?

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We'll check that. We saw down here that when you opened the hatch, you didn't get any drop in the current, and we suspect that the problem was the floodlight, but stand by on that.

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, would you go ahead and verify the position of the floodlight switch? Verify that it's off?

speaker: Conrad
text: Floodlights are off and exterior lighting in Off. We also punched the little button on the hatch and the floodlights went off.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We copy.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. You hear Pete Conrad and Al Bean speaking from the Lunar Module. They are currently going through the circuit breaker configuration at this time. Receiving updates from Ed Gibson, our Capsule Communicator at Mission Control Center. Ten hours, 45 minutes...

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, would you go ahead and open the Floodlight circuit breaker, Panel 16, and we'll troubleshoot. We'll be watching the current down here and see if we get a change.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, 12. When you pulled that circuit breaker [garble] the service testmeter dropped 0.4 of an amp - correction - 0.4 of a volt.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, 12. We confirm that. We show a drop in amps back to what looked to be the same before you went in. We'd like you to go ahead and leave that circuit breaker open, and you can leave it in that configuration when you leave the LM. When you go back in, of course, we'll just have to punch it in.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We're getting back out of the LM, Houston. Must be that switch in the hatch is out of adjustment somehow.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes. He can put - the switch works by me pushing my finger on it, but it may not cut it off - when it's closed any more.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. We concur with that.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Okay, you heard that last exchange. The amperage has been brought down and Ed Gibson did pass along the word to leave the floodlight circuit breaker Open when they depart the Lunar Module. When they made that switch...

speaker: Conrad
text: Hey, Houston. We're going to push the breaker hack in for just a second and go shut the hatch and watch our testmeter.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: When they made that switch, Flight Director Pete Frank said That did it, we're down where we were. We're at 10 hours, 48 minutes at the present time and we now show an altitude on Apollo 12 of 51,336 nautical miles [95,074 km]. Velocity now reads 8,044 feet per second [2,452 m/s]. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Hello, Houston; 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, go ahead.

speaker: Bean
text: Roger. I guess that's it. The - I left the service testmeter and he - Pete came back in and closed the hatch and locked it completely, and the testmeter didn't drop at all. So, we got back in and I'm going to pull the floodlight circuit breaker and now we're down to the bottom.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 10 hours, 53 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. We're in the process of returning Pete Conrad and Al Bean to the Command Module at this time. Their return is in progress. The floodlight referred to, by the way, is much like a refrigerator light. It's the kind of device that you can punch it with your finger to turn it off apparently and the hatch did not adequately shut it down. And so the procedure that has been taken has been to leave that circuit breaker open. Our amperage readings are now the same as they were prior to the first manned excursion into the Lunar Module. We'll stand by and continue to monitor at 10 hours, 54 minutes. And this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, a while back you read to us some Service Module RCS propellant quantities, and they showed Off-Scale High. Also the TM from that gage is still reading Off-Scale High, and we suspect a problem with the gage. We'd like to do some troubleshooting on that and have you look at those four propellant quantity readings again and also look at the Service Module indicator to put that at Helium Tank Temperature and read the four quantities. For your information - for your information, our calculations down here show your RCS total is 86; A is 84; B, 88; C, 84; and D is 89.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. I just checked all A, B, C, and D, and they're all still reading Off-Scale High. And then the - in the tank in the Service Module RCS indicator H e tank temp is reading 70 on A; it's reading 85 on B, 85 on C, and 65 on D.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. Copy 70, 85, 85, 65.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes. And something I forgot to pass on, I guess, I think I did. When we Sepped from the S-IVB prior to turning around, I believe it was Helium 1, B, barber pole; and system A, secondary propellant, barber pole; and that was it. We turned them both on and away we went.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. We copy that.

speaker: Conrad
text: We also, Houston, think that our PCM gauge is out. It's been reading zero. We changed our canister at the proper time and we had - when was it? During powered flight, then?

speaker: Gordon
text: During launch.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes, during launch we had a flashing CO 2 light along with a few others. This thing jumped all over the place and then all of a sudden it went to zero and then it moved off the peg, so I kind of got the suspicion that the PT CO 2 gauge was out.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. We confirm or suspect that down here.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. That's Pete Conrad now back in the Command Module doing this trouble shooting with Ed Gibson on the ground. We are now at 11 hours, 13 minutes into the flight of Apollo 12. Presently 53,187 nautical miles [98,502 km] above the Earth and now traveling at 7,870 feet per second [2,399 m/s]. This is Apollo Control, Houston; continuing to monitor.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello there, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Gibson
text: Say, since you got those two indications on the - two barber pole indications we'd like to have you barber pole indications we'd like to have you verify that you did complete the step of throwing the secondary propellant Service Module RCS to Close and then back to Off.

speaker: Conrad
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 11 hours, 25 minutes Ground Elapsed Time into the flight of Apollo 12. Now we have had no conversation with the crew of Apollo 12 for some minutes now; however, we thought we would pass along to you the current altitude and velocity reading. Our digital displays now show the Apollo 12 spacecraft at 54,092 nautical miles [100,178 km] above the Earth, velocity reading 7,786.9 feet per second [2,373.4 m/s]. We'll continue to monitor the air to ground loop and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go.

speaker: Gibson
text: Flight Plan at this time calls for terminating the Battery B charge. Because of the exercise this morning and the fact that it drained down the batteries, we'd like you to continue charging Battery B, and we suspect that it'll probably go on to about 13 hours. We'll give you a call when we'd like you to go to Battery A. Also, you can perform your O 2 fuel cell purge as planned, and if you hold out - or take that waste water dump down to about 15 percent rather than the nominal 25, you won't have to have another dump until about midcourse 2.

speaker: Conrad
text: Understand.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 11 hours, 35 minutes now in the flight of Apollo 12. Current altitude 54,812 nautical miles [101,512 km] for the Apollo spacecraft above the Earth. It is now traveling at 7,724 feet per second [2,354 m/s]. Because our conversational pace with the crew is spacing itself out once again, we will be taking the air-ground loop off the line and will play a tape of any conversations as they occur. If - and we will follow the same procedure as we did previously if the situation warrants to bring the line backup live, we will do so. So at 11 hours and 36 minutes and continuing to monitor; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston, we're going to turn off the dump now.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, 12.

speaker: Conrad
text: Say, Houston, how far out are we?

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by, Pete. We'll give you a good figure.

speaker: Conrad
text: Thank you. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, you are about 56,000 [nautical] miles [104,000 km] out now, and you are smoking along at 7,600 feet per second [2,300 m/s].

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Thank you. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Al, are you still at the window?

speaker: Bean
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston, at 11 hours, 58 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12...

speaker: Bean
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Bean
text: The Earth doesn't seem to be getting smaller too fast right now, but it is sort of funny. It just seems to hang out there. It doesn't - You can't see it rotate, you can't see it move or anything. It just sort of hangs out there in this black space, and the Moon just doesn't seem to be any bigger than it was when we left, but it looks more like a sphere also. It sort of looks like a ball that is being hung out there somehow. It's really crazy.

speaker: Gibson
text: Al, which way does it look like it is hanging from?

speaker: Bean
text: North Pole, naturally. Otherwise the string would get all tangled up.

speaker: Gordon
text: Just scientists are supposed to know that.

speaker: Gibson
text: You need some experimental proof.

speaker: Bean
text: That sub-solar point is over the water now, and it glints on the surface of the Earth just like a light on a billiard ball or something. There is a little spot there that gives you a little specular reflection, and then it's got a bright halo, or just a bright area, around it.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. How...

speaker: Bean
text: It looks like we can see the coast of China and Japan now. It's kind of hard to tell. You can see red Earth pretty well, but if there's greens or grays, it is very difficult to discern them from the blues.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Al. That glint, is that about a quarter of the way off the - about half-way between the terminator and the edge?

speaker: Bean
text: That's about right. [Music: 'San Antonio Rose']

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. Presently the Apollo 12 spacecraft is 56,766 nautical miles [105,131 km] above the Earth, now traveling at a speed of 7,555 feet per second [2,303 m/s].

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Commander Pete Conrad ask how far out they were. They have progressed some 795 [nautical] miles [1,472 km] since he asked that question. That was Al Bean vividly describing the Earth as they viewed it from in excess of 56,000 nautical miles [104,000 km]. At 12 hours and 3 minutes into the flight of Apollo 12, this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Al's getting homesick up here; we're just trying to keep him happy.

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, is that you singing?

speaker: Conrad
text: No. Unfortunately, it's not.

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, let's hear a little of that good music. [Music: 'San Antonio Rose'.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay, that's enough. Pete, I asked for a little of the good music.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger-Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: Just a minute. I'll go see if I can find it. [Music - 'Louisiana Man' by Rusty and Doug.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, all the folks down here feel that isn't half bad.

speaker: Gibson
text: All bad.

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, I'll tell you what it's done. It's precipitated a big search for the rest of the tapes. Al and Dick are scurrying all over the spacecraft.

speaker: Gibson
text: Can we help?

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. What about the waste stowage vent?

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, you can go ahead and close it now.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. And we'll hold off until we finish charging Battery B, before we dump the battery compartment.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Dick. That sounds good. [Long pause.]

speaker: Bean
text: Ed, I guess you might as well start logging this leak rate now for the LM. It's - Delta-P is plus 0.2 right at this time, and I don't think we'll be [garble] for a day or so now so we can start logging, and Zero on our gage is 0.1 plus 0.1.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. Copy Delta-P 0.2, and Zero is 0.1.

speaker: Bean
text: That's affirmative. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, this is 12. We went ahead and vented that Battery right now and it's on its way down to zero. It was up to 3 volts when we started.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, 12. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. At 12:24 it says here in our Flight Plan that we'll be full frame for a 500 millimeter and we have it out, and I presume that that time is still pretty good.

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by on that, Pete. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, was that a recent write-in to the Flight Plan?

speaker: Conrad
text: No, it's on our photo card.

speaker: Gordon
text: We just found that out before we left.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. [Music: 'Chattanooga Choo-Choo'.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, those values of the F-Stops you just questioned look good. That's F:11 for the Earth, F:8 for the Moon.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Thank you.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 12 hours, 21 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. The Apollo 12 spacecraft at the present time 58,160 nautical miles [107,712 km] away from Earth. It is now traveling at 7,439 feet per second [2,267 m/s]. Since our last report, we've had several conversation exchanges with the Apollo 12 crew. Interestingly enough, you will note that in these conversations, the conversations are interspersed with bits of music. And in most instances, the country and western style prevails. Commander Pete Conrad is an acknowledged country and western music fan.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control of Houston. The country and western style of music which predominated at least a goodly segment of that played down by the crew is courtesy of commander Pete Conrad, commander Conrad being an acknowledged country and western music fan. The music came to us from their tape cassettes aboard the spacecraft. At 12 hours, 27 minutes; our digital displays now show Apollo 12 at 58,586 nautical miles [108,501 km] above the Earth. It's velocity continuing at a steady decrease, now reading 7,404 feet per second [2,257 m/s]. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: ...is that any better?

speaker: Gibson
text: Well, we suggest, Dick, that maybe you continue scurrying around there.

speaker: Gordon
text: Oh, you're really hard at it today, aren't you? Okay.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 12 hours, 51 minutes now into the flight. Our displays currently show the Apollo 12 spacecraft at 60,257 nautical miles [111,596 km] in altitude, current velocity reading of 7,269 feet per second [2,216 m/s]...

speaker: Bean
text: That Earth view is really going to be something weird coming back, Houston, when you only got about a - just a little bitty sliver of the Earth, because, like I said earlier, you just can't see anything in the black. And when we had that eclipse at about 5 hours, I guess the Earth's going to completely disappear.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Al, copy. You see Australia coming up over the - over by the edge?

speaker: Bean
text: I sort of do. It's difficult to tell, unless the ground is - has a pretty good contrast to the -to the water. And I can see some red over there, and I'm not really sure whether that's Australia or exactly what it is. Makes you wish you had studied your geology harder in high school, or something- geography, that is.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. More music from the Apollo 12 spacecraft. We heard from both Dick Gordon and Al Bean during this transmission. That was Al talking about the Earth once again in referring to an earlier conversation. We've picked up the crew again and we will switch to that transmission, live.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay, Houston. We've got Australia. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. Say again.

speaker: Bean
text: Roger, we got Australia in sight now at the - oh, it's about the 8 o'clock position, with respect to the terminator.

speaker: Gibson
text: Al, are you able to pick out any small islands out there in the Pacific?

speaker: Bean
text: Pete's using the monocular right now and - what do you say, Pete?

speaker: Conrad
text: There's a lot of clouds out there, Houston. I can see a lot of fairly small clouds, but there is so darn much cloud cover out in the Pacific, except right off the Northeast coast of Australia, that I really haven't found any islands yet, but I am sort of scanning for them now.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This Apollo Control, Houston; 12 hours, 58 minutes now into the flight. We'll take the line down at this time and pick back up as the mission progresses. We currently show an altitude reading of 60,684 nautical miles [112,387 km] above the Earth. The velocity now shows 7,236 feet per second [2,206 m/s]. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hey, Houston, 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. Have you been plotting this PTC on the ball? How's it looking?

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Dick. We've been watching it; stand by. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, we've been looking at your trace here, and it looks as though you're up to around 27 degrees now; you're just sort of pig-tailing out. What gave you a large excursion was the waste-water dump. It looks as though you'll be heading back in; you won't really significantly improve -that is, you won't really get the alignment rate right down close to zero at the rate you're going, but you'll probably stay within 30 degrees, so just hold what you've got.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, Ed. Thank you.

speaker: Gibson
text: Apollo 12, Houston. We have a - some P37 PADs for lift-off, 25, 35, 45, and 60, when you're ready to copy.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Mr. Bean is busying himself finding the PAD at this time, and he'll be ready to copy in just a minute.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go.

speaker: Gibson
text: That's it, Al. Read back.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay, the last one I got before we lost S-band there with you was the 122, and I didn't copy the last part GET 400K.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. GET at 400K was 122:01.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay, read-back follows: 025:00, 4227 [garble]; 035:00, 6327, minus 166, 073:39; [garble] 0 [garble] 045:00, 4917, minus 168, 097:5 [garble]...

speaker: Gibson
text: Al, hold up; your transmissions are all broken.

speaker: Bean
text: I'll see if I can get a little closer to the Mike; do you want me to start over again?

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by, Al. We still have a lot of static on the line.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. [long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay, Al. Go ahead with your read-back. After 025:00 we pretty much lost all of it.

speaker: Gibson
text: Read-back correct, Al.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hello, Houston, 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. It looks like - get another calibration point for our Service Test-Meter. Looks like the Battery compartment is vented when it reads 0.4 of a volt. It's been on for about - well, 30 minutes and going [garble.] Can you take a look at that ?

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. Copy. Voltage for vented is 0.4.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. You confirm us closing that - at this time, starting on a Battery B charge, over -or a Battery Alpha charge.

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, we'd like to go ahead and close the battery manifold, but continue charging Battery B.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, we estimate another 30 to 45 minutes for charging Battery Bravo.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 13 hours, 22 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. Apollo 12 now 62,373 nautical miles [115,515 km] above the Earth. Our display currently shows the velocity reading 7,107 feet per second [2,166 m/s] as the spacecraft steadily slows down. For the past several minutes we've had, in the Mission Control center, had a replay of the Translunar Injection burn, those viewing the television monitors may have noted the world map was briefly taken down. This was done at the request of the guidance officer who was analyzing the data which had been received only a short while ago from Hawaii...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. Of the long listing of numbers exchanged between CapCom Ed Gibson, and Alan Bean aboard the spacecraft, were the representative P37 PAD. P37 is a return to Earth computer program. The numbers identified at 25, 35, 45, and 60 are plus times and hours from lift-off. At 13 hours, 31 minutes into the flight, we now show Apollo 12 with an altitude of 62,957 nautical miles [116,596 km]. Its velocity now reads 7,064 feet per second [2,153 m/s]. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, you can go ahead and stop charging Battery Bravo and start on battery Alpha. If you go ahead and charge that until you hit the sleep period, you'll be able to get 60 percent of the charge back in.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. We're going to go off Bat B and start charging Bat A.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. We're charging Bat A at this time.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, 12.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 14 hours, 2 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. Our displays currently show Apollo 12 at 65,043 nautical miles [120,460 km] above the Earth. Velocity now reads 6,911 feet per second [2,106 m/s]. Here in the Mission Control Center, we're in the process of having a pass over between shifts. Cliff Charlesworth, the Flight Director of the Green Shift is now in the Control Center and going over the status of Pete Frank's shift with Flight Director Pete Frank. They will be coming on shortly...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 14 hours, 4 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. We're sort of suggesting here that, when you terminate your PTC, you go directly to your P23 attitude as listed in the Flight Plan to do your P52. There should be good stars there and it will save one attitude maneuver later.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Lind
text: And at the P23 Optics Cal, the Roll is 204, Pitch 262, and Yaw 0.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Welcome aboard, Don. [Pause.]

speaker: Lind
text: You certainly had an exciting one this morning.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes. It keeps recurring in our conversation [laughter] throughout the day today.

speaker: Gordon
text: Anybody see anything from the ground in all that business?

speaker: Lind
text: That's affirmative. We saw lightning coming right down your plume, right to the ground.

speaker: Gordon
text: Are you kidding me, or not?

speaker: Lind
text: That's some of the reports we've been getting back.

speaker: Conrad
text: I believe it.

speaker: Lind
text: I keep telling you, you don't fly through thunder storms.

speaker: Conrad
text: I keep wondering why they write that in all the handbooks. They can write that in the Saturn V handbook now.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Houston, go.

speaker: Gordon
text: You know these marks are going to be good. Dick Gordon even used his eye patch this trip.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger.

speaker: Gordon
text: I was looking at the Earth a few moments ago. You can see the entire top of Australia. Sure is pretty, and hardly any clouds at all over it. And looks to me like it's to be about one and a half to two times the size of a golf ball at arm's length.

speaker: Lind
text: Should be a pretty impressive view from that altitude. [Long pause]

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, would you select Omni Alpha, please?

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. Didn't seem to change anything.

speaker: Lind
text: Houston, say again.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. We were watching the signal strength, and it didn't seem to affect it much.

speaker: Lind
text: We're anticipating.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Gordon
text: Say, Houston, 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Go.

speaker: Gordon
text: Our PICAPAR has put the star in the LM. Have you got a couple of stars to this attitude that would not have blockage by the LM?

speaker: Lind
text: Stand by.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12. It looks like you beat the computer down here. Procyon and Rigel are the ones that we're recommending, that's 16, Procyon, and 12, Rigel.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. And here's Noun 05 for you, and here's the torquing angles coming down.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. Houston. Are you copying those torquing angles?

speaker: Lind
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: Gordon
text: Have you got them, Houston?

speaker: Lind
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Lind
text: It looks like you've got a pretty good platform up there, since the last P52 you had - you show about 1.4 in negative drift in Z, and the other two axes are better than that, so we're quite pleased with that down here. Also, we would like you to confirm the position of your SCE power push.

speaker: Gordon
text: SCE power is in Normal.

speaker: Lind
text: In Normal. Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control; 15 hours, 8 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 12 presently 69,010 nautical miles [127,807 km] out from Earth, traveling at a velocity of 6,639 feet per second [2,024 m/s]. The crew of Apollo 12 at this time are running what they call Program 23 exercises, says Lunar Navigation, in which the included angle between the star and either the near Earth horizon or the far Earth's horizon is measured. The onboard computer has stored data on the stars and part of the 35 navigational stars used in the Apollo program. The techniques used are actually extensions, more sophisticated versions of the celestial navigation techniques, which for centuries mariners have been using to locate their position on Earth. In this case there is a third dimension added, space or depth...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control. We're now at 15 hours, 15 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Still a little over 2 hours until the scheduled rest period begins for the crew of Apollo 12, however, it's likely they will sack out a bit earlier than that. They still have an evening meal before they go into the 10-hour rest period and resume the Passive Thermal Control mode, which also is known as the barbeque mode, in which they revolve at about 3 revolutions an hour to stabilize the thermal response of the spacecraft to the alternate heating of the Sun. At 15 hours, 16 minutes Ground Elapsed Time, this is Apollo Control.

speaker: Bean
text: Hello, Houston, Apollo 9. Correction, 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Go ahead. Houston, 12.

speaker: Bean
text: Roger, Houston. What state vectors do you have in the LM slot? [Long pause.]

speaker: Lind
text: It's the CSM prior to the P23.

speaker: Bean
text: Thank you.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston. [Long pause.]

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. It looks like we're ready for PTC now, and when you start the maneuver we would suggest Omni Bravo.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger, Omni Bravo.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hey, Houston, how do those P23s look to the guys in the back?

speaker: Lind
text: They look great.

speaker: Gordon
text: They're real happy, huh?

speaker: Lind
text: They sure are.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. If they're happy, I'm happy. [Pause.]

speaker: Lind
text: 12, we've got an uplink to the gyro drift whenever you can give us the computer.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. It's all yours.

speaker: Lind
text: Thank you.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, the computer's yours again. Thank you. [Long pause.]

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston. We're finished with the computer. It's yours again.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Thank you.

speaker: Lind
text: Thank you. [Long pause.]

speaker: Lind
text: This is Houston, 12. Did you call?

speaker: Conrad
text: That's negative, Houston. Some other spacecraft must have called in.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. [Laughter] I was hearing you occasionally weak, and we're not sure whether it's you or the others.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger-Roger.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston. [Long pause.]

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. We wanted to make a couple of suggestion: for you before you settle down for the night, and we wanted to leave that up to your option, when you want to go to sleep after you eat. And a couple of items before - we wanted to remind you of - that you'll have to include before you settle down for the night. First one is that the H 2 tanks, both 1 and 2, should be in Auto. You would terminate the battery charge, and you'd change the lithium hydroxide canister, and then we wanted to leave it up to you when you wanted to terminate your activity today.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We understand about the battery charge, and we intend to change the canister on time; and more than likely we'll try to go to bed about the proper time although we may go a little bit earlier. We're all pretty tired.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. That's fine with us, and we can understand that you might want a little extra sleep.

speaker: Lind
text: 12, in case I was not clear on that, we suggest that you go with the heaters to Auto after you finish the pre-sleep checklist.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. H 2 heaters to Auto after pre-sleep checklist. Roger-Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control; 16 hours, 8 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 12 now 72,989 nautical miles [135,176 km] out from Earth. Velocity, 6,383 feet per second [1,946 m/s]. We have some tape accumulated and at the present time, spacecraft communicator Don Lind is discussing an earlier start of the sleep period after they complete the pre-sleep checklist and their last meal of the day. We'll roll the tape and then join any live conversation if it's still taking place at that time when the tape is completed. Let's hear the tape.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control. That completes the most recent exchange between the spacecraft communicator and the crew of Apollo 12 who at this time are settling in for the night and likely will be in their sleep periods somewhat early. At 16 hours, 14 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

speaker: Conrad
text: You guys calling, Houston?

speaker: Lind
text: Not us. You must be talking to somebody strange now.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston. [Long pause.]

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Lind
text: Listen, those transmissions you thought you heard a couple of minutes ago were us running some keying checks. We didn't think they were getting out, but apparently a couple of them did; so apparently, nobody is up there flying with you.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Very good.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. We liked your PTC maneuver down here. Looks pretty good. And just a reminder to - you can turn off the Auto RCS select switches now.

speaker: SC
text: [Garble.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Go.

speaker: Conrad
text: How about a E-memory dump?

speaker: Lind
text: We're all ready.

speaker: Conrad
text: Coming at you.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Lind
text: Could you give us that dump again? We switched bit rate on you in the middle and fouled ourselves up.

speaker: Conrad
text: Coming at you, Houston.

speaker: Lind
text: Thank you. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Hey, Houston, seeing we don't have any Service Module RCS propellants gauge that's working, could you give us our - what you think our present A, B, C, and D quads are, please?

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Go.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Did you get my last request?

speaker: Lind
text: Yes. We're trying to work those up, the RCS consumables.

speaker: Conrad
text: Oh, okay. Thank you.

speaker: Lind
text: Yes. We're working on it.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Lind
text: Okay. I've got your RCS propellants for you. The total is 83.2 percent; Alpha is 80.5; Bravo is 85.3; Charlie is 81.4; Delta is 85.4. That's the status as of about 2 minutes ago and also, we got your E-dump successfully.

speaker: Conrad
text: That's lovely.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control 17 hours, 08 minutes, Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 12 is presently 76,579 nautical miles [141,824 km] up from Earth. The velocity now 6,166 feet per second [1,879 m/s], continuing to decelerate as we approach the midpoint in the gravispheres between the Moon and the Earth...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo 12 Control - Apollo 12 now some 76,872 nautical miles [142,367 km] and while we watch the display it jumped to 76,884 nautical miles [142,389 km] out from Earth. Velocity continuing to decelerate, now 6,148.5 feet per second [1,874.1 m/s]. Total vehicle weight in Earth pounds, 96,440 [43,744 kg]. Extending a line outward from the Earth to the position of Apollo 12, it is presently directly over the equator, just north of the island of New Guinea, more specifically north of West Irian at 76,000 miles out. At 17 hours, 14 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Go.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. The pre-sleep checklist is complete. We have no medical crew status report, and - the - we're going to the normal Lunar comm mode except S-Band Normal, so forth and so on.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. Have pleasant dreams. We see you in the morning.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. The battery charge is going off at this time.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston. [Long pause.]

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Lind
text: Sorry to bother you again, Pete. We need pyro Bat readouts from you if we could. We'd also like to get a LM/Command Module Delta-P reading and a confirmation that the heaters are on Auto - the cryo heaters.

speaker: Conrad
text: 0kay. The heaters are on Auto; Bat C's, 37.1; pryo Bat A, 37.2; pryo Bat B, 37.2; and the LM/CS Delta-P is plus 0.4.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. We've got it all. Thanks very much and have a pleasant night's sleep.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control. That completes the wrap up of the last few moments of conversation prior to the crew sacking out for the night. Apollo 12 now 78,503 nautical miles [145,388 km] out from Earth traveling at a velocity of 6,055 feet per second [1,846 m/s]. And at 17 hours, 41 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control; 18 hours, 41 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 12 crew apparently asleep at this time. Now some 81,705 nautical miles [151,318 km] out from Earth. Velocity continuing to decrease 5,877 feet per second [1,791 m/s]. One clock here in the Control Center has been set to show the time remaining in the 10-hour sleep period. The clock now shows 9 hours, 17 minutes remaining; and at 18 hours, 42 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 20 hours, 16 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. The crew of Apollo 12 still apparently asleep at this time. Some 7 hours, 43 minutes remaining in the sleep period. The spacecraft now, 87,149 nautical miles [161,400 km] out from Earth. Velocity 5,592 feet per second [1,704 m/s]. The space flight meteorology group and the weather bureau said this morning that the weather conditions in the planned landing areas are expected to be satisfactory for the next 4 days. Ocean areas of concern should have partly cloudy to cloudy skies, winds 10 to 15 knots, seas 3 to 4 feet, temperatures in the Atlantic area in the upper 70s [Fahrenheit, approx 25°C]. Temperatures in the Pacific area in the mid 80s [F, approx 30°C]. Isolated showers in the Atlantic area and widely scattered showers in the Pacific area. And at 20 hours, 17 minutes Ground Elapsed Time; this is Apollo Control.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 22 hours, 18 minutes into the mission. The Apollo 12 crew still asleep. They show 5 hours, 41 minutes remaining in this rest period. All systems continue to function satisfactorily. Apollo 12 is 127,851 nautical miles [236,780 km] from Earth, traveling at a velocity of 4,039 feet per second [1,231 m/s]. The Flight Controller team led by Flight Director Gerry Griffin has taken over here in the Control Center. This is Mission Control, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 22 hours, 27 minutes. We have a correction on the last figures passed, the distance and velocity. Those figures were Moon reference figures, not Earth reference. The present Earth reference distance, 93,351 nautical miles [172,886 km]; velocity, 5,292 feet per second [1,613 m/s]. The previous figures were referenced from the Moon.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 23 hours, 18 minutes. Crew still has 4 hours, 41 minutes remaining in it's rest period. But the flight controllers here are, at this time, reviewing the playback of yesterday's television transcript, it's mission. Apollo 12 is 96,456 nautical miles from Earth [178,637 km]. Traveling at a velocity of about 5,149 feet per second [1,569 m/s]. Apollo 12 will be equal distance between the Earth and the Moon at an elapsed time of 29 hours, 16 minutes, 53 seconds. The distance to both bodies from the spacecraft will be 112,899 nautical miles [209,089 km] at that time and the CapCom on this shift is Astronaut Paul Weitz who has relieved Astronaut Don Lind. This is Mission Control, Houston at 23 hours, 19 minutes.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 24 hours, 18 minutes into the mission. 3 hours and 41 minutes remain in the sleep period for the Apollo 12 crew. Apollo 12 is 99,360 nautical miles [184,015 km] from Earth, velocity is 5,020 feet per second [1,530 m/s]. Total weight of Apollo 12 now at 96,869 pounds [43,939 kg]. The Flights Dynamics Officer using data gathered from the last look at the S-IVB has predicted its trajectory. This will be the last update on this predicted trajectory for the third stage of the booster. Its closest approach to the Moon will be 3,091 nautical miles [5,725 km]. Its velocity at that time will be 4,934 feet per second [1,504 m/s], and the elapsed time at which it reaches this closest approach is 85 hours, 48 minutes, 4 seconds. The S-IVB is then expected to go on into a solar orbit. This is Mission Control, Houston at 24 hours, 19 minutes.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 25 hours, 18 minutes. Apollo 12 is 102,203 nautical miles [189,280 km] from Earth, traveling at a velocity of 4,898 feet per second [1,493 m/s]. The Apollo 12 crew still has 2 hours, 41 minutes remaining in their sleep period. The TB-5 clock that shows on the monitors in the News Center is counting from zero Greenwich Mean Time on launch day. Some of the Flight Controllers, primarily the Flight Dynamics Officers, use this time reference in some of their calculations. It's counting from zero Greenwich Mean Time on launch day. We're projecting now a time for arrival at the lunar sphere of influence of 68 hours, 30 minutes, 22 seconds. This is Mission Control, Houston at 25 hours, 19 minutes Elapsed Time.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 26 hours, 18 minutes. Apollo 12 is 104,983 nautical miles [194,429 km] from Earth. Velocity, 4,782 feet per second [1,458 m/s]. The Apollo 12 crew still has 1 hour, 41 minutes remaining in its sleep period. All systems on the Apollo 12 spacecraft continue to perform in a normal manner. This is Mission Control Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 27 hours, 18 minutes. Apollo 12 is 107,698 nautical miles from Earth traveling at a velocity of 4,672 feet per second [1,424 m/s], and we will wake up the crew 41 minutes from now. All systems continuing to function satisfactorily. No problems. The crew wake up in 41 minutes. This is Mission Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Weitz
text: Good morning, Pete. [Pause.]

speaker: Weitz
text: Hello, 12. Houston here. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 27 hours, 54 minutes. Pete Conrad has beaten us to the punch by about 5 or 6 minutes. Just as Flight Director, Gerry - Pete is putting in a call just as Gerry Griffin is asking the CapCom Paul Weitz to put in a call to him. We'll listen.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Houston; Hello, Houston. Apollo 12. Over.

speaker: Weitz
text: Good morning, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Morning.

speaker: Weitz
text: You have everybody up and about there?

speaker: Conrad
text: Everybody's up. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: They give you a crew status report.

speaker: Weitz
text: I thought we just had it, but go ahead.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Everybody had 8 hours of sleep, and the PRDs for the CDR is 11005; for the CMP, 11005; for the LMP, 04006.

speaker: Weitz
text: Roger. Copy.

speaker: Weitz
text: Apollo 12, Houston. If you want to go ahead and stir your cryos, we can get good H 2 and O 2 readout for your consumables update.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, that's in work.

speaker: Weitz
text: A couple of words on your RCS, Pete. We're running a little behind the curve, a total of about 60 pounds low. We are recommending that you perform your maneuvers at your option at either 0.2-degree a second or minimum impulse in an attempt to reduce RCS usage. Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger.

speaker: Weitz
text: 12, Houston. Ready with your morning newscast if you are.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. Go.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Whoever answered me that time was way down in the mud and hardly readable. World attention is on the flight of Apollo 12. The Soviet Union held the crew as courageous; and Tass, the official Soviet news agency, reported the start of the mission and a brief factual report in both of its Russian and foreign language reports. Czechoslovak television carried a live coverage of the lift-off, complete with an explanation of technical details. In West Germany, all radio and television networks carried the launch live, as did the Japanese Broadcasting Company. The launch is being described by such adjectives as spooky and cliff hanging. Even President Nixon, a one-time Navy man himself, admitted he had some anxious moments but added, I'm really proud of those three men up there. Weather is a news item in Houston where temperatures are expected to dip into the 20s tonight. Automobile owners are being advised to put anti-freeze in their car radiators. Today's a voting day in Houston as Houston picks a mayor, eight councilmen, four school-board members, and decides upon a number of special issues. In sports, Houston Oiler Woody Campbell ended rumors and speculation yesterday by strolling into the Oiler training room and putting on his uniform. He says he's in good shape after 10 months as an MP with the First Infantry Division in Vietnam and hopes to be in action very soon. We're working up some ball scores for you; the only one available right now is a halftime score, it's Ohio State 28 and Purdue 7.

speaker: Bean
text: Houston, 12. Right at the end of the reports on Apollo 12, we changed the antennas. Did you want to relay some stuff up between that and the election in Houston? If so, would you repeat it?

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Yes, I got several paragraphs in there. Let me start over again and I'll read it on down to where - the election in Houston. World attention is on the flight of Apollo 12. The Soviet Union held the crew as courageous; and Tass, the official Soviet news agency, reported the start of the mission in a brief factual report in both of its Russian and foreign language reports. Czechoslovak television carried live coverage of the lift-off, complete with explanation of technical details. In West Germany, all radio and television networks carried the launch live, as did the Japanese Broadcasting Company. The launch is being described with such adjectives as spooky and cliff hanging. Even President Nixon, a one-time Navy man himself, admitted he had some anxious moments but added, I'm really proud of those three men up there. And weather is a big news item in Houston where temperatures are expected to dip into the 20's tonight, and there was a fairly heavy frost in the neighbourhood last night. And then we picked up with the voting, which I guess you got.

speaker: Bean
text: Roger-Roger. Thank you. [Long pause.]

speaker: Weitz
text: And I got a Flight Plan update when you have a chance.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay, Dick. At 30:30, we call for a waste water dump, which is back to our normal procedure of dumping down to 25 per cent on that one. And at 31:30, want to start a charge on battery Alpha. Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. We copy.

speaker: Conrad
text: Waste water dump 30:30, 25 per cent. Battery A charge, 31:30.

speaker: Weitz
text: Roger. [Long pause.]

speaker: Weitz
text: 12, Houston. Your PCO 2 sensor is powered through a circuit breaker on panel 5. If you haven't already checked it, would you check Transducer Pressure Group 2; Main Alpha circuit breaker?

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Wait one. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: They're all in, Houston.

speaker: Weitz
text: Thank you.

speaker: Bean
text: Houston, Apollo 12. How far out are we now?

speaker: Weitz
text: Stand by and I'll find out for you, Al. [Pause.]

speaker: Weitz
text: 12, Houston. Not quite halfway at a 110,000 [nautical] miles [204,000 km].

speaker: Bean
text: Roger.

speaker: Weitz
text: 12, Houston. Omni Delta, please.

speaker: Weitz
text: 12, Houston. We'll continue to manage your antenna here until you tell us that you're ready to take control of them. And I have a consumables update for you.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. We're eating breakfast, so we'll let you manage them for a while longer, and I'm ready to copy the update.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. The update was at 26:50; your total RCS is 83.2; reading Alpha through Delta, we have 80.5, 86.0, 80.8, 85.4. Your H 2 is 87.8 and 85.6; O 2 is 87.0 and 87.1. Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. 12 copies.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Weitz
text: Go ahead, 12.

speaker: Conrad
text: You got anything more to add to what happened yesterday? We've been sitting up here chuckling again this morning about it.

speaker: Weitz
text: Stand by and I'll get a recap on it, Pete.

speaker: Weitz
text: 12, Houston. Nothing new to report. It's - they're still considering it from two, three aspects, but nothing firm yet.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. [Long pause.]

speaker: Weitz
text: 12, Houston. We've got a half dozen or so scores of all games in progress, if you're interested.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Go ahead.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Final score, Syracuse beat Navy 15 to nothing; in the third quarter, Yale is leading Princeton 14 to 7; in the first quarter, Texas 21, TCU nothing. In the third quarter, Houston's ahead of North Carolina State 34 to 7; in the third quarter, Michigan State is leading Minnesota 7 to nothing; and that big game in the Big 10, in the third quarter, it's now Ohio State 40 and Purdue 7.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Thank you.

speaker: Gordon
text: [Garble] Paul, this is Dick. I understand that the University of Washington's homecoming's this weekend; will you wish them well for me, please?

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Sure will. We'll pass that on.

speaker: Conrad
text: Sounds like I should have [clearing throat] wished Princeton well a little earlier; maybe it's not too late.

speaker: Weitz
text: No, it's only in the first quarter. Maybe it will still work.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Bean
text: And I guess Texas doesn't need any help.

speaker: Weitz
text: Apparently not.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Pete Conrad is a graduate of Princeton. Dick Gordon a graduate of the University of Washington and Al Bean is University of Texas graduate.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 28 hours, 42 minutes. Apollo 12 is 111,436 nautical miles [206,379 km] from Earth; velocity, 4,525 feet per second [1,379 m/s].

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 28 hours, 50 minutes. This is a quiet time as the crew has breakfast...

speaker: Weitz
text: Hello, 12; Houston. We're not trying to press you, but we've got your uplinks and your PADs ready whenever you're ready.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay [clearing throat]. We'll give you the computer right now, and - and Al will be ready to copy the PAD in just a second.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. And also, for information, the burn attitude for MCC-2 will also be a good attitude for P52 and for all your star checks, if you want to come out of PTC and just go right to that attitude.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. That sounds good. Ready to copy, and the computer is yours. It's in P00 and Accept, and Al's ready to copy.

speaker: Weitz
text: Rog. It's MCC-2, SPS G&N: 63284, plus 0.96, minus 0.25, 030:52:43.68, minus 0060.1, minus 0012.6, plus 0005.6, 034, 095, 333. The Noun 44 blocks are not applicable; 0061.7, 0:09, 0057.2. Sextant star 22, 150.5, 30.9. Your boresight star is Vega, 036, up 250, 0 deflection, up and down that is - correction, left and right. The rest of the PAD is NA. Your GDC align stars are Sirius, 15; Rigel, 12. The angles are 256, 152, 069; no ullage; LM weight, 33585. Over.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 29 hours, 2 minutes. We are in contact with the crew passing up some PADs for the midcourse correction. Here's that conversation.

speaker: Weitz
text: That's all of Charlie, Al. [Long pause.]

speaker: Weitz
text: 12, Houston. The computer's yours.

speaker: Bean
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 29 hours, 16 minutes. We're a little less than 1 minute away from the time when Apollo 12 will be equal distance between the Earth and the Moon. At 29 hours, 16 minutes, 53 seconds; Apollo 12 will be 112,899 nautical miles [209,089 km] from the Earth and from the Moon.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Mark, equal distance. And the velocity is 4,470 feet per second [1,362 m/s]. Midcourse Correction number 2 will be performed at an elapsed time of 30 hours, 52 minutes, 44 seconds. Duration of the Service Propulsion System burn will be 8.8 seconds. Delta V , 61.7 feet per second [18.8 m/s]. This maneuver will take Apollo 12 off the free-return trajectory, put it on the hybrid trajectory. And make its closest approach to the Moon, if it does not burn Lunar Orbit Insertion, 60 nautical miles [111 km]. On the free-return, Apollo 12's closest approach was approximately 1,800 nautical miles [3,300 km]. However, on this hybrid trajectory, closest approach without Lunar Orbit Insertion will be 60 nautical miles.

speaker: Weitz
text: 12, Houston. You want some more ball scores, Dick, or are you busy?

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Sorry, Pete; it didn't work. The final score was Yale 17, Princeton l4. And for Al, Texas is leading TCU at the half 24 to 7; Washington, they haven't started on the West Coast. In the fourth quarter, fourth quarter that is, Pitt is leading Army 12 to 6. Dave's next to me; he just cringed at that. A final, Penn State beat Maryland 48 to nothing. Final, Houston beat North Carolina State 34 to 13. Here's a big one. In the third quarter, Mississippi is leading Tennessee 31 to nothing. The final in the Ohio State-Purdue game, Ohio State on top, 42 to l4. Minnesota beat Michigan State 14 to 10. In the first quarter, Arkansas is leading SMU l4 to 12. At half, Rice is leading A&M 7 to nothing. And that's all we have for now.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. Appreciate it very much. Thank you.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: And Dave Scott, the backup crew commander, has joined Paul Weitz at the CapCom console. Dave who cringed at that score, is a graduate of the Military Academy.

speaker: Weitz
text: Hello, 12; Houston. You're Go for MCC-2.

speaker: Gordon
text: Apollo 12. Roger.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, Apollo 12. The LM/CSM Delta-P is plus 0.7.

speaker: Weitz
text: Houston. Roger.

speaker: Weitz
text: 12, Houston. I have some High-Gain angles for you for the burn.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. Go.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. That will be pitch minus 85, yaw plus 28, and when you get to the burn attitude, would you give us narrow beam width, please?

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Pitch minus 85, yaw plus 28, and while we're in the burn attitude, go to narrow beam width.

speaker: Weitz
text: Roger. [Pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: And as soon as we roll around on this one to the right roll angle, we'll be going into the P52, Houston.

speaker: Weitz
text: Houston. Roger.

speaker: Weitz
text: 12, Houston. Give us Omni Bravo, please.

speaker: Weitz
text: Hello, 12, Houston. Over. [Long pause.]

speaker: Weitz
text: Hello, Apollo 12, Houston. Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead there, Houston.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay, on this - You've got a pretty tight LM, and it is going to have to be purged some. We have got two options. The Flight Plan calls for a CSM purge at 36 hours. The other option is to vent the LM down now. Instead of doing that, the pros and cons are that the cabin purge, the CSM cabin purge takes longer, and does slightly perturb the post-burn tracking. Now, all of other things being equal, and if it meets with your approval, we would like to request that you vent the LM down now. Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Roger. How far do you want it vented?

speaker: Weitz
text: This is Houston. You are broken. Say again.

speaker: Conrad
text: How far do you want it vented?

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. We would like to vent to a Delta-P of about 1.5 to 1.6. This should take about 30 to 45 minutes to go from the present 0.7 to those values. Over.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, okay. Are you looking at the DSKY?

speaker: Weitz
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. There's the torquing angles. Do you copy?

speaker: Weitz
text: We have only got one so far. There they come. We have them, Dick.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. Torquing on my mark. [Pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Mark.

speaker: Weitz
text: Got it.

speaker: Weitz
text: Hello, Apollo 12, Houston. I have a status report on the Phoenix 200 if you want it, Pete.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Al Unser is leading after 59 laps. Mario Andretti is second. Bobby Unser is third. A. J. Foyt was forced out of the race. My information doesn't indicate when. He was running with the leaders and his car was damaged in a collision. There were no injuries.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger-Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 29 hours, 55 minutes. Apollo 12's distance now is 114,559 nautical miles [212,163 km]; velocity, 4,405 feet per second [1,343 m/s]. We are 56½ minutes away from the midcourse maneuver and we should have television coverage during this maneuver. We are scheduled - the start of TV is at an elapsed time of 30 hours, 25 minutes. That's 4:47 pm Central Standard Time. We will have the capability to pick up slightly earlier than that, and that if the crew decides they would like to come in a little early as they did yesterday.

speaker: Bean
text: Houston. Apollo 12. The lithium hydroxide canister change out has been done on time.

speaker: Weitz
text: Roger 12. Thank you, and your platform looks real good. No updates.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay.

speaker: Weitz
text: Hello, Apollo 12, Houston. A hot flash on the Phoenix 200. Al Unser and Mario Andretti collided with each other and Bobby Unser is now in the lead.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Very good.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 30 hours, 4 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. We're apparently having a change over in flight control teams in Mission Control. At the present time Pete Frank is manning the Flight Director's console replacing Gerry Griffin and members of his Orange Flight Control team are taking their places at their respective consoles. As was reported earlier, Midcourse Correction 2 is currently scheduled for Ground Elapsed Time of 30 hours, 52 minutes, 43 seconds. This is done with Service Propulsion System engine. Time of burn - or burn duration - 8.8 seconds. Before this burn, Apollo 12 will be yawing around 168 degrees making the burn itself close to retrograde. Without the burn, or if we did not do this Midcourse Correction 2 burn, the point of closest approach for Apollo 12 with the moon would be 714.9 nautical miles [1,324.0 km]. With this...

speaker: Weitz
text: Hello, 12, Houston. A correction to my last update on the Phoenix 200. That collision was between Marlo Andretti and Bobby Unser. Al Unser still has the lead.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Very good. Do you know how far along they are in the race?

speaker: Weitz
text: No, we don't know right now, Pete. We will get it for you.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: With the burn itself performed as programmed, it should bring Apollo 12 within 60 nautical miles [111 km] as a point of a closest approach to the Moon. At 30 hours, 6 minutes into the flight of Apollo 12; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 30 hours, 10 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. We currently show the Apollo 12 spacecraft at an altitude of 115,165 nautical miles [213,286 km] above the Earth. Its velocity now reads 4,382 feet per second [1,336 m/s]. At Mission Control Center we're currently configured for receipt of our next television transmission, which is nominally expected some 15 minutes from this time. This is Apollo Control Houston standing by.

speaker: Weitz
text: 12, Houston. Can you give us a readout on the LM/Command Module Delta-P now, please?

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Just a second, let me go up there. I had a clock running for a while, and I was just going to check it in a minute.

speaker: Weitz
text: We just want to get a check on the rate.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. It's about 1.25 to 1.3 right now.

speaker: Weitz
text: Roger, understand. And here on the ground, we're configured for TV.

speaker: Conrad
