text: Okay. We're just setting it up in here, and the - we'll go back to LM tunnel Vent. You want to go to 16, right?

speaker: Weitz
text: That's affirmative. Between 1.5 and 1.6.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. It's back at Vent.

speaker: Weitz
text: Roger. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, you want the TV now?

speaker: Weitz
text: Stand by, Pete.

speaker: Weitz
text: While we're getting a reading on the TV, Pete, they stopped the race in Phoenix after 84 laps because of rain, if you can believe it; and they're going to wait a while and then restart when it slacks off.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Thank you.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 30 hours, 15 minutes into the flight of Apollo 12. Jerry Carr is in the Mission Control Center now replacing Paul Weitz as our Capsule Communicator. Meanwhile, we're standing by for receipt of television transmission in just about any time. At 30 hours, 15 minutes into the flight; this is Apollo Control.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. We're ready for a TV whenever you are, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We'll be coming at you in just a second.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. [Pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Apollo Control, Houston. You heard that response from commander Pete Conrad indicating that they should be coming at us with the television.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. We're giving you the TV. We'll be coming up Vox, and we'll let you watch what happens during the burn.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: We're receiving television, now.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, I guess I'm on Vox now. I've got to stow this helmet stowage bag. I'll stick it in this container A7 here.

speaker: Bean
text: No, not in A7.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Dick, I don't think your Vox is set quite right yet. Need some more sensitivity. Use the [garble] plug all the way.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Conrad
text: Let me get the big book.

speaker: Gordon
text: Pre-burn checks; 30 hours, 52 minutes, 43.68 seconds.

speaker: Gordon
text: Plus 5.6.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Got the TV yet, Houston?

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, 12. Looks beautiful.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We're just going through the pre-burn checklist at this time. Al's down in the bilge stowing some gear for the burn. Dick's in the left-hand couch, and I'm in the center couch right now, and we have the TV mounted so that you can watch the instrument panel and the switches throwing.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, let's see. The clock's in Sync now.

speaker: Gordon
text: They're in Sync 34, 27, and 25.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, do you want us to run the tape recorder during this TV or not?

speaker: Carr
text: Stand by.

speaker: Bean
text: We're concerned about the high bit rate while operating the TV.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. Better run the tape just during the burn.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Bean
text: We had the automatic stop on.

speaker: Conrad
text: Al, would you take the monitor and put it some place for a second? And Dick, hand me the [garble.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Put it over here.

speaker: Conrad
text: [Garble] tool E, so I can go up and check the Delta-P in the LM again.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, yes.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, we've got just a little bit to go.

speaker: Gordon
text: Got all your shoulder straps tucked away where they won't go anywhere?

speaker: Conrad
text: We're at 1.4 on these water bags. Need a drink of water, Dick?

speaker: Gordon
text: Got it.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Gordon
text: Well, let's see, we got to do something with the water gun. Let's stick her down here.

speaker: Conrad
text: Can't, with that thing on, can you?

speaker: Gordon
text: Uh-uh. Not unless it would go in backwards, which it will.

speaker: Conrad
text: That's super.

speaker: Gordon
text: There you go.

speaker: Conrad
text: I'll hold on to tool E. I'm gonna - I'm gonna shut-off the vent a minute anyhow.

speaker: Gordon
text: We're almost there. If the our stowage bag falls off the wall, we're going to have garbage all over the place.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. There's another one.

speaker: Gordon
text: Great Scott.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay.

speaker: Conrad
text: Got the DAP, 11 loaded?

speaker: Gordon
text: DAP's loaded. Rot Control Power, two of them, AC/DC.

speaker: Conrad
text: AC/DC.

speaker: Gordon
text: DET is set.

speaker: Conrad
text: It's set.

speaker: Gordon
text: And we have several choices. You can either go to P40, or we can sit where we are, or you can go over to P00.

speaker: Bean
text: Might as well sat here for a few minutes, I guess, and watch the clock, and see how they do.

speaker: Conrad
text: Deadly TV monitor keeps floating around here. Get her and put her out of the way.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, let me check that LM Delta-P again.

speaker: Conrad
text: No not quite.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Now, weren't we flowing some O 2 before? Wonder why we're doing it now?

speaker: Gordon
text: We haven't opened anything. You got any of the vents open down there, Al?

speaker: Bean
text: Let me check. I don't think so. I don't think we're flowing anything.

speaker: Gordon
text: Everything's closed in here and the Delta-P...

speaker: Conrad
text: No, it's in tunnel vent, I'm venting the LM down.

speaker: Bean
text: No, not a thing is venting as far as I can see.

speaker: Gordon
text: Oh, you just may be making up some in the cabin.

speaker: Conrad
text: Do you see anything loose, now?

speaker: Bean
text: I think I've got it all stowed.

speaker: Conrad
text: Very good.

speaker: Bean
text: Trouble is, some of those things hang up in under the seats and float so still that you don't see them. Think they're part of the seat or something. You're not used to looking in those places on Earth.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We got 30 minutes to the burn.

speaker: Bean
text: All righty.

speaker: Conrad
text: Set 10 minutes on your little ding-ding timer there, will you, Al. And then fasten it to that tunnel vent so I don't forget. it.

speaker: Bean
text: All right.

speaker: Gordon
text: Give all these circuit breakers a quick cage [garble].

speaker: Conrad
text: Go for the burn, time is 9 seconds; to shut-down is burn time plus one, and we trim x to within two tenths, less than 2. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Apollo 12 now 115,735 nautical miles in altitude. That's essentially Pete Conrad and Dick Gordon talking back and forth within the spacecraft. That's Pete Conrad wearing the ball cap that you're seeing on your screen.

speaker: Gordon
text: Did we ever dump the waste water down to 25 per cent?

speaker: Conrad
text: No. We can do that right now. Okay, waste water dump coming up. Hey, Al, you want to check - want to watch the gauge?

speaker: Bean
text: Okay.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Conrad
text: And Houston, we're going to dump the waste water down to 25 per cent at this time.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, 12. We're standing by.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, check - Okay, vent valve is closed, and I'm going to dump A.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay.

speaker: Gordon
text: There you go.

speaker: Bean
text: You got 50 per cent, around there, about 49.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Gordon
text: [Garble.]

speaker: Bean
text: Huh?

speaker: Gordon
text: I need the Auto dump vent B system book.

speaker: Bean
text: Pete's got it.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, I'm going to - I'm reading 1 point - Houston, I'm reading 1.5 on the LM Delta-P now, but I think I'll let it go to 1.6 because the gauge has about a tenth error in it when it's equal.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay, Pete, that sounds fine.

speaker: Gordon
text: How is the waste water doing, Al?

speaker: Bean
text: It's doing good. It's just down to about 45.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. Say, how's the focus on the TV? We usually don't become focused on this monitor up here.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hey, Houston, what do you think of the hats our boss presented with us?

speaker: Carr
text: We were just going to ask you for a little fashion show here, troops.

speaker: Gordon
text: Well, we've got a space - qualified beta clothes and all those good things.

speaker: Carr

text: Apollo Control, Houston; 31 hours, 3 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. MCC-2, the burn, was some 9 seconds in duration. A preliminary evaluation following this burn would put Apollo 12's point of closest approach to the Moon at 64 nautical miles [119 km].

speaker: Conrad
text: Hey, Houston, if it's all right with you, we will go ahead and secure the TV.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay, 12. You guys are looking real fine. That was a nice burn.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Carr
text: Our compliments to your cameraman.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay.

speaker: Bean
text: Yes. You have to help us on the focus. We can frame it and everything up here, but the focus is difficult to see up in this monitor.

speaker: Carr
text: Al, if that's you talking, you're still not too good. Yes, the focus was real fine the last half of the show there, and right there when we were fiddling with it, it went bad and then you went through a good focal point and off to a fairly reasonably one, and it seemed to improve later on then.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: We have lost our television picture at this time. We now read 31 hours, 4 minutes into the flight of Apollo 12. Coming up momentarily in the MSC News Center, will be a change of shift briefing with Flight Director, Gerry Griffin and Capsule Communicator, Paul Weitz.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay, I think the problem is if I zoom in on something, it's difficult to focus. I went back and was not zoomed in, and then it's a fairly easy situation.

speaker: Carr
text: That's affirm. It seemed to be pretty nice.

speaker: Bean
text: Thanks, Houston for your help. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. We're starting the data dump now. [Pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: We copied you, Jerry - you can see us dumping now.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: And, Houston, we're planning to make a dump now. Is that okay?

speaker: Carr
text: Say again, 12.

speaker: Conrad
text: We're planning a urine dump now, if that's okay. [Pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Yes. No problem, 12. Go ahead.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 31 hours, 8 minutes now into the flight Apollo 12. The change of shift news conference is due to start in the news center at approximately 2 minutes ...

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. Did you do a fuel cell O 2 purge before the burn?

speaker: Conrad
text: Negative. We didn't.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. We'd just as soon you'd delay it until your next opportunity at 40 hours.

speaker: MS
text: [Garble.]

speaker: Conrad
text: ...40 hours. Thank you. Well, we're sorry we missed that.

speaker: Carr
text: No sweat, 12.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. It looks like your rates are low enough now to start PTC; we notice your CMC Mode switch is in Hold position and you should be in Auto.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Gordon
text: There she goes, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, 12. [Pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, this is 12. Do you want us to save all jets or just work in this 30-degree deadband until our sleep period?

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. You can turn them off now if you want to.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. I'm just saving a couple that may fire on us or something, huh.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead, Jer.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Go S-band antenna to Omni and Omni Bravo.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. Omni to Omni Bravo.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston, at 31 hours, 34 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. Apollo 12 is currently 118,620 nautical miles [219,684 km] away from Earth. It's velocity now reads 4,235 feet per second [1,291 m/s]...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. Although we are looking at a relatively blank Flight Plan for the remainder of the evening and expect a quiet evening, we will leave the release line up live at least for a while. If we continue to have long intervals between conversations with the crew, we will take the release line down and play back the tapes at periodic intervals. At 31 hours, 37 minutes into the flight; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. Go.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Battery vent is - Battery compartment has been vented and we started charging Bat A at 31:37.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, we just got a Master Alarm with nothing on the panel. Got any idea what that might have been?

speaker: Carr
text: Stand by, 12. We'll start checking.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. We don't see much out of the ordinary, Pete. We are on a low bit rate right now, and we will be in high bit rate shortly where we can look at things a lot more closely. About the only suspicious item is your O 2 flow rate is just a shade high, but we see nothing else.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We're venting the - the urine system - that new one, and we're just letting it run. I'll go shut her off.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Looking at the Earth down there, Houston, it looks like you are littler than a golf ball at arm's length now. Sure looks pretty though. The terminator looks like it's - it's kind of hard to tell from this distance - looks like it's passing somewhere just west of Tallahassee.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. It's just getting dark out here now.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Your accumulator cycled just about the time you got that Master Alarm, so it may have been an O 2 flow high, and you may have just had a flicker on your matrix panel.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 31 hours, 48 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. We currently read a velocity on Apollo 12 at 4,214 feet per second [1,284 m/s]. Its present altitude, 119,204 nautical miles [220,766 km].

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, Houston, we have settled down to a normal routine during the day.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, 12. We'll have some scores for you shortly.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Houston. Do you read 12?

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. Reading you loud and clear on voice.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Did you get the transmission a little while ago?

speaker: Carr
text: We got a few words and a little bit of music, and then it quit.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. I think you lost our antenna about then.

speaker: Conrad
text: We're trying all these things we didn't have in Gemini, like toothpaste and shaving and - We are really having a ball up here.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Carr
text: All dressed up and no place to go.

speaker: Conrad
text: Oh, we're going someplace. We can see it getting bigger and bigger all the time. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. I have a little sports news for you.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. The Phoenix 200 is still in a hold status; they apparently couldn't get past the thunderstorms. And here are some scores.

speaker: Conrad
text: We were...

speaker: Carr
text: ...Go ahead.

speaker: Conrad
text: No, go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Some scores: Texas Tech 41, Baylor 7 - these are all finals - Texas 69, TCU 7; Arkansas 28, SMU 5; Rice 7, the Aggies 6; Northwestern 30, Indiana 27; Michigan 51, Iowa 6; Wisconsin 55, Illinois 14; Ole Miss 38, Tennessee 0; Missouri 40 and Iowa State 13. And the scores on the West Coast are starting to come in now. Dick, you'll be happy to hear Washington and Southern Cal are tied 7 to 7 in the third quarter, and Oregon is - in the third quarter - is ahead of oh - UCLA 10 to 7.

speaker: Gordon
text: Jerry, I - makes me happy but I'll bet it doesn't make you happy, does it?

speaker: Carr
text: Game's not over, Dick.

speaker: Gordon
text: We've been trying to look at the United States through the monocular, and it just looks like most of the States is covered with clouds. Are you having bad weather generally over the country?

speaker: Carr
text: We'll have to take a look at an overall map, but here in Houston, it's been CAVU all day and beautiful, a wonderful, clear fall day.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. Dick, I got bad news for you. A final: USC 16, Washington 7.

speaker: Gordon
text: Boy, you sure changed that in a hurry, didn't you.

speaker: Carr
text: I didn't want to give you too long to gloat over that one.

speaker: Gordon
text: I think you were sandbagging me, Jerry. I was about to bet you.

speaker: Carr
text: I should've waited. [Pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. We currently show Apollo 12 at an altitude of 119,954 nautical miles [222,155 km].

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. I've got a weather map here for the United States. All up through the northeast part of the country it looks like it's either overcast or broken. And then in the Southeast and in the South and up through about the panhandle of Texas down into Florida it's all clear. And then, moving on further west, you get into New Mexico, Arizona, California, and you begin to pick up overcast skies again, all the way from Montana all the way down to Arizona. Montana has got a few broken and scattered clouds in the eastern side and then it's pretty bad over on the western side.

speaker: Gordon
text: Yes, we - we could - We were having a hard time picking out exactly where we were looking at. Even with the monocular everything is now - tends to be brown - and having a hard time picking out the land from the water, but it seems like that part of the country that we can see is pretty well covered with clouds.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. It looks like the whole West Coast is socked in [Pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. The weather system is a great big high sitting down over, oh, Gulfport - Biloxi area, so that's why we are so clear down in the Southeast. We have a weak high up around the four corners area of Utah, Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona. And then everywhere else is just bad news.

speaker: Conrad
text: I see.

speaker: Conrad
text: How are our families doing, Jerry?

speaker: Carr
text: Haven't talked to them, but I'll make a few calls and give you some answers.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Appreciate that every day if you could.

speaker: Carr
text: We'll do her. Everybody is probably at supper right now, so probably catch them all at home.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. We are at 32 hours, 10 minutes into the flight.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston. We are just looking out of the window now and we were all talking about old project FSMOE. You remember that?

speaker: Carr
text: I guess that one doesn't compute, 12.

speaker: Gordon
text: Say again.

speaker: Carr
text: That one doesn't compute.

speaker: Gordon
text: Project FSMOE? Full-Scale Mock-up Of Earth?

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hard to tell which one we've got out the window.

speaker: Carr
text: Is it blue or gray?

speaker: Gordon
text: Pretty blue and white [Long pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Hey, Jer, somebody's probably already said this before, but - That place looks like an oasis down there.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Dick.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 32 hours, 17 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. The Apollo 12 spacecraft at this time 120,348 nautical miles [222,884 km] above the Earth. It is now traveling at 4,172 feet per second [1,272 m/s]. At this time we will take down the live release line and come up at periodic intervals with taped replays. We expect relatively quiet period with regard to conversation between our capsule communicator, Jerry Carr, and the crew. At 32 hours, 18 minutes into the flight of Apollo 12; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston, at 32 hours, 42 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. Since our last report, we have had no further conversation with the Apollo 12 crew, no doubt who are relaxing at this time after an active day and half in space. Mission Control Center now at this time, they - what would appear to be a somewhat powered-down mode? Very little activity aside from the individual flight controllers looking at their displays; perhaps one or two having sandwiches being brought in to them. At present we show an altitude above the Earth for Apollo 12 at 121,393 nautical miles [224,820 km]. Apollo 12's velocity now reads 4,134 feet per second [1,260 m/s]. And at 32 hours, 43 minutes; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. Go.

speaker: Conrad
text: What's your preliminary look at the midcourse show?

speaker: Carr
text: Stand by a second, Pete. While they're ginning up the answer, got some nice warm words for you on your SPS burn. Evaluation shows that your ISP is within one tenth of a second, and your thrust is within 20 pounds on that engine so you got a real hummer there.

speaker: Conrad
text: Very good. I guess we can thank Mr. Thibodaux [NASA propulsion expert] for that one.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hey, Jerry, it says in the Flight Plan to perform housekeeping chores. We're having a devil of a time finding a housekeeper up here.

speaker: Carr
text: Who's the Junior man, Dick?

speaker: Gordon
text: He's on the Exer-Genie right now. He thinks he made Captain already, but he's got a surprise.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Your next midcourse looks like about a foot per second.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. So I guess maybe we won't need to do any of those, huh?

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Looks real good for here anyway. Another little gem of wisdom we got for you here, when you entered PTC, you collapsed your deadband when you used Verb 37 Enter to get the P00, so just as a little helpful reminder, we want you to remember that when you come out, you're going to zap to your Noun 22 attitude as soon as you activate your jets unless you come out in SCS.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Understand.

speaker: Carr
text: We figured you already knew it, but we wanted to show you how smart we were.

speaker: Conrad
text: Good, thank you [Long pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, 12. What do you think now? I just redid a Verb 79.

speaker: Conrad
text: Will that do it?

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. You just cured it.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. I guess we called a P21 in there or something; we got curious to see how far out we were and that must have collapsed it.

speaker: Carr
text: That's affirmative, that's what you did.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 33 hours, and 9 minutes now into the flight Apollo 12. At present the Apollo 12 spacecraft is 122,405.6 nautical miles [226,695.2 km] above the Earth. Its velocity steadily decreasing now reads 4,098 feet per second [1,249 m/s]. Since our last status report of some 20 minutes ago we've had only brief conversations with the crew of Apollo 12...

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Dick, you listening?

speaker: Conrad
text: No, Dick's not on the horn.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. How about Al, is he listening?

speaker: Bean
text: I'm listening, yes.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay, Al. I checked home for you and Sue got back this afternoon from the Cape. She said to say yesterday was a pretty exciting day for her, kind of wet, too. And she wanted to let you know that she had attended a birthday dinner party that was honoring Vice President Agnew yesterday and had a real fine time. She says her Mom and Dad are there with her at home now. They just finished dinner, and the kids are headed for bed, and she wishes you Godspeed.

speaker: Bean
text: Thanks, Jerry.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. Pete, I guess Jane and the boys are...

speaker: Conrad
text: Dick's up now.

speaker: Carr
text: Pete, I guess Jane and the boys are out to dinner, I haven't been able to get a hold of them yet. And Dick, you up?

speaker: Gordon
text: Go.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. Barbara says that Barb and Norman and your mother are all there now, and everybody's doing fine, and they've had enough excitement for a while, thanks. And if you don't mind, they just as soon you lay off the spectaculars.

speaker: Gordon
text: Why? What in the world has happened?

speaker: Carr
text: [Laughter.] She said Aunt Dorothy is passing through Houston now, and she called in to say hello, and she said also to let you know that Bill Der Bing is there with them, and he's doing a great job.

speaker: Gordon
text: Very good, thank you.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. The Mr. Thibodaux who is thanked very early in that exchange by Pete Conrad is Mr. Guy Thibodaux who is the Chief of the power and propulsion division at the Manned Spacecraft Center. The reference was an obvious reference with regard to the performance of the engine on Midcourse Correction 2. Bill Der Bing who is referred to later in Jerry Carr's report is also an MSC employee who is a member of the special events office of the Public Affairs. At 33 hours, 15 minutes into the flight; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Houston, 12.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. Go.

speaker: Conrad
text: Say, you know, yesterday we talked to you about this stuff that's all over the windows, and on Dick's rendezvous window - window 2 - We've got some kind of a white deposit that's like a - I don't know, it's like an ash and it's not flush on it, it's built up in little humps and tabs of it sticking out, especially in the upper right-hand corner. What we'd like to do is photograph this for you. We don't have much to do right now. We thought we'd photograph these windows and thought maybe you'd come up with some recommended settings and everything. Seems to me I remember somewhere we had those procedures for photographing windows back in D or something because they were bad.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. We'll get somebody going on that right away.

speaker: Conrad
text: We expect this stuff will be long gone after re-entry.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. We've been kind of dying to ask you too about the ice situation. How long did it take that to sublime off?

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, now, that's a funny thing. The ice was sublimed off, but it's left a white deposit all along the perimeter of the number 1 window, that - that's on the black surface of the outside of that window, and it's up along the side of the window too. It's similar to the same stuff that's on the rendezvous window. Now, the ice that was on the inside of the outer pane in the number 1 window - that's sublimated, too, since we started PTC. We have a - a fine deposit of water droplet; whatever was in the water - has adhered to the window and that's all in streaks and dots and splatters, so we kind of think some of this may have come when - when the tower was jettisoned; we're not sure, and I guess what we want to do is try and photograph this as best we can for you to see - because I haven't heard [garble] before either.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. How long did it take for that outer layer of ice on window 1 to sublime? How long was it before it was gone?

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes, it didn't go until we were finally asleep last night or - we stopped looking at it. It was still there, I think, when we went to bed last night.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Carr
text: 12. Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. The polls are closed now and - soon as we get enough election results to give you a meaningful information here, we will run you up some returns.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. I'm going to run to get a bite to eat right now and your friendly AFD is going to be monitoring the line for you.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger-Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston, at 33 hours, 29 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. Our displays in Mission Control now show the Apollo 12 spacecraft at an altitude of 123,206 nautical miles [228,178 km] above the Earth and now traveling at 4,069 feet per second [1,240 m/s]...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. The election results referenced by CapCom, Jerry Carr, are from the Houston city elections. We will try to pass these along to the crew sometimes later this evening and as you heard in that last comment, Jerry is now out of the Mission Operations Control Room grabbing a bit to eat. At 33 hours, 34 minutes into the flight; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. I've got some words for you on the camera settings.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. Wait 1 [Long pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Step number 1: make sure the Sun is incident to the window but not shining directly into the camera. Step number 2: set the focus at 3 feet, and then do as best you can to hold your camera 3 feet from your target, realizing that this focal length is pretty sensitive to the distance. Your shutter speed is 1/250th. And if you don't have the spotmeter out, use an f-stop of 5.6 and take a picture of each window, and then go to an f-stop of 4 and take one of each window. And if you do have the spotmeter out and want to use that, then the only caution here is to be sure that the spotmeter is focused on the window or the target itself.

speaker: Gordon
text: Understand, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston, with some election news.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. About 10 per cent of the votes are in and counted now, and Mayor Louie Welch is leading his nearest contender, who is Curtis Graves, by 10,000 votes to 3,000; these are approximates. In the six City Council positions that are up for grabs, all the incumbents are leading at this time, and the housing code question in Houston is running about 8,800 for and 6,200 against.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. Thank you.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control Houston. The photo settings passed up were to allow the photography of the white deposits around the spacecraft windows. That was Al Bean talking with Capsule Communicator Jerry Carr.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: We've just picked up another conversation with the Apollo 12 crew and we'll play that for you very shortly.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control Houston at 34 hours, and 4 minutes now into the flight. The Apollo 12 spacecraft is presently 124,563 nautical miles away from earth. Its velocity, continuing to decrease and now reading 4,022 feet per second ...

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: We have a - some little bits of information here on the P23 that you've done so far. Also, it's generated a few questions that we'd like to ask. The first batch that you did showed a Delta-H of 49.2 kilometers, and the second batch showed 24.8 kilometers, and the marks that you took in each batch, in each set, were consistent. And the uncertainty both times was about 4 kilometers, so we've got four questions to ask you which might possibly help us decide which Delta-H to use. Over.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. First question. Did you notice any difference between the horizons on the two batches; in other words, did you select a new horizon the second time?

speaker: Gordon
text: Abso - absolutely, on the first one, they used top of the haze layer; on the second one, the haze layer was hardly discernible, used - what considered the true Earth horizon.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay, Dick, and the second question is - well, you've answered the second question essentially. We wanted to know if you used the same technique, or did you put the star below or above the upper part of the horizon, but that's answered. Next, is - were the stars...

speaker: Gordon
text: Well, Jerry, the reason I...

speaker: Carr
text: Go ahead, Dick.

speaker: Gordon
text: The reason I did that, the second batch, that haze layer was hardly discernible at all, and the Earth's sphere was so sharp at that point, that I used it.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay then, Dick. Then, I guess you're saying then that you liked the second batch better than the first hatch. Is that affirmed? [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. Did you get my last question, Dick? Is - I'm assuming that you liked the second batch better than the first batch then.

speaker: Gordon
text: That's affirmative, it was much sharper, much easier to define the horizon on the second batch.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Dick. We kind of got the impression that the altitude seemed to be a function of the star of magnitude and we're wondering, were the star images pretty well focused?

speaker: Gordon
text: That's affirmative. I didn't seem to notice that. The only thing I can say about the first batch is that they were at the very top of the - of the haze layer where it just starts to turn that very light blue, and I thought it was a lot further away than I expected it to be.

speaker: Carr
text: . Roger, Dick. And last question, was there any noticeable stray light and was it different on each batch?

speaker: Gordon
text: No, the optics appeared to be excellent, they didn't have any problem with stray light whatsoever.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. Thank you, Dick.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control Houston. That was Dick Gordon critiquing with Jerry Carr, the Program 23, the star sighting navigation program onboard the spacecraft. We're now at 34 hours, 12 minutes into the flight and we show Apollo 12 registering at an altitude of 124,872 nautical miles [231,263 km]. Its velocity now reads 4,011 feet per second [1,223 m/s].

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Carr
text: Go ahead, 12.

speaker: Conrad
text: We've been having a little discussion here on this photograph in the windows. We had the exterior color - I presume, really what you wanted was the CEX - HCEX rather than the normal color.

speaker: Carr
text: Stand by a second, Pete; I'll check on it.

speaker: Conrad
text: Well - We were showing for the color exterior, the 368, that we should have shot at a much slower speed, so that prompted us to think you meant us to use the HCEX, and so maybe you'd better clarify that.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. They're checking right now.

speaker: Conrad
text: Thank you.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. While we're looking for that answer for you, I've got an LOI minus 5 flyby PAD - maneuver PAD for you if you want to grab out a form.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Wait one.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We're ready to copy.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. LOI minus 5 flyby, SPS/G&N: 62633, Noun 48, plus 0.90, minus 0.17; Noun 33, 078:27:16.61, Noun 81, plus 0068.4, minus 0206.0, plus 0579.3; roll, pitch, and yaw is 052, 217, 338; Noun 44 is NA, NA. Delta-V T 0618.6, 1:26, 0613.6; sextant 32, 184.6, 38.6; boresight is NA, NA, NA; Noun 61, plus 07.38, minus 169.95, 1165.9, 36231; GET 0.5 g's, 145:52:20; GDC Align stars are Sirius and Rigel. Roll is 256, pitch 152, yaw 069. Ullage, none. Other burn is SPS docked. The LM weight is 33585. Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. LOI minus 5, SPS/G&N, and I may have screwed up on this [garble] 62633, plus 0.90, minus 0.17, plus 078:27:16.61; Noun 81, plus 0068.4, minus 0206.0, plus 0579.3; roll, pitch, and yaw 052, 217, 338; Noun 44, NA, NA. Delta-V T 0618.6, 1:26, 0613.6; 32, 184.6, 38.6, NA, NA, NA; Noun 61, plus 007.38, 1165.9, 36231, 145:52:20. The stars Sirius and Rigel, roll 256, 152, 069, ullage none, SPS docked, LM weight 33585.

speaker: Carr
text: That's affirmative, 12.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That was Commander Pete Conrad taking down the T minus 5 hour...

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Houston; 12. Do you read?

speaker: Carr
text: 12, this is Houston. Your read back was correct.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Very good. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Pete, you guessed us right. The data we sent you was based on HCEX film. So that is what you ought to use.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Thank you.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston, at 34 hours, 33 minutes since lift-off. Apollo 12 is now 125,686 nautical miles [232,770 km] away from Earth. Velocity now reads 3,982 feet per second [1,214 m/s]. We've had discussions with the crew who asked about the type of film to be used in their window photography. Additionally, we passed up one of the contingency PADs to them for storage in their computer...

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. Can we put our headsets back on now?

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes. That's Dick's music.

speaker: Gordon
text: They're friends of yours. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. You might consider taking a stereo pair with that camera on the window.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We'll give her a try.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. You heard the reference from Jerry Carr jokingly saying can we put our headsets back on. That was Pete Conrad responding that it's Dick's music. At 34 hours, 42 minutes of the flight, this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Carr
text: Go ahead, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Does it look like we are going to have to reinitiate the purge or not on the CSM?

speaker: Carr
text: Pete, dumping the tunnel down to 1.6 eliminated the requirement for it.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Very good.[Pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Hey, Pete. If you're looking for something to do, we got a geology pop quiz for you.

speaker: Conrad
text: [Laugh] Oh, thanks a lot.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead, give it to them.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. Go.

speaker: Conrad
text: We think we have the S-IVB in sight. We've - had a - an object which is in the same place all the time and appears to be tumbling. We've had it ever since yesterday, and it just seems to be tagging along with us, so I guess that's the S-IVB. It's usually out our center hatch window when our roll angle is about 35 degrees right now. Maybe that'll give you a clue, and somebody can figure out if that's what we've really looking at.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston, at 34 hours, 56 minutes now into the flight. Apollo 12 is presently at altitude of 126,547 nautical miles [234,365 km]. Its velocity now reads 3,953 feet per second [1,205 m/s]...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. That was Jerry Carr offering Pete Conrad and Al Bean a geology pop quiz if they wanted something to do and we literally could do that in Mission Control Center now. Astronaut/Geologist, Jack Schmitt has joined Jerry Carr in the Control Center and in fact was a source of inspiration for Jerry Carr's offering. You heard Dick Gordon, Command Module Pilot, who will not go to the lunar surface, suggest that we give them the quiz. That was Pete Conrad who reported sighting an object out the window, which he thought, might be the third stage of the Saturn V launch vehicle. At 34 hours, 59 minutes now in the flight of Apollo 12; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control Houston at 35 hours and 29 minutes since lift-off. We've had no voice contact or communications with the Apollo 12 crew since our last announcement. However, we currently show an altitude of 127,808 nautical miles [236,700 km] for Apollo 12. Its velocity now reads 3,910 feet per second [1,192 m/s]. So at 35 hours, 29 minutes; this is Apollo Control, Houston continuing to monitor.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 36 hours, 6 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. Since our last communication, we have not attempted to contact the crew nor have they called the Mission Control Center. Our present altitude, as shown on our displays, reads 129,204 nautical miles [239,286 km] above the Earth. Velocity now reading 3,862 feet per second [1,177 m/s] for Apollo 12. So at this time we continue with a very quite phase of the mission and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: 12,Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. That thing you saw off the hatch, at a roll of 35 degrees, we figured there's probably three possible answers. Number 1: it could be the S-IVB, or possibly a SLA panel, or it could be the backup crew flying trail on you.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Actually we have two objects out there. One's not anywhere near as bright as the other, so I think the real bright one's the S-IVB and the other one's probably a SLA panel. They're about 20 degrees apart. And as far as the backup crew goes, tell them we'll meet them on the back side of the Moon.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. Best as we can tell down here now - best as we can tell down here now, the S-IVB should be near Denebola, and if it's SLA panels - correction, what you are saying now ought to be near Enif; is that correct?

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes, it's near Enif.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. And the words here are that the S-IVB is about 180 degrees away, near Denebola.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. I wonder what that could be.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. We'll go back to our drawing board.

speaker: Conrad
text: The object's very bright - The object's very bright, and it's obviously something that's tumbling. It's tumbling about 1½ rev's per second, or at least it's flashing at us about that. And Dick - Dick is going to tell you what star it's near. He's messing with his chart right now.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. We're standing by.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Pete, as best as we can tell, looking at things down here, on those SLA panels, we assume that they weren't imparted any great amount of Delta-V, like anything more than 1 or so feet per second when they separated. Your SLA panels would probably only be about 300 miles away from you right now.

speaker: Conrad
text: That could be true but, gee whiz, when we turned around, I saw one of those SLA panels leaving the area at a high rate of speed; it looked to me like it was leaving us pretty - pretty rapid clip, like it got a lot more than a foot per second or so.

speaker: Carr
text: Well, since we don't really have any idea how they left or what their trajectory could be, it's kind of tough really to say just what the heck that could be.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. We'll assume it's friendly anyway, okay?

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. If it makes any noises, it's probably just wind in the rigging.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Understand.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 36 hours, 36 minutes into the flight of Apollo 12. Apollo 12 is presently 130,289 nautical miles [241,295 km] above the Earth. It's velocity now reading 3,825 feet per second [1,166 m/s]. Capsule communicator Jerry Carr has been passing along to Apollo 12 some of the Mission Operations Control Room insights as to the tumbling object, which the crew reported seeing earlier. We will play that conversation to you now.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. So we have no definite agreement as to what the crew may have sighted. Our best estimates place the S-IVB to be about 2,500 nautical miles [4,600 km] away from Apollo 12 at this time. The SLA panels that were not attached at the time of the S-IVB as slingshot maneuver. A smiling Dave Scott was in the control room when they remarked about the back up crew following was made. That was Dick Gordon from the spacecraft who makes the assumption that whatever they saw must be friendly. At 36 hours, 40 minutes into the flight; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 37 hours, 26 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. The Apollo 12 spacecraft is now 132,125 nautical miles [244,696 km] away from Earth. It's velocity now reads 3,763.7 feet per second [1,147.2 m/s]. Since our last announcement, we have had no further contact with the Apollo 12 crew and quiet studied atmosphere predominates in the Mission Control Center. Although you saw the midcourse correction burn performed on television earlier today, and knew that it was performed as advertised, we will pass along the official statistics from the Flight Dynamics Officer's log. The Time Of Ignition for that burn was 30 hours, 52 minutes and 43 seconds Ground Elapsed Time. Its Delta velocity was 61.8 feet per second [18.8 m/s] and burn duration was 8.82 seconds. Although the requirement for additional midcourse corrections is considered very slight at this time the Flight Dynamics Officer will continue to evaluate his vectors and the option will remain open at least for the time being. At 37 hours, 28 minutes into the flight of Apollo 12; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Carr
text: Hello, 12. Go.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. Go.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Huh?

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, if you haven't got anything to do down there, how about telling us where - what longitude line the terminator of the Moon is on.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, 12. It's in work. Sure you don't want that geology pop quiz?

speaker: Conrad
text: Al's all eager. He says give it to him. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 37 hours, 59 minutes. At the present time Apollo 12 is at an altitude of 133,311 nautical miles [246,892 km] from the Earth, traveling at a speed of 3,724 feet per second [1,135 m/s]...

speaker: Bean
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. Go.

speaker: Bean
text: Roger. We're getting close enough to the Moon now so that, even with the - the monocular, the Moon looks a lot like these photographs that you see taken from many of the observatories that are around the center. We were looking at it through the sextant a minute ago, and it really looks spectacular. It's starting to take on less of a silver color and more of a gray color when you look at it up close.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Al. Watch those color descriptions.

speaker: Bean
text: You said it.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. We're working on that question of yours. Also, it's about time now to terminate battery A charge. Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. That's in work.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: That terminator longitude is between 7 and 8 degrees east. Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Thank you.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control. We're getting a bit of noisy communications here as the spacecraft rotates through one Omni antenna and on to the next. The change of shift is presently going on in Mission Control. Flight Director Clifford Charlesworth is coming on to replace Flight Director Pete Frank and his team of flight controllers. The capsule communicator on this shift will be astronaut Ed Gibson replacing astronaut Jerry Carr. At 38 hours, 10 minutes into the flight of Apollo 12, the spacecraft is now 133,689 nautical miles [247,592 km] from Earth, traveling at a speed of some 3,700 feet per second [1,130 m/s].

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 39 hours, 10 minutes. Apollo 12 presently at an altitude of 135,809 nautical miles [251,518 km] from Earth, traveling at a speed of 3,642 feet per second [1,110 m/s]. We've had no further conversations with the crew since our last report. Flight Director Clifford Charlesworth went around the room and polled each of his flight controllers for a status shortly after coming on shift. The spacecraft continues to function normally and no problems. The crew is scheduled to begin a 10-hour rest period at 43 hours into the mission or about 4 hours from now. The spacecraft is continuing to maintain a stable Passive Thermal Control attitude, rotating at a rate of about 3 revolutions per hour. At 39 hours, 11 minutes; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Hello, troops. Looks like a good burn today. Good show. Say, Pete, we got some folks sitting next to us here who would like to get some Biomed data on the three of you tonight. Why don't you kick it around and give us a reply?

speaker: Conrad
text: What do you want us to do? Keep our Biomed hooked up tonight?

speaker: Gibson
text: That's affirm.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. You want it on all three?

speaker: Gibson
text: That's correct. One thing they'd like to do is to get a baseline to help them during the EVA. They'd like to get - Apparently they use some of that data for input to the equations which they'll be using during the EVA.

speaker: Conrad
text: Sleep - stuff?

speaker: Gibson
text: That's what we're told.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We'll leave it hooked up unless it bothers us.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay.

speaker: Conrad
text: I'm not exactly sure how you get it inside the sleeping bag.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. That sounds good. Thank you.

speaker: Gibson
text: Hello, Houston; Apollo 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: Hello, 12; Houston. Go ahead. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Hello, 12; Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Houston; Apollo 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. Go ahead. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Hello, 12; Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. The LM/CSM Delta-P is plus 1.7.

speaker: Gibson
text: We copy. 1.7.

speaker: Conrad
text: And we'll be bringing the purge line heaters on at 40 plus 35 per the Flight Plan.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: And what do you want us to dump the waste water to - 25 per cent or 15 per cent?

speaker: Gibson
text: Let's take it down to 10 per cent this time. That'll give you a pretty good margin.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Ten per cent.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 40 hours, 2 minutes. Apollo 12 now traveling at a speed of 3,585 feet per second [1,093 m/s] and 137,600 nautical miles [254,835 km] from Earth. We're in conversation with the spacecraft at this time...

speaker: Gibson
text: You folks have been pretty quiet. What's up?

speaker: Conrad
text: Nothing. We're just exercising and listening to the tape recorder and looking at the Moon and looking at the Earth - or reading the books.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. How's that tape recorder? Is the RPM up to nominal?

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes. It works pretty good here in zero g. It works better than it does down there on the ground.

speaker: Bean
text: It just doesn't have much in the way of volume up here with a 5 psi.

speaker: Gibson
text: How's that cloud cover over the Pacific at this time?

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, Australia is real clear again, and it doesn't look quite as cloudy north of Australia. It's sort of a - It's got a rectangular shape to it, whatever the system is north of Australia there. It's kind of funny looking.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. What's the smallest piece of land you can pick out? Can you see any of the Pacific islands?

speaker: Conrad
text: [Laughter] No, we haven't - We can't see any of them. One of - Dick just says he can see Borneo right now. He's looking through the monocular.

speaker: Gordon
text: You can't see it with your naked eye, though.

speaker: Conrad
text: I think one of the problems is that - The only thing that we could see would be close to the curve. All the - the terminator - We're not looking at that much of an Earth and all the water in the Pacific that's close to the terminator has a very shallow Sun angle on it, and it's fairly washed out.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. You still getting a pretty good glint off the surface then?

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes. Dick says the subsolar point is just west of Australia. By the way, how far out are we now?

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. The board's showing a little over 140,000 - Stand by. We'll give you a little more accurate.[Pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.[Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, you're now 137,720 [nautical miles, 255,057 km] out, and you're going along at 3,580 feet per second [1,091 m/s].

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger.[Pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We're going to ask the DSKY and see what it thinks.

speaker: Conrad
text: Not bad. 137,750.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We're showing...

speaker: Conrad
text: ...[garble]...

speaker: Gibson
text: ...755 right now.

speaker: Conrad
text: It'll only read to the nearest tenths, and the velocity is 3,579.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We're just about the same as you, Pete.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. We have some unofficial results from the elections today. It looks as though Mayor Louie Welch was re-elected to a fourth term. His closest competitor, Curtis Graves, got about 59,000, and the mayor's up to 98 now. According to - that's the first time since, I believe, 1927 we got a fourth term for a mayor.

speaker: Conrad
text: Very good.

speaker: Gibson
text: Say, Al, is that Moon beginning to look a little bigger to you now?

speaker: Bean
text: It sure is. We were watching it through the sextant a while ago, and the features on the Moon are much more pronounced than they are - than we've seen before we left Earth. They looked almost like one of these strip pictures you see from an Earth-based telescope. The terminator is about 7 or 8 degrees east, and it's right on the edge of a maria and running through some of the terra, and it's very stark and beautiful from this point of view. I imagine tomorrow it's going to be even more impressive.

speaker: Gibson
text: Probably be very impressive from a distance of around 3 or 4 feet.

speaker: Bean
text: That, too.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control. We're now about 3½ hours from the scheduled beginning of the crew sleep period. It continues to be quite quiet, both from the spacecraft and from here in Mission Control. The crew scheduled to begin a eat period at about 41 hours, 30 minutes; about an hour from now. Spacecraft presently traveling at a speed of 3,561 feet per second [1,085 m/s], has reached an altitude of 138,330 nautical miles [256,187 km] from Earth. At 40 hours, 23 minutes; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, if you hold off on the waste water dump and the fuel cell purge until 41:20, you'll minimize the effect on PTC.

speaker: Gordon
text: Sounds like a good suggestion. We'll do that.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 40 hours, 58 minutes into the flight of Apollo 12. The spacecraft now traveling at speed of 3,523 feet per second [1,074 m/s] and an altitude up to 139,509 nautical miles [258,371 km]. Continues to be very quiet here this morning. We have had one brief conversation with the crew since our last report requesting that they hold off on the scheduled waste water dump until about 41:20:00 at which time will be any more favorable position from standpoint of the Passive Thermal Control, and have the minimum impact on the Passive Thermal Control...

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. Apollo 12 is dumping waste water and purging fuel cells.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, can you see any ice crystals from that?

speaker: Conrad
text: You can see the water dumps; there's no doubt about that. There's all kinds of it. In fact, they look like a regular snowstorm.

speaker: Gibson
text: Does the snowstorm tend to hang around or does it move off pretty quickly?

speaker: Conrad
text: It moves out pretty fast.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hello, Houston; 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hey; Roger, Ed. I don't think that water dump did that PTC any good at all.

speaker: Gibson
text: G&C concurs with that down here. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, let us watch it a little while. We haven't seen you - much travel since you made that dump. You're around 25 degrees out now. We'll be keeping an eye on it and see which way you're going.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 41 hours, 50 minutes. Apollo 12 now traveling at a speed of 3,467 feet per second [1,057 m/s] up to an altitude of 141,270 nautical miles [261,632 km]. The crew advised us a short while ago that they were performing the waste water dump and fuel cell purge as listed on the Flight Plan. A little while after that Dick Gordon reported that apparently the energy imparted by dumping the waste water had affected the Passive Thermal Control attitude apparently setting up some sort of a mild rate in the slow rotational rate that we have. We're watching that in Mission Control now to see if it's going to be necessary for the crew to damp out the movements about the spacecraft axes and reestablish the Passive Thermal Control before they go to sleep.

speaker: Gibson
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: In looking at your - your angles here, it looks as though you might be pretty touch and go during the sleep period if you don't go ahead and re-initialize the PTC, and when you do that, give us a little better - a little better propellant margins. We'd like you to go ahead and reinitialize the DAP to 0.2 degrees per second rather than the 0.5 you have in there now.

speaker: Gordon
text: Got you.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control. As you heard, CapCom Ed Gibson advised the crew to re-establish the Passive Thermal Control mode. This is primarily because of the wobbling motions imparted to the rotational rate of the spacecraft by the water dump. It's felt that if the wobble is allowed to continue during the sleep period, it could conceivably grow to the point during the night where it would be necessary to awaken the crew to damp out this wobbling movement. Rather than take that chance and perhaps have to awaken the crew during the night, we've elected to go ahead and re-establish the Passive Thermal Control mode after stabilizing the spacecraft and the roll rate. And the new Passive Thermal Control mode will be about 2 revolutions per hour. The purpose of this, of course, is to maintain the proper temperature balances within the spacecraft as the vehicle rotates putting first one side and then the other toward the sunlight. Apollo 12 now 34 - out of 141,562 nautical miles [262,173 km] from Earth and traveling at a speed of 3,457 feet per second [1,054 m/s]. At 41 hours, 59 minutes; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Apollo 12, Houston. We've got a state vector for you, if you'll give us Accept.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. The state vector is in, and we're ready for the E-Mod, whenever you want. No hurry.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Gibson
text: State vector's in; the computer is yours. We're also ready to pick up on the roll now, Dick; and we're ready for the E-Mod dump, no hurry on that. Also, we have a question; have you cycled the water quantity indicator switch recently?

speaker: Gordon
text: Yes, which one do you want it in? [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Your position - I guess you have it in Waste right now - is fine. No problem either way, we just wanted to know whether you cycled it because we saw a funny down here.

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, it's in Potable right now, do you want it in Waste?

speaker: Gibson
text: Affirmative, Pete. Waste is good.

speaker: Conrad
text: What was the funny? Okay. It's in Waste, and what was the funny? [Pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, we saw the water quantity go from 101 per cent down to 72 per cent and remain there for a period of time and then work it's way back on up to 101 per cent, and if you had cycled that switch, that would do it. That's the reason for the question.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. I don't really remember, but we may have cycled it a couple of times.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Conrad
text: E-memory dump coming at you.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We're standing by.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control; 42 hours, 29 minutes. Apollo 12 now 142,546 nautical miles [263,995 km] from Earth; 3,426 feet per second [1,044 m/s]. The crew is presently going through their pre-sleep checklist, getting the spacecraft prepared for the sleep period. They are scheduled to begin an eat period at about this time and then begin their rest cycle - a 10-hour rest period at 43 hours, or about 30 minutes from now. We have had a couple of brief conversations with the crew since our last report. Pete Conrad advised a short while ago that they were going to dump the erasable memory for a routine check. The pre-sleep check list also [garble] plus chlorinating the onboard drinking water and setting a number of switches in the proper positions prior to beginning the sleep period.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. We have the E-Mod.

speaker: Conrad
text: 12, Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, it appears we will have no further conversation, at least for the time being. I probably will hear from the crew at least once more before they begin their sleep period. Probably within about 30 minutes. The spacecraft continues to function normally, all systems normal. We are now 142,814 nautical miles [264,492 km] from Earth, traveling at a speed of 3,417 feet per second [1,042 m/s]. At 42 hours and 37 minutes; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Let me give you the onboard readouts: Bat Charlie, 37.0; pyro Bat A, 37.0; pyro Bat B, 37.1. We have no RCS quantities. The indicator is on Main A. Pre-sleep checklist is complete, and we'll be going to our Comm configurations for sleep here in just a minute. And we're still doing some housekeeping chores, so you'll see some Biomed on and off, a little bit, while we get ready to go to bed.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. We copy. 37, 37, 37.1. And we have the RCS consumables if you're interested.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Ready to copy.

speaker: Gibson
text: RCS total 80.9, A 78.9, 83.1, 79.2, 82.8. And that's at 40 hours even.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger.

speaker: Gibson
text: And we are assuming a negative crew status report.

speaker: Conrad
text: That's right.[Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 43 hours, 4 minutes. The crew just called in and reported that they have completed the pre-sleep check list, and will be beginning their sleep period shortly.

speaker: Gibson
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Gibson
text: Before you go on off to sleep, would you take the - clear the DSKY and do it with a Verb 45 or Verb 66 rather than 37?

speaker: Conrad
text: Is there any reason why we can't leave the clock time up there? [Pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Yes. We just prefer, although it's not a strong desire, to clear the DSKY so you're not working the relays in the DSKY, give you a little longer life.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Gibson
text: And, 12, your PTC is looking good; we expect less than 6 degrees excursion during the sleep.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: The crew sleep period is scheduled to last some 10 hours, beginning at about 43 hours as scheduled in the Flight Plan. Apollo 12 is presently 143,833 nautical miles [266,379 km] from the Earth. The spacecraft velocity down now to 3,386 feet per second [1,032 m/s]. At 43 hours, 9 minutes into the flight; this is Mission Control, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 43 hours, 38 minutes. We have not heard from the crew since Conrad announced about 30 minutes ago that they were going to be in their 10-hour rest period. The spacecraft velocity now is 3,355 feet per second and altitude 144,801 nautical miles. The Guidance and Control Officer reported a short while ago that the spacecraft is maintaining good stable Passive Thermal Control attitude rotating at the rate of about 2 revolutions per hour to maintain the proper temperature control during the time the crew are asleep. This sleep period is scheduled to end at about 3:30 this afternoon. At 43 hours, 39 minutes this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 44 hours, 18 minutes. Apollo 12 presently 146,029 nautical miles from Earth. Spacecraft velocity continuing to drop off slowly, now down to 3,317 feet per second. The flight surgeon reported that the crew appears to be settling down and getting to sleep at this time. They are about 1 hour into their scheduled 10-hour rest period. All spacecraft systems continue to function normally at this time. At 44 hours, 19 minutes, this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 45 hours, l8 minutes. It's been a little over 2 hours now since Pete Conrad advised that the crew would be beginning their 10 hours sleep period. The flight surgeon reported about an hour ago that the 2 crewmen on whom we have biological data, Conrad and Bean, appeared to be getting to sleep at that time. Apollo 12 is now traveling at a speed of 3,257 feet per second and the altitude continuing to increase gradually, 147,977 nautical miles from Earth. All spacecraft systems are functioning normally at this time. It's been a very quiet night. We do not expect to hear from the crew until about 3:30 this afternoon Central Standard Time. At 45 hours, 19 minutes, this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 46 hours, 18 minutes. The Apollo 12 crew is asleep. There is 6 hours, 41 minutes remaining in this rest period. Apollo 12 is 149,827 nautical miles from Earth; velocity is 3,200 feet per second. System performance continues to be normal. This is Mission Control Houston at 46 hours, 18 minutes.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 47 hours, 18 minutes. Systems performance continues normal, Apollo 12, as the crew continues in its sleep period. 5 hours, 41 minutes remaining in that rest period. Apollo 12 is now 151,654 nautical miles from Earth traveling at a velocity of 3,144 feet per second. This is Mission Control Houston at 47 hours, 18 minutes.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 48 hours, 18 minutes into the mission. Apollo 12 is 153,414 nautical miles from Earth, traveling at a velocity of 3,091 feet per second. All spacecraft systems continue normal, and 4 hours, 41 minutes remaining in the crew's sleep period. This is Mission Control Houston at 48 hours, 18 minutes.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 49 hours, 18 minutes. Apollo 12 is 155,198 nautical miles from Earth. Its velocity 3,037 feet per second. Three hours and 41 minutes remain in the sleep period for the Apollo 12 crew. All systems continuing to operate normally. We are showing a total weight in space of 96,218 pounds. This is Mission Control, Houston, at 49 hours, 18 minutes.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 50 hours, 18 minutes. Apollo 12 is 156,922 nautical miles from Earth. Velocity 2,986 feet per second. Two hours and 41 minutes remaining in Apollo 12 crew's sleep period. Flight Dynamics Officer reports after studying all the tracking information that Midcourse Correction number 3 will not be required. To repeat, we do not intend to perform Midcourse Correction number 3. This is Mission Control, Houston, at 50 hours, 18 minutes into the Mission of Apollo 12.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 51 hours, 18 minutes. One hour, 41 minutes remaining in Apollo 12 crew's sleep period. Apollo 12 Spacecraft is 158,627 nautical miles from Earth. Velocity is 2,935 feet per second. This is Mission Control, Houston at 51 hours, 18 minutes.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 52 hours, 18 minutes. We're 41 minutes away from crew wake up time. Apollo 12 is 160,294 nautical miles from Earth, velocity 2,886 feet per second. All systems performance still normal. This is Mission Control, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 52 hours, 56 minutes. CapCom Paul Weitz is getting ready to put in a call to the crew now.

speaker: Conrad
text: Good morning, good morning.

speaker: Weitz
text: Good morning, Pete. [Pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: We're just getting stirring up here, and we'll be with you in a few minutes.

speaker: Weitz
text: okay.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Apollo 12 is 161,436 nautical miles from the Earth; velocity 2,852 feet per second. We'll continue to standby for air to ground conversation after the crew gets a little bit organized.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, 12. We're ready for the consumables update.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay, 12. Your consumables update for GET of 53 hours. RCS total is 80.2 - for information, Pete, that puts you 95 - that's 95 pounds below the how goes it. Reading Alfa through Delta 77.5, 82.4, 78.5, 82.5. Your hydrogen is at 80.6/78.8. Oxygen is 81.0/80.7. Over. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Copy. [Long pause.]

speaker: Weitz
text: 12, Houston. No update to the Flight Plan this morning.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: And, Houston, on the crew status report, the CDR slept approximately 8 hours, CMP approximately 9, LMP approximately 8. PRD readings for the CDR, 11010; CMP, 11009; LMP, 04010.

speaker: Weitz
text: Roger 12.Copy.

speaker: Conrad
text: Everybody's at attention in here.[Long pause.]

speaker: Weitz
text: 12, Houston. Let me know when you're settled in the breakfast nook, and I'll give you your morning news.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We'll be with you in a minute.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: The CapCom is Astronaut Paul Weitz.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Houston, 12. We're ready for the news now.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay, 12. The news reports on the flight of Apollo 12 are highlighting yesterday's midcourse correction and the fact that the flight is moving along smoothly. One wire service story calls attention to the improvement in the food menu on this flight. Local, as well as network stations, played video taped highlights of your television show yesterday. Prayers for the flight's success were said in churches everywhere. In Houston, Mayor Louie Welch won his fourth consecutive term by defeating five candidates. He won 53 percent of the vote. His nearest opponent was Curtis Graves, who received about 31 percent of the vote. A minimum housing code and a freedom-of-choice integration plan won strong support. That's about it for news. A recap of how the top 10 teams did yesterday. Ohio State beat Purdue 42 to 14; Texas beat TCU 69 to 7 - I guess they're trying to edge Ohio State in the ratings. Tennessee lost to Mississippi; final score on that one was 38 to nothing. Arkansas beat SMU 28 to 15; Penn State over Maryland 48 to nothing; Southern Cal edged out Washington 16 to 7; UCLA over Oregon 13 to 10; Missouri beat Iowa State 40 to 13; Notre Dame won over Georgia Tech last night 38 to 20; and, of course, Purdue lost to Ohio State. Some pro scores today as they're in - these are finals - Dallas beat Washington 4l to 28; Detroit over St. Louis 20 to nothing; the Minnesota Vikings squeaked by Green Bay 9 to 7; and Kansas City, in the American League, beat New York 34 to 16. And we'll keep you posted on them as they come in later.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Weitz
text: Hello, 12, Houston. We'll be handing over from Madrid to Goldstone in 2 minutes. You may get a momentary Loss Of Signal.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 53 hours, 31 minutes. Apollo 12's distance is now 162,315 nautical miles velocity 2,826 feet per second. The change of shift news conference in the MSC news center will be at 4:30 Central Standard Time, 4:30 p.m. for the change of shift news conference.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 53 hours, 43 minutes. This is a quiet period as the crew is having breakfast. We are in the midst of a shift changeover here in the Control Room ... This is Mission Control, Houston; at 53 Hours, 43 minutes.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 53 hours, 57 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. The Apollo 12 spacecraft, at this time, 162,988 nautical miles in altitude. Its velocity now reads 2,807 feet per second. In Mission Control Center we've just had a turnover in Flight Controller teams. Pete Frank and members of his Orange team are now aboard replacing the Jerry Griffin team. Our Capsule Communicator for this shift will be Don Lind who has just taken over the console from Paul Weitz. As was reported earlier, the Midcourse Correction No. 3 burn will not be done and the crew, the Apollo 12 crew, presumably at this time, is having breakfast. They were awakened approximately an hour ago with the call of reveille. The Change of Shift News Conference is scheduled to begin as previously announced at 4:30 and will include Flight Director Jerry Griffin and the Public Affairs Officer, Jack Riley. At 53 hours, 58 minutes into the flight, this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Lind
text: Pete, we've looked at the situation here. We don't think that a Midcourse Number 3 is going to be required. We're still evaluating number 4 it'll be small if we need it at all - so there will be no Midcourse Number 3. Also, we'd like you to balance the hydrogen for the fuel cells by turning tank number 2 heater Off, and - until we get those back in balance. Also, for your information, the Phoenix races were rained out after 53 laps, yesterday, and so they're going to be rerun today, and we'll let you know the outcome.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, very good. And hydrogen tank 2 heater is Off.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. How's breakfast this morning?

speaker: Conrad
text: It's in work right now. Very good.

speaker: Lind
text: Fine.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Go. 12, this is Houston; go ahead, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: CDR Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston. Go ahead. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Apollo 12. [Long pause.]

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston. Go.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Two questions: one, how far out are we; and two, what time do we reach the lunar sphere of influence?

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. I'll get those numbers for you, Pete. You might want to turn your uplink squelch Off. We're kind of low on signal strength. And you may not hear us very well. I've called you several times. So, that may be a cure.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes, I think we were just in the process of switching antennas or something.

speaker: Lind
text: Okay. Pete, the time for your crossing the lunar sphere of influence is 68 plus 30 plus 19. Your altitude above the Earth is 163,280. Your altitude above the Moon is 63,190.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, and how fast are we going now?

speaker: Lind
text: 2,797. Now, that's referenced to us...

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, thank you.

speaker: Lind
text: ...down here.

speaker: Conrad
text: Understand.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Lind
text: Pete, a question. We wanted to know whether you wanted to manage the antennas or whether you I want us to continue switching back and forth.

speaker: Conrad
text: We've gone to High Gain now. We'd like you to switch back and forth.

speaker: Lind
text: Okay, if - if a - you're going to leave control of that down on the ground, they would prefer to stay in Omni only and turn off the High Gain.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We'll go back to Omni.

speaker: Lind
text: Fine. Thanks very much.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 54 hours, 22 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. The spacecraft presently 163,645 nautical miles in altitude. Now traveling at 2,787 feet per second...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. That time passed to Apollo 12 - that time for crossing the lunar sphere of influence was ground elapsed time of 68 hours, 30 minutes, 19 seconds. You just heard Commander Pete Conrad talking back and forth with the Capsule Communicator in Mission Control Don Lind. At 54 hours, 27 minutes now into the flight, this is Apollo control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Houston, Go.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, this is Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston. [Pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Lind
text: 12, go ahead.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. We changed out the LiOH canister and the LM/CM Delta-P is 1.8.

speaker: Lind
text: 1.8 what?

speaker: Lind
text: Roger, thank you. It seems like every time you call, you catch us with our uplink signal down. Lithium hydroxide is changed and 1.82 for the Delta-P.

speaker: Conrad
text: You're breaking up. I think we are changing antennas. Say again.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. Confirm. Got your lithium hydroxide change out and Delta-P at 1.82.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Lind
text: For your information, the Phoenix 200 is over. We still have only unofficial results, but the unofficial results show Al Unser as the winner. Number 2 is Ruby, and number 3 is Don Dallenbach.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Thank you very much.

speaker: Lind
text: Very good.
