speaker: Gordon
text: Hello, Houston; 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Don. Everybody has had breakfast, brushed their teeth, combed their hair, and we're even thinking about shaving today for you. But the big question I've got, I want to do that P52 option 3, the one that the Flight Plan has optional at 55 hours or so, and I want to remain in PTC while I do it. Do you concur?

speaker: Lind
text: We concur. Fine. Sounds like you're ready for another busy day.

speaker: Conrad
text: It really doesn't look that way, really. I think we'll just practice for a while.

speaker: Lind
text: You're all cleaned up and nowhere to go.

speaker: Conrad
text: We're going somewhere; we're not sure where.

speaker: Lind
text: We are.

speaker: Gordon
text: It doesn't look like we've moved very far for 2 days now.

speaker: Lind
text: It'll be a long way home. You've been travelling a long way.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 54 hours, 47 minutes now into the flight. Apollo 12 now 164,328 nautical miles above Earth. Its velocity now reads on our digital displays 2,767 feet per second. We've just passed up to Commander Pete Conrad the Phoenix 200 unofficial but final race results...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. That was Dick Gordon making the report that they had completed breakfast, brushed their teeth and combed their hair and might even shave. The P52 reference is a platform alignment and Command Module Pilot Gordon did indicate he would like to do it around 55 hours ground elapsed time. We are at 54 hours, 52 minutes now ground elapsed time and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Apollo 12. Are you looking at the DSKY?

speaker: Lind
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. You've cut out on the [garbled] antenna.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. We are watching your DSKY.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, do you have the torquing angles?

speaker: Lind
text: That is affirmative.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We're going to go ahead and torque.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 55 hours, 14 minutes, now in the flight of Apollo 12. We presently show Apollo 12 at 165,029 nautical miles above the Earth. Its velocity now reads 2,747 feet per second. Now we pick up conversation with Apollo 12 while the computer alignment program is in process...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That was Commander Pete Conrad talking with Don Lind and at 55 hours, 16 minutes into the flight, this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Houston. Go.

speaker: Bean
text: Roger. Just looking through the monocular again at the Earth, and looks like it's dark everywhere except the lower left-hand corner of California. Right in there - L.A. and San Diego, and I can't see Baja California. It may be just twilight there. It's kind of hazy - not hazy, but insofar as the dark light relationship, it's kind of difficult to tell. The lower left corner of California is the only part we can see in the sunshine right now.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. What does the weather look like out there?

speaker: Bean
text: Looks beautiful. See it real well. It doesn't appear to be any clouds - any large cloud formations near it. There's a nice crescent-shaped large weather system that appears to be several hundred miles out to sea, but I don't know if that will affect it or not. But the whole area around that southern tip of California there is nice and clear.

speaker: Lind
text: Very good.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston, at 55 hours, 43 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. We currently show an altitude for the spacecraft of 165,802 nautical miles. Velocity now reads 2,725 feet per second...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: At 55 hours, 46 minutes now into the flight, this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Bean
text: Been looking at the Earth some more through the monocular, and I think maybe the part of the U.S. that I thought was the lower left-hand corner, the Los Angeles area, it was just about to have sunset, was really not. I don't think I could see that because of the - it's color-related to the blue of the rest of the Earth. I think maybe it was the desert area around Phoenix and around in there, just thinking about the time it is now. And I'm not able to discern at all the lower left-hand corner of the U.S., I think, because of the colors.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. A little smog out there in L.A.? Can't see through it?

speaker: Bean
text: No. I don't think its smog. I can't see any of that area. I think it's probably just that the Earth out there has more trees, shrubs, and the like, and that makes it sort of a gray-green which is sort of like the ocean whenever you look at it from this view. And they just blend in together, and you're not able to tell exactly where one starts and one ends. We noticed that a little bit as we were closer to earth and then now as we get out this far, about all we can see is something contrasting very greatly with those blue-grays or blue-greens. In this case, it was sort of a reddish-brown [garbled]...

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston. [Long pause.]

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston. [Long pause.]

speaker: Bean
text: Hey, Houston; Apollo 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. Go. We lost the very end of that transmission because we were switching antennas, but it sounds like you got a great view up there. [Pause.]

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.[Long pause.]

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. We were switching antennas there. Lost the last part of that transmission, but it sounds like you got a good view out there tonight.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes, not too bad. Hey, Don, how'd the Saints and the Oilers make out today?

speaker: Lind
text: The Oilers tied on the last play of the game. 20-20 was the final score.

speaker: Conrad
text: What was the score?

speaker: Conrad
text: 20-20, huh? How'd the Saints do? They were playing the Giants.

speaker: Lind
text: 25 to 24 for New Orleans.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Thank you.

speaker: Lind
text: Very good. Hey...

speaker: Conrad
text: Got some good news?

speaker: Lind
text: Yes. Say, listen, can you see any of Antarctica from your position in the daylight?

speaker: Conrad
text: That's affirmative, Don. We can see a large portion of it, as a matter of fact. It's continually in sunlight.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger.

speaker: Lind
text: Listen, I've got some other scores for you, if you are interested.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Lind
text: Okay. AFL: Houston and Denver 20-20; Kansas City over New York 34-16; Boston over Cincinnati 25-14; Buffalo over Miami 28 to 3; Oakland took San Diego 21-16; in the National, as I said, New Orleans over New York 25-24; Chicago 31, Atlanta 48; Philadelphia 17, L.A. 23; Detroit took St. Louis 20 to nothing; Dallas hl, Washington 28; and L.A. over Philadelphia, 23 to 17.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Thank you very much.

speaker: Bean
text: And could you give us the exact longitude the terminator is on the Moon at this time?

speaker: Lind
text: Wait 1. We'll get it for you.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 56 hours, 15 minutes now into the mission. Apollo 12 is presently shown at 166,616 nautical miles above the Earth. It's presently traveling at a speed of 2,701 feet per second.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. That was Capsule Communicator Don Lind giving the football scoreboard report. We are at 56 hours, 22 minutes now into the flight and this is Apollo Control.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Lind
text: The terminator on the Moon now is 1 degree west. We're trying to get it more accurately for you than that, but 1 degree west is the present terminator.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Thank you.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Conrad
text: We were just talking about the TV show this afternoon, and I guess what we'd like to do - it probably hasn't been seen before that I remember - If we could get a High-Gain antenna angle and the Sun in our center hatch so we could get as much light as possible into the Command Module, we'd like to use the TV and try and show the removal of the hatch, probe, and drogue and then take the TV over into the LM.

speaker: Lind
text: Very good. We'll get those angles for you. Sounds like a good show.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Lind
text: Just a note for the director of your TV presentation: We'll get the first 29 minutes of that presentation live; the rest of it will be recorded at Honeysuckle and shipped back to us. We'll get it in several days. But we'll only get directly through Goldstone your first 29 minutes.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We'll move it up and make sure we get into the LM by then, anyway.

speaker: Lind
text: Okay. Just wanted to make sure you got all your best performance in the first period. [Pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: We'll figure out something, Don.

speaker: Lind
text: Very good,

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 56 hours, 41 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. The Apollo 12 spacecraft at this time 167,298 nautical miles away, its velocity now reading 2,682 feet per second. Don Lind has just had conversation with Apollo 12 concerning our upcoming television show now scheduled or now set for 1:52 AM tomorrow morning.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. That was Pete Conrad who first brought up the subject of television. As you heard that final comment from Dick Gordon, we could move up the time of Lunar Module transfer - the transfer of the crew to the Lunar Module to coincide with the scheduled television time. We are now at 56 hours, 44 minutes into the flight and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 57 hours, 10 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. We've had no conversation with Apollo 12 since our last report. However, we thought we would pass along altitude and velocity updates at this time. Apollo 12 is presently shown at an altitude of 60 - 168,023 nautical miles, its velocity now shown at 2,660 feet per second. This is Apollo Control Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Hello, Houston; Apollo 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Go ahead, 12.

speaker: Bean
text: How about asking the food experts down there, we had a can of tuna fish spread salad last night, and there's about a half a can left today, and that stuff's still good to eat, isn't it?

speaker: Lind
text: We'll check. I'll be right back with you.

speaker: Bean
text: Thank you. [Long pause.]

speaker: Bean
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Lind
text: The surgeon suggests you try a new one. New can. [Pause.]

speaker: Bean
text: Well, Dick has this one in his hot hand, and we just opened it last night. You sure that one isn't all right?

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Lind
text: We're still checking with some people down here whether there's, any problem over that tuna fish, but why don't you hold off eating it until we get a better answer for you?

speaker: Bean
text: Okay.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 57 hours, 35 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. We currently show Apollo 12 at 168,650 nautical miles above the Earth. It's velocity now reading 2,642 feet per second...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. At least for now, the consumption of tuna fish spread one-day opened remains an open item. We'll keep you posted on developments. At 57 hours, 37 minutes into the flight, this is Apollo control Houston.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston. [Long pause.]

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Lind
text: You can't imagine what consternation your tuna fish question has raised down here. We have a wide diversity of opinion.

speaker: Conrad
text: I decided it was...

speaker: Lind
text: The...

speaker: Gordon
text: I decided it was okay.

speaker: Lind
text: Well, we have a vote that it's okay. The majority says throw it away; there's a minority report that says everybody can eat it except Dick Gordon.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. That's done.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. They recommend that you probably throw it away.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 1 - at 57 hours, 44 minutes into the flight of Apollo 12. Apollo 12's altitude now reads 168,882 nautical miles. Its velocity now 2,635 feet per second. We've closed the tuna fish question.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: At 57 hours, 45 minutes of the flight, this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 58 hours, 23 minutes now into the flight, of Apollo 12. We've had no conversation with the Apollo 12 crew since our last report. Presently we show an altitude of 169,851 nautical miles for Apollo 12. Its velocity now reads 2,607 feet per second. We're at 58 hours, 23 minutes and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Hello, Houston; Apollo 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, go ahead.

speaker: Bean
text: Roger. Do you have a report on the families' activities today?

speaker: Lind
text: Negative. We'll see if we can find out what's been going on over here.

speaker: Bean
text: Thank you.

speaker: Conrad
text: Meanwhile, Houston, I can tell you what we've been doing since we got up this morning, just for your information.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: We cleaned the spacecraft fore and aft and all lower decks and ladders; cleaned up the garbage and re-stowed everything. And everybody had a bath and everybody shaved. And Al's studying the Moon. I'm studying descent. Dick's been fitting the S-158 making sure it fits and works, and that's occupied us for about the last 3 hours.

speaker: Lind
text: Ah, very good. Where do you put the garbage when you haven't got a fantail to throw it over?

speaker: Conrad
text: We've defined the area below the window shade box and down next to the O 2 mass as the fantail, and we have rigged a garbage bag down there. And we retransfer all of the gear out of the TSB's and neatly wrapped and packaged them and made sure they all had their pills and good things in them.

speaker: Lind
text: Very...

speaker: Conrad
text: ...and configured down there.

speaker: Lind
text: Very good. You sound incredibly neat.

speaker: Conrad
text: Haven't got much else to do, pal.

speaker: Lind
text: We'll get your - the reports on your families...

speaker: Conrad
text: Also on the...

speaker: Lind
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Also, as we're approaching the Moon, of course, we're beginning to notice less and less of the Moon. We're moving out in front of it, and although - although the terminator is coming around, we're beginning to see less and less the illuminated portion of the Moon, and it's of becoming quite noticeable to us now.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 58 hours, 35 minutes now into the flight. We presently show Apollo 12 at an altitude of 170,159 nautical miles. Its velocity now 2,599 feet per second. We have just received a report from Commander Pete Conrad speaking for the all-Navy Apollo 12 crew describing what they've been doing today...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That was Capsule Communicator, Don Lind speaking with Pete Conrad aboard the Apollo 12 spacecraft. We're at 58 hours, 38 minutes now into the flight, and this is Apollo control, Houston.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. Just checked with your families. Pete, Jane reports that they've had a very quiet Sunday afternoon there. Everybody is home, and everybody is well, and there just really is not much excitement going on. It's just been a very quiet afternoon over at your house. Dick, Barbara says...

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Lind
text: Barbara reports to you, Dick, that Sharon and Lynn Diamond are over for the evening, and they're expecting the Irwins over momentarily, and Jim McDivitt just left. She says the boys have gone back to school, and she thought things were going to be pretty quiet; but, between Barbara and Karen, she's got so many giggling girls around there that it's more noisy than she thought. The other thing she pointed out was that Father Connolly had been over and had noticed Barbara having a nap this afternoon, and coming out of church this evening he commented in front of some of the people standing there in the church that the last time he saw her she was - she had been asleep. And this was much to her consternation. Also, Barbara asks that you guys talk a little bit more. She says she certainly expected more conversation out of you than she's been getting. Al, your wife reported that they're all missing you. They're extremely proud of you.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston. How do you hear? [Pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. How do you hear now, Pete? [Pause.]

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston. [Long pause.]

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston. [Pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Hello, Houston; 12.

speaker: Lind
text: 12, Houston. Do you read? [Pause.]

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, 12. Are you locked up now?

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston. Do you read me now?

speaker: Gordon
text: I read you loud and clear. How us?

speaker: Lind
text: I read you very fine. Sorry about switching antennas there. Al, your - As I started to say, your wife says that the family is missing you; they're very proud of how the flight is going along; and that they'll certainly be watching tomorrow. The children are all fine.

speaker: Bean
text: Great break.

speaker: Conrad
text: We're not getting you at all, Don. What are you having, a site hand-over or something? We've only gotten about two or three words in the last 5 minutes.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. How do you hear me now? We - We've just switched the antennas.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. You're loud and clear, and you started cutting out after you said that Father Connolly was over and Barbara was taking a nap. Can you go back to that point?

speaker: Lind
text: Oh, yes. Yes. Father Connolly had been over in the afternoon and had seen Barbara taking a nap. So coming out of church this evening, in front of some of the members of the congregation, he said that the last time he had seen her she was asleep. And this was very embarrassing to her at the moment. Also...

speaker: Gordon
text: ...Well, that is better than what he could have said.

speaker: Lind
text: [Laughter] Also, Barbara had the comment for the whole crew that she's a little disappointed in how much you're talking. She certainly wanted you - expected that you'd talk more than she's been hearing lately.

speaker: Gordon
text: We're talking. She's just not hearing.

speaker: Lind
text: She also requests that when you talk, try to be a little funnier. Al, talked to your wife. She said that the family are missing you and that they're extremely proud of how the flight's been going. They'll be watching tomorrow; and, also, she wanted you to know that all the children were fine. This evening when Amy was going to bed, she turned to her mother and she said, I want to see my daddy. I want to touch him. So, you're being missed. Also, she concurs with the decision on the tuna fish. She definitely was happy that you didn't eat the day old tuna fish. That's about all the family has to report.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. Thank you, Don.

speaker: Lind
text: Say, one other item for Pete. The board of directors has had a meeting, and the VFR has been replaced with IFR Conrad from now on.

speaker: Conrad
text: [Laughter] I understand. Okay. Very good.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger.

speaker: Gordon
text: Don, we're all decided up here that we're going to have to get another Saturn V ride because we sure missed the last one.

speaker: Lind
text: Very good [laughter].

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 59 hours, 3 minutes into the flight. Apollo 12 now at an altitude of 170,851 nautical miles. Its velocity now reading 2,579 feet per second. Capsule Communicator, Don Lind, has just passed along family reports to the Apollo 12 crew.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Lind
text: Things are going so well we've decided that you do not need a state vector update at this time. So things are going along very nicely.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. What's your first hack on MCC 4?

speaker: Lind
text: Just about 3 feet a second.

speaker: Conrad
text: Are we going to do it or not?

speaker: Lind
text: We're still evaluating.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Lind
text: Would you give us H 2 tank heater number 2 to Auto?

speaker: Conrad
text: H 2 heater number 2 to Auto.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. Thank you.

speaker: Conrad
text: You're welcome.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Apollo Control, Houston. That was Dick Gordon that suggested the Apollo 12 crew might need another ride on the Saturn V. We are at 59 hours, l0 minutes now into the flight and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 59 hours, 29 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. Apollo 12 presently at an altitude of 171,497 nautical miles. Its velocity now reading 2,560 feet per second...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That was Commander Pete Conrad aboard the spacecraft and at 59 hours, 30 minutes into the flight, this is Apollo Control Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Go ahead, 12.

speaker: Bean
text: We been looking out at the Sun with our monocular, and we put the sunglass that goes with the telescope over the front of it. Been looking at the Sun and looks like there's two or three dark spots on the west limb of the Sun. Maybe 30 - 40 degrees in, about the equator. Other than that, it doesn't - we can't see anything else. Over.

speaker: Lind
text: Very good. If they're 30 or 40 degrees in, you won't have to worry about any flare particle from them.

speaker: Bean
text: Who's worried?

speaker: Lind
text: Sounds like you guys are having a real good review of astronomy this afternoon.

speaker: Bean
text: We've been studying astronomy, geography, geology, a few other things up here.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger.

speaker: Bean
text: Really not a lot to do on the way out. You've got your systems to monitor, and you got to eat, and keep yourself clean, get some sleep, and except for that, you're free to do a little looking out the window and studying the checklists and maps and things that you're going to be using when you get to the lunar orbit.

speaker: Lind
text: You're in [garble] Rev.

speaker: Bean
text: So it's got to be a pretty pleasant trip. Yes, we'll make it all up starting tomorrow.

speaker: Stafford
text: Beano, this is your old Social Director speaking. One thing, I'll guarantee that those dark spots on the sun aren't clouds.

speaker: Bean
text: [Laughter] I thought it was particularly appropriate, since we were going to the Ocean of Storms, that we bailed out of the Earth in the midst of one of them.

speaker: Stafford
text: How about that.

speaker: Conrad
text: We thought for a minute we had a caution and warning failure because they all came on.

speaker: Stafford
text: Understand.

speaker: Conrad
text: What are you doing up so late, Social Director?

speaker: Stafford
text: Oh, I just thought I'd keep check on you, Pete. Looks like everything is just going great.

speaker: Stafford
text: [Laughter] There's not too many places we can go.

speaker: Stafford
text: Yes. Watching the plot up here...

speaker: Conrad
text: [Garbled].

speaker: Stafford
text: It's quite a view out there, isn't it, Pete?

speaker: Conrad
text: Sure is. Did you all learn any special tricks about viewing the Earth or the Moon? Did you think we haven't tried?

speaker: Stafford
text: No. I think we've passed on all the basic information and guess it's quite a view to see it rotate through the windows there and take pictures of it.

speaker: Conrad
text: Because, during launch, I usually tell Al which lights are on, if he has an electrical problem. Friday, all I could do was look over and tell him, I said, Hey, Al, they're all on.

speaker: Stafford
text: No, we can probably plan some good simulations from now on.

speaker: Bean
text: We talked about it before; and Pete said, Don't worry. He says, If you ever have anything go wrong in flight, it'll be something you've never seen before in your life. He was right.

speaker: Stafford
text: Yes. That's - that's the way it always happens. [Pause.]

speaker: Stafford
text: One thing you've got the advantage of us. We couldn't see the Moon until we got just - right nearly to it by that westerly site. You've probably got a pretty good view of it now.

speaker: Bean
text: Yes. Of course, it's getting - The illuminated portion as we move out in front of it is getting less and less all the time. We're really beginning to notice that we're seeing less and less of it.

speaker: Stafford
text: Roger. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 59 hours, 39 minutes now into the flight. Apollo 12 presently at 171,728 nautical miles in altitude. It's velocity now reading 2,554 feet per second...

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, 12. Since we're not doing MCC 3, do they want to do an alignment here or just do another REFSMMAT alignment?

speaker: Stafford
text: Negative. We don't need that. Things are really ...

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. How's that platform looking then, this morning? [Pause.]

speaker: Stafford
text: Your platform's looking really good, we'll try to get you some drift numbers.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Stafford
text: Apollo 12, your drifts are 1.2 mERU on all axes or less. One of there's even lower than that.

speaker: Stafford
text: Apollo 12, Houston. [Long pause.]

speaker: Stafford
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Stafford
text: Did you get that drift report? Your platform is less than 1.2 mERU on all axes.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. The gentleman in Mission Control Center who prefaced this conversation with Beano, this is your old Social Director is Colonel Tom Stafford who, as you will recall, was the Commander on Apollo 12. Shortly after Tom came on the line, the Commander of Apollo 12, Pete Conrad, chimed into the conversation. We are at 59 hours, 44 minutes...

speaker: Stafford
text: Apollo 12, Houston. How's your sleeping bags working out up there, Pete?

speaker: Conrad
text: Real good, Tom. The first night I slept in a bag, and Al slept in a bag, and Dick slept up in the seat. He didn't sleep too well. And last night, I slept up in the seat, and Dick slept in my bag, and all of us like the bags. And one of the problems with the seat is that - and we're going to take care of that tonight - it's rattling around in here, and every time somebody stirs down below, why the seat bangs off the wall and that naturally wakes up the guy that's sleeping in it. It's kind of spring loaded, anyhow.

speaker: Stafford
text: Roger. Looks - you getting plenty of sleep? Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes, plenty. We're getting more than I need.

speaker: Stafford
text: Good. The reports look real good down here. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Hey, Tom. What do you think of our RAD count?

speaker: Stafford
text: Say again?

speaker: Gordon
text: What do you think of our PRD count?

speaker: Stafford
text: Stand by 1, Dick, I'll check. [Pause.]

speaker: Stafford
text: Well, from down here, it looks like the total Rad count showed that you got practically nothing up there.

speaker: Gordon
text: Well, I wouldn't go so far as to say we've got nothing.

speaker: Stafford
text: At least, they call it 90 millirads.

speaker: Stafford
text: That's less than 1/300th of what atomic workers can get.

speaker: Stafford
text: And I'd nearly bet that the calorie count that you people can see up there just nearly zero.

speaker: Gordon
text: I wouldn't bet on that either.

speaker: Conrad
text: I would. The calorie count. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 59 hours, 48 minutes now into the flight. Apollo 12 presently at 171,942 nautical miles. Its velocity now reading 2,548 feet per second. Tom Stafford has just called the crew to ask about their sleeping bags and generally carry on a chat session...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Apollo Control, Houston. That was Pete Conrad first talking with Tom Stafford; then followed by Dick Gordon. We're at 59 hours, 50 minutes into the flight and continuing to monitor. This is Apollo Control Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 60 hours, 17 minutes now into the flight. Apollo 12 presently at an altitude of 172,658 nautical miles. It's velocity now reads 2,527 feet per second. We have not spoken with the crew since our last report, and the atmosphere in mission control, at this time is quiet. As the various flight controllers making notes, looking into their consoles and planning ahead for a more active day tomorrow. We're at 60 hours, 18 minutes and this is Apollo control.

speaker: Lind
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Lind
text: Roger. We'd like to check and see if the expanded deadband has been collapsed. We'd like to check your load by looking at Noun 79, so we'd like to ask you to enter a Verb 79 for us.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, how's that? Proceed on that and I'll be okay, huh?

speaker: Lind
text: Load looks all right to us. You can go ahead and proceed.

speaker: Gordon
text: Are you looking at it, Don?

speaker: Lind
text: That's affirmative. You can go ahead and proceed.

speaker: Gordon
text: Looks okay to me, too.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hey, Don, I think all of us up here are gaining weight on this food; it's been so good.

speaker: Lind
text: Say again, 12.

speaker: Gordon
text: Pete and I just had frankfurters and - say, this food up here has been so good, I think we're going to gain weight.

speaker: Gordon
text: Pete and I just polished off four frankfurters and some apple - applesauce; Al Bean hasn't quite eaten his yet, but it's really been good.

speaker: Lind
text: Hey, you're just killing me, man. I'm sitting down here without anything to eat.

speaker: Gordon
text: You mean the Tastee-Freeze isn't open?

speaker: Lind
text: I haven't been in it for a while. Just remember to do your mild exercise today so you don't gain weight.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston, at 60 hours, 40 minutes now in the flight. At the present time we show Apollo 12 at an altitude of 173,196 nautical miles. Velocity now reads 2,512 feet per second. Still very quite in the Control Center and at 60 hours, 40 minutes, this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Lind
text: Go ahead, 12.

speaker: Bean
text: Roger. At 61:15, do you want an O 2 fuel cell purge and waste water dump like the Flight Plan calls for?

speaker: Lind
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay, and what do you want us to dump the water to, 10 percent? [Pause.]

speaker: Lind
text: 12, we'd like to recommend that you dump to zero since we're going to have quite a time before we'll have another opportunity for a dump.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 60 hours, 54 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. Apollo 12 presently shows an altitude of 173,531 nautical miles above the Earth. The spacecraft velocity now reads 2,502 feet per second. Capsule Communicator, Don Lind has conversed briefly with Apollo 12.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That was Lunar Module pilot, Al Bean aboard Apollo 12 talking with Mission Control in Houston. We're at 60 hours, 55 minutes, and this is Apollo control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Lind
text: 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. One waste water dump, one O 2 purge coming up.

speaker: Scott
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: Who's that? David?

speaker: Scott
text: Good ear.

speaker: Conrad
text: What are you doing ...

speaker: Gordon
text: Good evening, David.

speaker: Conrad
text: ...up so late?

speaker: Scott
text: Watching after you.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control of Houston at 61 hours, 19 minutes now into the flight. Apollo 12 continuing on its course to the moon presently at an altitude of 174,130 nautical miles Continuing to slow down, it's velocity now reads 2,485 feet per second. Pete Conrad just called in and received a bit of a surprise. The gentleman at the Capcom console at least for this moment, is Dave Scott, backup commander for Apollo 12...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Apollo Control, Houston. As was previously reported, Midcourse Correction number 3 was deleted from the Flight Plan. The requirement for the Midcourse Correction number 4 burn is still being evaluated at Mission Control. In any case, if this burn is accomplished it's magnitude will be at most very small, perhaps in the order of 3 feet per second. Television is scheduled for tomorrow morning, which is rapidly approaching for tomorrow morning at 1:52 a.m. Central time and as reported by the crew earlier they will probably move their Lunar Module transfer time forward to coincide with the 29 minutes of television which will be carried live. We're at 61 hours, 21 minutes into the flight and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Scott
text: Apollo 12, Houston. We see zero on your waste water. Thanks very much.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control Houston at 61 hours, 48 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. Our displays presently show Apollo 12 at an altitude of 174,824 nautical miles. Its velocity now reads 2,465 feet per second.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control Houston. Meanwhile in Mission Control Center, Houston discussions have been taking place regarding the possibility of moving the television time forward or in advance of that shown in the Flight Plan. These times have not yet been defined. As soon as they become known to us we will pass them along immediately. We're now at 61 hours, 49 minutes into the flight and this is Apollo Control Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hello, Houston; 12. [Pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Hello, Houston; 12.

speaker: Scott
text: Go ahead, 12. [Pause.]

speaker: Scott
text: Apollo 12, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hello, Houston; Apollo 12.

speaker: Scott
text: Apollo 12, go.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger, Houston. Looks like that water dump has kind of ruined our PTC, here. I was just wondering if you want us to do anything with it or just stand by and wait until the - the fixed attitude at 63 hours.

speaker: Scott
text: Roger. We - We followed your water dump maneuver.

speaker: Scott
text: Wait 1. 12, we'll just continue to watch your attitude changes for a while, and - if anything -if your yaw swings too far, we can come out of it, but let's stay in the attitude you're in now for a while.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Scott
text: In PTC for a while is what I intended to say.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. Understand.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 62 hours, 1 minute now into the flight of Apollo 12. Apollo 12 presently 175,119 nautical miles away from Earth. It's velocity now reading 2,057 feet per second. A change of shift is presently taking place in the Mission Control Center with Cliff Charlesworth's Green team of Flight Controllers relieving Pete Franks' team of Orange Controllers...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Apollo Control, Houston. We still have no firm time yet for the next scheduled television transmission. However, there is a very definite possibility that this time will be moved forward from the 63 hours, 30 minutes, ground elapsed time as reflected in the flight plan. We will pass along an update time, as soon as it becomes available and at 62 hours, 04 minutes into the flight, this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Just want to remind you to charge Battery B, please.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. Battery B charge.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Thank you.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, 12.

speaker: Carr
text: Go ahead, 12.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Apollo 12, Houston. How do you read me? [Pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston. Go. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Apollo 12, this is Houston. Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. Go.

speaker: Conrad
text: What's going to be the roll angle, so we can start thinking about where we're going here - for this TV?

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Your roll angle is 285 degrees, pitch 90, and yaw is 0.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. We've got a checklist change for you for coming out of PTC. Would you open your checklist to page F 9-7? Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Got it. Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. On step number 1 to exit G&N PTC, because you're so far out of the deadband, you ought to put your Man Att 3 to Accel Command before you put your Auto RCS Selects to Main A and B. And we suggest we put the - this ...

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger.

speaker: Carr
text: ...into the checklist change for good.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes, that's probably ...

speaker: SC
text: [Garble] okay?

speaker: Conrad
text: ...a good idea. [Pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. And we think you probably ought to come on out of PTC now. That's one of the reasons why we're having a little trouble with Comm.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. And what we'll do - we'll slide on over to the 90, 0, 285.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control; 62 hours, 21 minutes Ground Elapsed Time. Apollo 12 presently is coming out of the passive thermal control mode, bar-b-que mode going to the attitude hold mode because of disturbance set up by waste water dump, also because of the LM checkout, which is scheduled, - normally starting at about 64 hours however, there is some discussion going on here in the control center moving that up, also, accompanying the television transmission from the spacecraft. We're standing by for a resumption of conversation...

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control. Some numbers while we're waiting for resumption of conversation, and the altitude above the Earth - here we go.

speaker: Carr
text: Apollo 12, Houston, with a Flight Plan update.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. Ready to copy.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Your TV pass at 63 plus 00. Number 1, stop your PTC roll at 285, and this is what you need to put the Sun through the hatch window. Step number 2 is your High-Gain antenna angles are pitch 19, yaw 268. Step number 3, put the ALC switch to the In position, and open the camera aperture to Full Open for your tunnel pictures.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. We got it.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Back to distance and velocity. 175,763 nautical miles out from Earth. Velocity now 2,439 feet per second. Continuing to monitor air to ground as the crew of Apollo 12 prepare to man Intrepid for housekeeping chores and fairly extensive checkout of the Lunar Module.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Apollo 12.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. Go.

speaker: Conrad
text: When do you want us to start this show, now?

speaker: Carr
text: Pete, we're ready whenever you are. Your option.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. That's what I figured. So, we're starting to pressurize the Command Module now, and we'll start here directly.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control. The spacecraft apparently now in attitude hold. We've had solid lock-on with the high gain antenna through the Goldstone 210-foot dish. We're standing by now for the television transmission and the subsequent manning of the lunar module, Intrepid. Standing by live on the air-ground circuit.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Houston; 12.

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. Go.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We're coming up Vox at this time, and we're getting ready to give you the TV. Al will get it going in just a second.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Standing by. [Long pause.]

speaker: Bean
text: [Garbled] properly dressed.

speaker: Gordon
text: Jerry, we've got to dress Al yet. We have to put on his hat.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Lights! Camera! Action! [Pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: I'm down here [garble] up in here, I guess.

speaker: Bean
text: Let him get over here where the Sun comes in.

speaker: Gordon
text: Shortly too.

speaker: Bean
text: There you go.

speaker: Gordon
text: Who, me? Okay? [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. You putting it out? Wait a minute. You got it on the ground yet, Houston?

speaker: Carr
text: Not yet, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We'll hold until you get the picture.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. We're not copying any FM downlink as yet. [Pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: 12, Houston. We have you in blushing black and white. And the color's coming in now.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger.

speaker: Gordon
text: What happened to the color?

speaker: Bean
text: There you go.

speaker: Carr
text: Takes a little for the processing.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. As you can see, Dick's up there in the tunnel, and he's opening the vent valve now, and he's starting to pressurize the LM.

speaker: Conrad
text: And we have a Delta-P of about 2.3 at the moment.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. It's going down to about 2.2.

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, no. The Delta-P went up when we pumped up the cabin.

speaker: Gordon
text: Delta-P is 1.8.

speaker: Bean
text: What's the cabin? Okay. Just about do it. We're down to 1.3 Delta-P. Okay, 1 psi Delta-P.

speaker: Conrad
text: While we're equalizing the cabin, Houston, the attitude that you have us in, out our number 1 window, we have the Earth; and out the number 3 window, we have the Sun shining in; and out the number 5 window, we have the Moon. And, of course, we're too far from either the Earth or the Moon to see any motion, so it just seems to us that we're in suspended animation out here.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Gordon
text: What's the cabin pressure, Al?

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes, it is. And you just brought the cabin Reg on and that ought to be okay so ...

speaker: Carr
text: We're reading you 4.7 on your cabin pressure now; and, Al, we're not reading you at all.

speaker: Bean
text: [Garbled] How do you read me now?

speaker: Carr
text: Okay, now, Al.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. And the hatch is open.

speaker: Gordon
text: What in the heck is this thing doing up here? Here it goes - there's another one right there. You may not want to move it. There you go.

speaker: Bean
text: All right.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Pretty good - How's the lighting down there, Houston? Looks pretty good on the monitor.

speaker: Carr

What happens is, Pete stands right behind those scribe marks you can see right at the top; There's - where the horizontal line is, that's 0 degrees, and then there's a 10 down, 20 down, and 30, 40, and on down. Right at the top then, left and right, there is also some angular marks. As we proceed in the descent and we pitch over where the lunar surface is visible, about 7,000 feet, Pete's going to be looking out through the window at those marks. I'll be reading from the computer, and the computer will say where it's taking us to land, relative to those marks. For example, probably the first thing you will hear me say is 42 degrees, so Pete will look out at the 42-degree mark, and he will see if that is the Surveyor crater. We spent a lot of time learning which crater the Surveyor is in and a lot of the more interesting craters around there, the more easily identifiable craters. He will look out and see if the craters in the right place, I mean if the 42-degree mark's in the right place. If it is, then we'll just continue on the present trajectory. If not, he can use his control stick to put a certain number of inputs in to change the direction we are headed; for example, if he saw it at 40 degrees instead of 42 for the crater we wanted, he could pitch down a couple or pitch up a couple, depending on what he wanted to do. If he saw it at 40, he would pitch down a couple of hits of the stick and, hopefully very shortly, the computer would notice this and start heading for the 40-degree point. I'd continue reading the numbers, and he'd continue to monitor them all the way down. When we got down to a low altitude, then we would be in a good position for Pete to take over manually and land next to the point we're headed for. This is called the LPD or Landing Point Designator. It allows the Commander to keep up with where the computer thinks it should land and then tell it to land at a different place if he feels it should.
