speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 120 hours, 34 minutes. Yankee Clipper has 12 minutes acquisition time left in this 19th lunar revolution. The crewmen of Intrepid are recharging the portable life support systems, refilling with oxygen and getting the LM reconfigured. After they complete that, we will have a short debriefing session between the ground and the Intrepid on this first EVA. Mission Control Center flight controller teams will change shifts right after that briefing. We are estimating the Change Of Shift news conference for 11:30 a.m. Central Standard Time.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, [garble].

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston. Did you call?

speaker: Gordon
text: Intrepid, [garble].

speaker: Gibson
text: Clipper, we copied that P52 torquing angle.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. Thank you, [garble].

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, you'll never believe what we've been doing for the last 35 minutes.

speaker: Gibson
text: Go ahead. We're waitin'.

speaker: Conrad
text: I am going to take this 35-cent [meaning cheap] scale that they sent out here to weigh these bags with and break it over somebody's head.

speaker: Gibson
text: I take it you're having a malfunction with the bag. The bag and the scale.

speaker: Conrad
text: The nut... [Responding to Gibson] No, just the scale. The nut came off the top of the adjustment; and that's the end of the scale [that is, they can't get it to work].

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, we're busy activating the scale experts. [Long Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Hey, tell me where they stowed the pliers in here.

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by, Pete. [Long Pause] Pete, our first cut [that is, first guess] on the plier location is in one of the PPKs [Personal Preference Kits].

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. [Long Pause while somebody in Houston digs out a stowage list]

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, it's in the lower lunar boot compartment.

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, 1 minute to LOS.

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston [Pause] Intrepid, Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Al, how you coming on weighing the water?

speaker: Gibson
text: Our suggestion is that, if you don't see that you're going to be able to do it in a short period of time, that you move on. Suggestion is that you look for something where you can accurately measure its volume, and we'll calibrate it when you come back. And the last alternative is [to] just plain guess at the volume [of water]. [Pause]

speaker: Bean
text: Okay, Houston. Well, let us think about it a minute. We're still working on the scale. [Pause]

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Al. We copy. [Long Pause]

speaker: Bean
text: Eureka; we did it! Got the nut back on.

speaker: Gibson
text: Well done, Intrepid.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston! One RCU weighs 3.8 kilograms on this nickel/dime scale.

speaker: Gibson
text: [A bit incredulous] Copy, 3.8 kilograms.

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, if that's what KG stands for at the top of the scale. I'm sorry. Make it point three eight. 0.38.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We copy 0.38. You had us wondering down here - a few of us. The metric fellows were wondering.

speaker: Conrad
text: [Chuckling] Me, too.

speaker: Bean
text: This [feedwater collection] bag is really filling up. Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Al. Is that the CDR's?

speaker: Bean
text: That's right. [Long Pause]

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, for your information, your EVA went 4 hours and 1 minute [from 3.5 psi cabin pressure to 3.5]. And, Al, you were the shortest in terms of quantity remaining. Your PLSS H2O was down to 47 minutes remaining [an estimate since they are still measuring the residual water]; and, Pete, your O2 was most critical on you. And you had still 2 hours 7 minutes left.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. [Long Pause]

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. Pete's water bag weighs 0.26 kilograms.

speaker: Gibson
text: Copy, 0.26.

speaker: Conrad
text: Say, Houston. While we're doing this, what was our BTU output level, do you figure?

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by. [Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: I say, what BTU level do you think we were working at?

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, you averaged out at 900 BTU; and, Al, you averaged out at 1000. [Long Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: What kind of signals are you getting from the ALSEP? Is that running all right?

speaker: Gibson
text: That's affirmative. It's running real well. The PSE and LSM are up and working; and they're just going through the activation phases for the remainder.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. [Long Pause]

speaker: Bean
text: 0.17 kilograms for the LMP's water.

speaker: Gibson
text: 0.17. Got it. [Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: And, Houston, I'm going to go ahead and top off our PLSSs [with oxygen]; and, while we're doing that, I guess we ought to get into our EVA debriefing with you.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We're standing by for that.

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, Houston. We also have your lift-off block data for Rev 20 to 24.

speaker: Bean
text: Wait one. [Long Pause while Al gets out the Flight Data book so that he can write the times in a pre-printed table] Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: That's correct, Al. [Pause]

speaker: Bean
text: Say, Houston, I'm a little bit puzzled about that TV camera. Do you think it had some sort of mechanical failure or did we point it at the Sun too much?

speaker: Gibson
text: That's a question right now, and we're trying to figure it out. We got mechanical and Vidicon-burn people taking sides. We're not sure right now.

speaker: Conrad
text: We got lots of room. We'll bring it back for you.

speaker: Gibson
text: That is a possibility, Intrepid.

speaker: Conrad
text: Say, Houston. Do you have any questions that you wanted to ask us about the EVA?

speaker: Gibson
text: That's affirmative. We'd like to get your comments first if we could, and then we'll take up the questions and recommendations that we can come up with.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. My first comment is that I got water in both my boots, and it's driving me buggy.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. Copy. Water in the boots.

speaker: Conrad
text: My second comment is that the EVA went pretty well as planned. I think that most everything - once we got to a task the way we had practiced it back there - we got it done. It was kind of the unforeseen, as usual, which almost got us behind. I will say one thing. It very definitely took about 10 minutes or so to adapt to what was going on, but as soon as I did, I really got the hot-foot, and I think that Al felt the same way.

speaker: Gibson
text: I think from our end down here, Pete and Al, you did a tremendous job. You were able to go along, as you said, on the nominal things and take care of the off-nominal also. There were quite a few points there where we might not have met the objective had you not played heads up ball.

speaker: Bean
text: [Referring to the troubles they'd had getting the fuel element out of the cask] Yeah; that's the handy of having a hammer aboard.

speaker: Conrad
text: My heart was in my throat when he couldn't pull that cask out of there. [Pause] I mean the element out of the cask.

speaker: Gibson
text: Al, you should have been a surgeon.

speaker: Conrad
text: As far as the geology goes... [Stops to listen to Gibson] That was me that was beating with the hammer, not Al. [Pause] As far as the geology goes, we really didn't have a chance to look too hard; but I think it's very obvious that there are a variety of different kinds of rocks. I would also like to say that I think that we're in a most favorable position to get to the Surveyor. I don't think we want to walk down the crater wall from... the crater-wall side that the Surveyor is on. I think what we want to do is walk down in the crater right from the LM across the bottom and walk up to Surveyor. It looks far too steep to approach from the other side - near the upper part. That's number one. Number two, I think that we're pretty well game for any kind of a [geology] traverse that you want us to make. You know, what we can do here in a few minutes is sit down with our book and put together the best of spot 3 and 4. And y'all can do the same thing. [Pause]

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay, Pete. We're leaning right now towards the traverse for site 4 , although we wouldn't take it necessarily in the same order it's spelled out there. If you want, you can get out your notes on board for site 4, and we could give you a tentative spell out of the order in which you would hit those points. And in looking at it, I see it would take you down the western wall of the Surveyor crater, which is, I believe, the way you want to go.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yeah. Let me find number 4 here, just a second; I'll be right with you. [Long Pause] Say, that ought to work out pretty darn clever, actually, to start at F-C which is essentially where we landed there.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. That's affirmative. We show our present thoughts on where you landed are R-2, 15.0. And, if you like, I'll go ahead and give you the order in which you could hit those points that are spelled out. A through G.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hey, wait a minute. I'm going to improve your knowledge of where we are. It just came to me what crater I'm looking into here. I am sitting approximately 120 feet northeast from the number 3 crater - that's 3 in age - that is on the east side of the Head Crater. Which would be. Q... No; as a matter of fact, we're right on about Q-5 and about 14.1.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. We copy that. [Pause] The back room will be thinking about that, and we'll get back to you on it.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Gibson
text: That puts you pretty close.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Now give me some words about the water in my boots. I'm not kidding. I've got water in my boots and I want to know what to do about it. I didn't get any water out of my drain hoses, but I'm just beginning to pick up water in my left boot. I had it in my right boot for a while.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. Stand by, Pete; we will be right with you.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. I tell you, the first thing I am going to do is disconnect the suit hoses.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. We're thinking about that, Pete, and why don't we go on with this debriefing? And we'll get back to you as soon as we can come up with a good recommendation. [No answer]

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, can we go ahead with the debriefing? What I'd like to do is give you the recommended order for the points in traverse 4.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Just a second. I disconnected my hoses. This blue hose is really pumping out pretty moist air. I'm just going to let it pump it out. The air is ice-cold air and I think that's part of the problem. Is there some way we can warm up this air?

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by with that, Pete. [Long Pause] Pete, would you give us the position of the suit temperature control valve and also confirm that the LCG pump circuit breaker is pulled?

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Suit Temp [control] is full Cold. I guess we'll go to full Hot on that.

speaker: Gibson
text: Affirmative.

speaker: Conrad
text: And the LCG pump breaker is out [meaning that the breaker has been pulled and the pump is off].

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. [Long Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Go ahead; give me your recommended sites now.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. Okay. Number 1 would be F, and that's Head Crater; number 2, B, Bench Crater; number 3, A, Sharp Crater; and we might possibly delete this depending on how you are doing on the timeline at that point. Number 4 is C, Halo Crater; number 5, D, Surveyor Crater; 6 is E, Block Crater; and we'll omit G. [Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Now where is A? [Pause] Oh, it's Sharp Crater, is that right?

speaker: Gibson
text: That's affirm. A is Sharp Crater. And we may just cut across that corner depending upon how you are doing with the timeline.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yeah. But don't we also want to get out here on this possible Copernican ray stuff? [Pause] Oops, excuse me, Uel Clanton, material.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We do want to get off after [that is, go get] that Copernican ray material. Two points: one is it's further out than you might be able to hack in a normal traverse for the documented samples; and, two, we're not too sure exactly where that line [that is, the edge of the supposed ray] really lies. If you can, go on over into that area without taking a lot of time away from the other documented sampling; press on.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Now, in looking at the map, we got all the way over to... If you go to, what is it, the general map, map 5, or whatever you want to call them, we got over in that Shelf Crater [Middle Crescent Crater]. That's where you sent us, and we got to that fellow, so some of that stuff we picked up might be of that Copernican ray material. We also had photographs down there of that shelf, which everybody thought was interesting. I took a set of stereos in that thing, all the way around that big crater. Now, we made it over there with no strain. Matter of fact, we ran over and ran back in nothing flat. So, I think it's reasonable to go as you have indicated. Which would be one, starting at F, which is right in front of the spacecraft, then going to Sharp, then going to Bench, then to Halo, then to the Surveyor crater, then to Block, and back to the spacecraft. How's that sound?

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. That sounds real good. Understand you'd like to go Sharp [Crater] and then Bench [Crater].

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, yeah; we can try that.

speaker: Gibson
text: Rog. No problem. [Pause] Okay, Pete, if you would, take a look at the information you have there on those sites, and we'll be getting back to you in the pre-EVA briefing and talk a little bit more about the location of the sampling, the core tubes, and the trench site sampling.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Gibson
text: You may have some pretty good ideas on that now, after being able to look at it first hand. [Pause] And, Pete, we have several questions for you related to the EVA. We'd like to move through these pretty quickly, as we know we ought to get you off to bed pretty quickly.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Gibson
text: First, a question on the water in the boots. When was the first time you got water in the boots, Pete; and, Al, do you have any [in yours] at the present time?

speaker: Conrad
text: Al doesn't have any. I noticed it just starting before... I just got off the suit loop to Prep for EVA. It started in my right boot when I came back in. And these hoses - blue hose, of course - pumped out about three or four three-quarter-inch balls of water when I first disconnected it, just a few seconds ago.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. Thank you, Pete. [Pause] Question for you, Al. In the EVA Prep, the PLSS Comm check took longer than nominal. What corrective action did you take; and do you think we may have a problem the second time around?

speaker: Bean
text: None at all. It was completely my error. At the front of the RCU, there's a switch, it goes Main, Off, Push-to-Talk or something like that... Momentary, it is. And we should have had it at Main and we didn't. And so we were a little confused there for a while.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Bean
text: It was entirely an onboard problem.

speaker: Conrad
text: Question for you, Houston. How long was our total EVA Prep time?

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by on that one. [Pause] Pete, your total EVA Prep time was 2 hours and 8 minutes.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. I believe we'll do it in about 1 plus 45 tomorrow as planned. Like Al said: one, we made a couple of mistakes; and the other one, we just had our heads up and locked. Something we didn't have on the checklist and we should have known better.

speaker: Gibson
text: Al, second question. When you put the core tubes in, do you now think it's feasible to join two core tubes together and perhaps get at least one and a half core tube lengths in? Something on that order?

speaker: Bean
text: Yeah. It was getting harder as I drove it in, just like it does back on Earth. But I think if you wanted to stand there and pound, maybe three times as long as you would have to drive in one, you could do it. And I don't know if we could do that now, though, with those pins in, but maybe we could take those pins out and put two of them together. I'd sure be willing to give it a try if you'd want to do it.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. We'll be thinking about that one and get back to you with it. Apparently, the augering is what made the difference there. If you're looking at your map...

speaker: Bean
text: That and you've got to pound the... [Stops to listen to Gibson]

speaker: Gibson
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Bean
text: No comment there. [Long Pause]

speaker: Gordon
text: Hello, Houston; Clipper.

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston. Read you loud and clear.

speaker: Gordon
text: [Garble] stand by [garble] the E-memory dump [garble].

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. Stand by on that Dick.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. If you're watching the computer, I'm going to bring it out of Standby and put it back in again to update the clock time.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Intrepid. [Long Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: There's another one of those downlink too-fast alarms.

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston. We're ready for the E-Mod.

speaker: Gordon
text: Here it comes.

speaker: Gordon
text: [Garble] the onboard readouts [garble] I have for the Batteries; 36.1 volts, Battery C, pyro Bat A, pyro Bat B.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Intrepid. Copy 36.1 volts, and would you say which ones those apply to?

speaker: Gordon
text: Say again, Ed.

speaker: Gibson
text: Clipper you gave me a reading 36.1 volts. I didn't copy; for which batteries were you reading that out?

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. That's three of them on battery C, pyro Bat A, and pyro Bat B.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. And we'll be up to you with an RCS update in a minute.

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, for the sleep period in order to get a little extra signal margin on the Omni's, we'd like first of all - you'll be turning your High Gain to Off; S-Band, Normal; Voice to Off; S-Band, Auxiliary; Tape to Off. If you have to call ground, do it on Downvoice Backup.

speaker: Gibson
text: Clipper, did you copy?

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, Houston. Would you give us aft Omni? [No answer] Intrepid, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: First, would you give us [the] aft Omni [directional antenna]? And we are ready to pick up with the debriefing.

speaker: Conrad
text: Aft S-band? Is that what you want? [Long Pause]

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, negative. That's the VHF antenna.

speaker: Conrad
text: [Garbled] [Stops to listen] [Long Pause]

speaker: Gibson
text: And, Intrepid, we're ready to pick up with the debriefing.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. Two questions related to the mounds which you saw out there. Is the object at R-5, 13.1 a mound or a rock? And, secondly, confirm that you did get a sample of the mound material.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes. We got a sample of the mound material; we got lots of them. And would you say again the coordinates?

speaker: Gibson
text: Coordinates are R-5, 13.1. [Long Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: No. I don't think so, Houston. This mound is too small to show up like that. I believe. I'll look at it a little bit more here for a minute and think about it. The mound... I'll tell you where the mound is. The mound is not seen on the map. What you gave me was a crater.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We copy that. And on that mound sample, you got material from the mound as well as material around the mound itself.

speaker: Conrad
text: That's right. We can get, tomorrow, a documented sample if you want.

speaker: Gibson
text: We will talk to you about that in the briefing before the EVA, Pete. And a question on the number and sizes of rocks. What was the ratio of fines to rocks that you finally ended up with? [Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: I put two of the large scoops worth of fill [that is, regolith] in one bag that had three rather large rocks in it; I think it's three. And the other bag of rocks fills half of the rock box, and I guess there were, what would you say, Al, 10 [or] 12 rocks in there? And the rock box is full to the top. I couldn't get anything more in there, I'll tell you that, and get the core tube in there. That's it.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We copy that. One question on the SIDE dust cover. Was the SIDE dust cover well aligned after reclosing? And the reason for asking that is in case we suspect a misalignment, we would try to activate that now and if it doesn't work, we'd have a manual backup.

speaker: Bean
text: The SIDE dust cover popped off about three times, Houston. And the last time it popped off was when we just finished aligning it neatly [and] level and we put out the cold cathode ion gauge. And the cover popped off again, and we didn't want to disturb the experiment to try and put the cover back on. We'd spent already overtime on it, so we just left the cover off. So, as the experiment sets right now, the cover is off. Now if this is not acceptable, I guess we can take a swing by there tomorrow and try to put the cover back on. And we can put it on lined up accurately as it was to begin with, if that is what you want.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. Stand by on that, and we'll be massaging that one tonight.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. My recommendation is - unless it is going to hurt the SIDE - to leave it just like it is, because it is just a precariously balanced experiment over there and it is going to take time to do it right.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We copy that, Al. And, Pete, could you give us an estimate of the number of rocks that you have on board?

speaker: Conrad
text: I really didn't get a count, Houston. Well, let me see. I guess it would be about, [to Al] wouldn't you say, about 15 to 20 rocks is all.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. We are looking for really the quantity of rocks, pounds of rocks.

speaker: Conrad
text: That rock box is heavy, I'll tell you that. I think it is right up to Max.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. That is good enough. One last question, Al. When you took the fuel element out, in the extraction, what was the force profile like? In other words, did it all of a sudden come free at one point or did it gradually come free as you extracted it?

speaker: Bean
text: Well, Pete started pounding on the side; and, as it came out, an eighth of an inch at a time - make that a sixteenth of an inch at a time - until it was about three-eighths of an inch out. And once it was three-eighths of an inch out, it slid out rather easily.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We copy that.

speaker: Conrad
text: What is the fuel cask made out of?

speaker: Gibson
text: That's graphite.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Well, I pretty well was beginning to bang it up pretty badly. As a matter of fact, I think I cracked it. I had better go look at it tomorrow. But I was rapping it as hard as I could and was getting about an eighth of an inch at a time until he finally got about, what would you say, Al, an inch and a half out, and then it came all the way.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. [Pause] Pete, no problem with that. You don't have to go back to it.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. [Long Pause]

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, we have a procedure here in order to get the water out of the suit loop. First, [put the] suit loop... [correcting himself] or the Suit Isolation [Valve to] Disconnect, both; [then] disconnect the O2 hoses. [Next, put the] Suit Isolation [valves] to Suit Flow, both; lower the outlet of the hose to floor for about 2 minutes. [After that, put the] Suit Isolation [valves] to Disconnect, both; connect both O2 hoses; [and, finally, put the] Suit Isolation [valves to] Suit Flow, both.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, I understand that one, and we'll do it in a little bit. We're eating right now. I got my hoses disconnected anyhow.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. And we don't see a real easy way of getting the water out of the boots. If you turn the heat way, way up, we may be able to dry some of it out. And the other thing is to use gravity in whatever way you could use it.

speaker: Conrad
text: I don't have that much water in there, and it's drying up. Or, at least, it's as warm as I am right now, so it's not bothering me and it's no sweat.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: I just want to make sure the suit loop's running right, that's all.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete.

speaker: Bean
text: Say, Houston. Question for you.

speaker: Gibson
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Bean
text: Here's a question for you, Houston. With the tapemeter being like it is and those erratic readings we seem to be getting approaching PDI, as far as the backup perilune monitor check. How are we going to use that tapemeter tomorrow when we're trying to update the AGS in range and range rate [during rendezvous]?

speaker: Gibson
text: That's a good question, Al. We'll be working on that one. That's another one for tomorrow. We're going to have a lot of people thinking hard over the sleep period.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, I think we could just call Noun 78 with P20 running. Isn't that right?

speaker: Bean
text: You could do that...

speaker: Conrad
text: And the first thing that I'd propose doing, Houston, is we'll get a quick airborne check after we launch and I get a manual lock-on or something, go do a Verb 63, and check the tapemeter against the DSKY .

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: That's no big deal.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Intrepid.

speaker: Gibson
text: We recommend, also, that you shoot for the 3-1/2-hour EVA. [Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. And we'll wake you up at the nominal time in the flight plan [which is 129:55].

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston.[Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston.[Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, Clipper. Go ahead.

speaker: Gibson
text: Clipper, you have A-C rolls selected in the DAP. Would you verify that your A-C thrusters are also enabled?

speaker: Gordon
text: [Garble] select [garble].

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, we also have a lift-off block data for Rev 20 through 24 when you're ready to copy and the RCS totals, if you're interested.

speaker: Gordon
text: Yes, I sure am interested in the [garble] just a second, though.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Dick.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. Go ahead.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. Copy. Thank you very much. Is that it for the day?

speaker: Gibson
text: You're welcome, Clipper. And say again the question.

speaker: Gordon
text: I said, Was that it for the day?

speaker: Gibson
text: Clipper, again you were broken; repeat the question.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, I guess that's it for the night, huh?

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. That's it, Dick, except for one thing. Would you verify that your pyro Bat readings are 36.1 rather than 37.17.

speaker: Gordon
text: They are 37 - 37.1.

speaker: Gibson
text: Copy, 37.1. Thank you. We'll talk to you in the morning.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 121 hours, 59 minutes and in Mission Control, we are changing shifts at this time. Flight Director Glynn Lunney has taken over from Flight Director Jerry Griffin. Our Capsule Communicator is astronaut Paul Weitz. Our Change of Shift press conference will begin shortly in the Houston news conference. The participants are leaving Mission Control at this time. At 121 hours, 60 minutes, 122 hours, rather, this is Mission Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Intrepid.

speaker: Weitz
text: Go ahead, Intrepid.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. When do you want us to change the... Give me a time for the [ECS Primary] LiOH cartridge change, would you, please?

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Sure will, Pete. Now we got a couple more questions to get rid of some Irish pennants here; and when you answer these, we can turn you loose to go to sleep.

speaker: Weitz
text: First off, what are your intentions for your suit-hose configuration for sleep? Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: Al says he's hot, and he's going to leave his connected to blow air. I'll probably sleep with mine [his suit hoses] off.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Understand. Secondly [as per checklist], how about, for our friendly surgeon, a crew status report and a medication and radiation status?

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. The crew's in super shape; no medication; and let me look at my little Rad[iation] counter here, just a second.

speaker: Bean
text: [Sounding quite stuffy] LMP had one of those decongestant pills just prior to EVA.

speaker: Weitz
text: Understand, Al.

speaker: Conrad
text: And my Rad counter is 11020.

speaker: Bean
text: And mine's 04020.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay, thank you. One last question. Did you have any problems with the tapemeter during your descent other than it reading high on the perilune check?

speaker: Bean
text: We had it in Altitude/Altitude Rate on the descent, naturally; and it looked to me like it agreed pretty closely with the PGNS's numerical readout on the DSKY . That's what kind of concerns me about the rendezvous radar. Also, that low transmitter power - maybe they're hooked in somehow.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Thank you.

speaker: Conrad
text: I disagree on low transmitter power. We got surface lockup when the command module went by at a good P22. The tapemeter did not run in the P22 like it does in the simulator, I'll say that for it. And secondly, it was off - I don't remember the number now - but it was off from its normal reading in self-test. Although the PGNS portion of rendezvous radar self-test was absolutely correct. So I suspect that there may be just something wrong with that tapemeter. I don't think there's anything wrong with the rendezvous radar itself.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay, thank you. And it was not in agreement; it was not erratic in operation in any way, was it?

speaker: Conrad
text: Nope; it runs just perfect - not erratic. I think there's just... My impression of these perilune altitude checks, I think, [is that] there may be a bias on it, like 30 or 40 feet per second.

speaker: Weitz
text: Roger, Intrepid. Thank you. [Long Pause] Intrepid, Houston. Pete, the second time you disconnected your suit hoses, did you get any water out of the hoses then?

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, it was the second time that I got all the water out of them. I took them off the first time and put them on the floor as advertised and didn't get any water out of them. I put them back on again; I started getting water in my boots, so I took them off that time, and I never put them on the floor; I just took them off and it blew three three-quarter-inch water balls right out of it, that splattered all over the spacecraft. And, since then, it's been pretty good. And we turned the suit-dealie [the suit-circuit temperature control] here up full-hot, and we'll see how that works.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Thank you. [Long Pause] Intrepid, Houston. Has Al done the same thing with his hoses, Pete? And, if he has not, we would like to request that he do so before you turn in.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yeah, he hasn't gotten any water, but he's going to drain them right now. Now, look, you got us down here for an hour to eat tomorrow. We're in one-sixth g and it doesn't take us anywheres near that long to eat; we can whistle through things a lot faster. I think we can pretty well stick to the nominal timeline and get a good night's rest. It may turn out, that after 6 or 7 hours worth of sleep, we're going to get stirring because we're both up. And we're not going to sit here. So, we'll give you a holler whenever we get up, and we're going to start cooking right then and there and be ready to go over the sill ASAP [as soon as possible] so we can get as good a EVA out of it as possible and not cut ourselves at the end.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. That will be fine, Pete.

speaker: Weitz
text: Intrepid, Houston. Request that Al go to Suit Flow while he's disconnected so [that], if there is any water in there, it will blow it on out.

speaker: Bean
text: [Expressing his pleasure, with perhaps a small hint of sarcasm] That's a pretty reasonable request.

speaker: Weitz
text: Hello, Intrepid; Houston. Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Pete, can we have the results of Al's suit loop check?

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. He got two drops of water. That's it.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay; understand. And on that lithium hy[droxide]...

speaker: Bean
text: It's one of those mysteries of life, Paul. I don't have any water in mine, to speak of, and Pete has his coming out all the time. We've been shifting over to [Water] Separator B, but I really don't think that's the answer. Must be something to do... Just like on Neil's spacecraft with [garbled] hoses or the way it turns or something else.

speaker: Weitz
text: Roger, Al. Understand. And also, on the lithium hydroxide canister change, if it fits in with your activities at that time, we would like to have it changed out at 130 hours on the clock. And, for your information, you're 12 minutes past the halfway mark in your total mission time.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. And you want the LiOH out at 130:00?

speaker: Weitz
text: That's affirmative. [Long Pause] Intrepid, Houston. Let us know when you're getting ready to turn in, Pete, and we won't bother you any more.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We're still doodling around here a little bit; we're just getting ready to rig the hammocks now.

speaker: Weitz
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: Al wanted to go EVA again, and I restrained him until tomorrow.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Good show.

speaker: Conrad
text: Say, Houston, do you want us to go to Down Voice, Backup and Power Amplifier, Off?

speaker: Weitz
text: Stand by there, Intrepid. [Pause] Intrepid, Houston. That's affirmative, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We're going Down Voice, Backup and Power Amplifier, Off, at this time and configuring for sleep.

speaker: Weitz
text: Roger, Pete. Nighty-night.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, and I understand 129:55 is reveille [as per checklist]. Is that right?

speaker: Weitz
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We'll gauge it on that. Nighty-night.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 122 hours, 57 minutes. During the Change of Shift Briefing we said goodnight to the crew of Intrepid and also to Dick Gordon aboard Yankee Clipper. We last heard from our Yankee Clipper at about 122 hours. The CSM has now gone behind the Moon and we're scheduled to reacquire at about 34 minutes...we said goodnight to Conrad and Bean in Intrepid at 122 hours, 37 minutes.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control...we'll continue to stand by live now. We have about 24 minutes until reacquiring Dick Gordon in the Command Module and it's been about 30 minutes since we said goodnight to the crew of Intrepid on the lunar surface...at 123 hours, 9 minutes this is Apollo Control Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 124 hours, 1 minute. It has been about 1 and 1/2 hours since we said goodnight to the crew of Intrepid, Commander Pete Conrad and Lunar Module Pilot, Al Bean, and it has been about 2 hours since we last heard from Dick Gordon aboard Yankee Clipper. At Mission Control we have monitoring systems on both spacecrafts. Everything continues to look normal. Flight Director Glynn Lunney has been reviewing the status of the Extra Vehicular Mobility unit for the upcoming second EVA. We'll continue to leave the air-to-ground circuits up live should we have any conversation from the spacecraft. The scheduled wakeup time is 129 hours, 55 minutes. Pete Conrad advised before beginning the rest period that if he and Al Bean were to awake earlier than the scheduled wakeup time, they would expect to get up and get going working toward their EVA. At 124 hours, 2 minutes, this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 125 hours, 3 minutes. The sleep period is scheduled to end about 5 hours from now. The Command Module, Yankee Clipper has been behind the Moon now for some 20 minutes. We're scheduled to reacquire in about 26 minutes from now. The last look we had at the Command Service Module, before it went behind the Moon, everything looked good. We last heard from Dick Gordon, aboard the spacecraft, at about 122 hours at which time he advised that he was beginning his rest period. And we last heard from Pete Conrad and Al Bean aboard Intrepid at 122 hours, 37 minutes. Scheduled to wake up at 129 hours, 55 minutes. We'll continue to leave the air-to-ground circuits open throughout this sleep period should we get any conversation from the crew. In Mission Control it has settled down to a very quiet period now. We've completed reviews of the portable life support systems status and activity now is involved primarily with keeping an eye on the spacecraft's systems. At 125 hours, 5 minutes this is Apollo Control Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 126 hours. We have some 4 hours left in the rest period for both the Intrepid crew and for Dick Gordon aboard the CSM, Yankee Clipper. The sleep periods scheduled to end at 129 hours, 55 minutes. We have about 41 minutes of acquisition left on Yankee Clipper. The Command Module now in its 22nd revolution of the Moon as the spacecraft came around to the front side, the EECOM engineer reported that all systems look good on the CSM. Of course we've been monitoring systems on the LM continuously since the landing and all systems there look nominal at this time. The preliminary coordinates on the landing site are 3 degrees 2 minutes, 10 seconds south, 23 degrees, 25 minutes, 5 seconds west or expressed as a decimal figure that would - be 3.036 degrees south and 23.418 degrees west. This is a preliminary figure and we expect that there would be some refinement to that, particularly after the data, which is - data during the lift-off is worked back into the assessment of the landing site. At 126 hours, 2 minutes this is Apollo Control Houston continuing to stand by.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 127 hours, 9 minutes. We have about 19 minutes before we reacquire the Command Module, Yankee Clipper on its 23rd revolution of the Moon. A flight surgeon reports that all three crewmen are sleeping at this time. We have about a little over 2 hours, 45 minutes left in the sleep period. That sleep period is scheduled to end at 129 hours, 55 minutes. Prior to beginning the rest period, at about 122 hours, 37 minutes, Pete Conrad advised us that should he and Al Bean awaken prior to the scheduled wakeup time, they would begin preparations for Extra Vehicular Activity, and would, as he put it, go over the sill as soon as they're ready. The current orbital parameters or the Command Module, Yankee Clipper are 61.8 nautical miles or the apolune 58.7 nautical miles for perilune. The orbital period is 1 hour, 58 minutes 50 seconds. The Flight Dynamics Officer reports that the plane change maneuver performed by Yankee Clipper at 119 hours, 47 minutes and 12 seconds was nominal. The maneuver was targeted to move the ground track of the Command Module 3.8 degrees north of the present, of its previous ground track at the point it crosses lunar landing site number 7. This is to put the Command Module in plane with the Lunar Module at the time of lift-off. We're now 17 minutes from reacquiring Yankee Clipper, continuing to monitor systems on the Lunar Module. Everything continuing to look good at this time. At 127 hours, 11 minutes, this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 128 hours, 6 minutes. We are now somewhat less than 2 hours away from the scheduled end of this sleep period. The Command Module, Yankee Clipper, will shortly be passing over landing site 7 and Intrepid, we have about 34 minutes of acquisition left with the Command Module on the path. Yankee Clipper now in its 23rd revolution of the moon. We've had no conversations with any of the crewmen on either spacecraft since they began their sleep period. Dick Gordon, we last heard from, at about 122 hours and we heard last from Pete Conrad aboard the Intrepid at about 122 hours, 37 minutes. On a couple of occasions during the sleep period, the LM environmental systems engineers reported telemetry indications that Al Bean was making minor adjustments to his suit circuit, probably for temperature control, in one case raising the temperature and in the other reducing it slightly. Other than this there has been no activity from the spacecraft and no communications. And biomedical data on Pete Conrad indicates that he is sleeping soundly. We also have minor update to the coordinates for the Intrepid landing site based on Pete Conrad's description where he thought the spacecraft had touched down. The new coordinates that we have for the LM are 3.036 degrees south and that figure shows no change from the previous one and 23.416 degrees west, which is a change from the previous 23.418. The new figure again 23.416 degree west. Using the same coordinates - system for the Surveyor spacecraft, we have it at 3.04 degrees south and 23.411 degrees west. At 128 hours, 9 minutes into the flight of Apollo 12, this is Mission Control, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 128 hours, 51 minutes. We're still about 1 hour from the scheduled end of the sleep period. However, the flight surgeon reports some indications in the biomedical data that the crew may be beginning to stir. So, we'll be standing by live for any call from the spacecraft. The sleep period began for Dick Gordon in the Command Module, Yankee Clipper, at about 122 hours. We heard from Pete Conrad aboard the LM about 37 minutes after we last heard from Yankee Clipper or at about 122:37 Ground Elapsed Time. Conrad advised us at that time if he and Al Bean were awake and ready to go early, they would begin preparations ahead of schedule for their Extra Vehicular Activity. We're currently showing a Command Module in an orbit of an apolune of 61.8 nautical miles and a perilune of 58.7. The last figure we had on an orbital period for the Command Module was 1 hour, 58 minutes, 50 seconds. We'll be reacquiring Yankee Clipper in about 33 minutes and 30 seconds from now. At 128 hours, 53 minutes, this is Apollo Control standing by.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Houston; Intrepid. How are you this morning?

speaker: Weitz
text: Good morning, Intrepid. How did you sleep?

speaker: Conrad
text: Short, but sweet. We're hustling right now, and we're going to eat breakfast, have a little talk with you, and get about our business.

speaker: Weitz
text: Sounds good.

speaker: Bean
text: Houston, Intrepid. What's the local time down there, Paul?

speaker: Weitz
text: It's 19:25 now, Al. [7:25 p.m. U.S. Central Standard Time]

speaker: Bean
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. We both slept 5 hours. My PRD is 11020, and Al's is 04021.

speaker: Weitz
text: Rog. Copy, Intrepid. For information, Pete, can you see the ALSEP out the LM window?

speaker: Conrad
text: Sure can.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. When you get a chance, what I would like for you to do is: they are not getting the readings they expected from the CCIG [Cold Cathode Ion Gauge]. If you can, we would like you to give a look-see at it with the monocular to see whether you can tell whether it is right side up and whether the port has been opened or not. Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Wait one [minute]. We left that in a rather precarious position due to that cable last night, and it wouldn't surprise me if it is not upside down, face down, because that is exactly where it wanted to go.

speaker: Weitz
text: Yeah, understand, Pete. They've given a command to open the ports, and the pressure has not gone down in it at the rate they expected.

speaker: Bean
text: When we left it last night, Houston, we left it sort of on its back facing about 80 degrees from the horizontal. That was the best we could do.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Understand. [Long Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Unfortunately, Houston, it is on the opposite side of the SIDE, which is supposed to be lined up with my view of it. It does look like it's roughly the same position as we left it last night. But I can't really tell. We'll run over there after we get out and look.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Thank you, Pete. [Long Pause] Intrepid, Houston. I have got a late change for you that came in a couple of hours ago. On the rocks you are bringing back in the jettison bag , Grumman has come through and, along the way, several people have decided that the allowable weight to be stowed in the bags on the deck there should be reduced from 35 pounds to 20 pounds. That's 14 pounds of rock and one 6-pound bag.

speaker: Conrad
text: I didn't quite get the end of that. Say it again.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Stand by one, Pete. [Long Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, while you are working that problem, I would like to know if there are any restrictions on when we go over the sill. [Pause]

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Stand by, Pete, and we will give you the word on that.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. I would like to go as soon as I can get ready without hurrying. And I've kind of got the suspicion, looking over the Prep card, [that] a good bit of this stuff is done, and it is pretty much a deal of hooking up the PLSSs and going. And I think we are going to be able to get out somewhere around 131:30 to 132, and let me look at the timeline and see what we should be doing then normally.

speaker: Weitz
text: Rog, Intrepid. [Long Pause] Okay, Intrepid; Houston. That's affirmative, Pete. Whenever you're ready, at your own pace, you can go over the sill. Of course, we do want to talk to you about the briefing on the traverse before you go out.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. I'll give you a call in about 3 or 4 minutes. We have some sprucing up to do; and, while we are eating breakfast, you can give us the hot word on geology.

speaker: Bean
text: Also give us some word on the families, if you would.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay; sure will. Did you get that on the allowable weight of the materials to be brought back in the [spare] jettison bags being changed from 35 pounds to 20 pounds?

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. How far down on the scale is that? I can't remember.

speaker: Weitz
text: It's 1 inch, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: One inch. Rog. [Long Pause]

speaker: Weitz
text: Intrepid, Houston. They want the TV camera brought back, so I've got some changes to your surface checklist to cover stowing it for return when you are ready to copy.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, wait one.

speaker: Bean
text: What [checklist] page?

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Page 65 to start with.

speaker: Bean
text: We're there. Go ahead.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Down under the block that contains words rest periods, about the fourth item down is voice-to-voice. We want to insert in there a step to stow utility towels from the hammocks in the upper boot box. These will be used, as I will describe to you later, to protect the TV camera when you stow it for return.

speaker: Conrad
text: Shucks. We already took them out to use to keep ourselves nice and clean.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. [Pause] Okay. Now, on page 67 of the surface checklist.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. On the right-hand column under EVA-2 Prep, about the eighth or ninth line down, it says remove ECS lithium hydroxide cartridge and bracket. Do not remove the bracket. Keep it on the engine cover. Over.

speaker: Bean
text: Good idea.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Now, on page 77 . [Long Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Go.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. On the right-hand column under LMP, next to the last step after Verify circuit breaker, insert a step to open the TV circuit breaker.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay, Houston. In other words, you say to turn the TV on to begin with and then before I get out to open it. Is that the plan?

speaker: Weitz
text: That's affirmative, Al. I should have made that clear. They want to try one more look to see if something short of a miracle occurred, and then you will open the circuit breaker again before you get out.

speaker: Bean
text: Sounds good. Be sure to remind me because it's not on my cuff checklist, and I won't have this one [the LM checklist] out. And what's the latest thinking on that, too?

speaker: Weitz
text: You mean on why it didn't work, Al?

speaker: Bean
text: That's right.

speaker: Weitz
text: That hasn't been resolved yet.

speaker: Bean
text: Man, I worried about that one all night.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Don't sweat it. On page 78 now. [Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Go.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Under the CDR. Now, we're going to have you use your Surveyor dismantling tool, I guess, on this TV camera - the [bolt] cutters - to get it apart. So add a couple of steps here, Pete, at the end of your list. We want you to cut the TV cable on the spacecraft side of the camera connector, below the adapter. And then stow the TV...

speaker: Conrad
text: Yeah. I understand.

speaker: Weitz
text: And then stow the TV camera in the ETB.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. We'll remind you of these steps since they're not on your checklist.

speaker: Bean
text: Also mention...[Stops to listen to Weitz] That's right, because they're not on the cuff.

speaker: Weitz
text: Rog. [Long Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Go ahead, Paul.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Now, on page 93 . [Long Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. In the right-hand column, the fourth or fifth line up, after Unstow 70 millimeter cameras, add a step to unstow the TV camera from the ETB and stow on the engine cover.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. Next step. [Pause]

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. It's been written on page 97 , Pete. [Pause]

speaker: Bean
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Let me read it over here a minute, and I'll paraphrase it for you. We want to fold the TV camera. We're going to stow it in the lithium hydroxide canister [means bracket].

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. Do you want us to pack it with the towels as best we can, huh?

speaker: Weitz
text: That's affirmative. And they want it...[Pause] Just wrap the remaining...Fold the handle; wrap the cable around the camera as best you can; and stow it in the lithium-hydroxide-canister bracket on the engine cover and stow it with the lens up. Over.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. Now has anybody checked to make sure that we can fit the camera and all the cables and stuff in that fitting?

speaker: Weitz
text: That's affirm...

speaker: Bean
text: You probably can, but I don't know.

speaker: Weitz
text: That's affirmative. They had and...

speaker: Bean
text: Oop. [Pause] Okay. The only reason I wondered is in case it...We'll make it work.

speaker: Weitz
text: Rog. The lens will stick up. It's been checked out; the lens will protrude up out of the canister stowage about 6 [or] 7 inches and they then want you to wrap some utility straps around the end of the camera to hold it in place.

speaker: Bean
text: We'll do it. [Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Consider it done. [Let's] press [on].

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. And one other thing, on your tiedown of this bag with the extra rocks in it, they want you to run an additional strap...Stand by one. [Pause] Okay. After you get the bag secured on the deck there between you, they want an additional strap run from the straps holding the bag down up to the ISA D-ring for additional support. Over.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. We'll do it.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. That takes care of our procedure changes this morning. I'll give your families a call and get the word back up to you in about 5 or 10 minutes.

speaker: Bean
text: Sounds good.

speaker: Conrad
text: What's the Yankee Clipper doing, sleeping?

speaker: Weitz
text: Yeah. He's cutting off a few Z's there. [Pause] Clipper's scheduled to sleep until 131:30, and our intention now is to let him sleep until then, if he does.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. I got a couple of messages for you here I'll read up to you. The officers and crew of the USS Independent or - correction - of the USS Intrepid extend their best wishes to all three of you. They're following your progress closely as you write another intrepid chapter in American history. And, from the blue Caribbean, they wish you smooth sailing on your voyage across the vast ocean of space and their thoughts and prayers are with you.

speaker: Conrad
text: Thank you.

speaker: Conrad
text: Say, Houston; Intrepid. I'm going to bring the computer out of P06 and put it back to bed again.

speaker: Weitz
text: Stand by. [Long Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. I've got another one of those 1105 alarms, which is uplink too fast. I don't know why that happens all the time, but it does. I'm going to go ahead and put it back to sleep again.

speaker: Weitz
text: That's fine, Pete. [Long Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. It's back in Standby.

speaker: Weitz
text: Roger.

speaker: Weitz
text: Hello, Intrepid; Houston. I have a consumables update for you, if you want it, Pete; and, after that, I've got some lift-off block data. [Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Go ahead with the consumables update, and then the block data.

speaker: Weitz
text: All right. RCS [Reaction Control System] Alpha is 80 percent; Bravo is 76; oxygen is 76 [percent in the descent tank] and 96 [percent in the ascent tank]; water, 47 and 99; and your amp hours [remaining] is 850 and 572.

speaker: Weitz
text: The lift-off block data for Rev 25, which is T13, is 132:11:35; Rev 26/T14, is 134:09:59; Rev 27/T15, 136:08:25; Rev 28/T16, is 138:06:50. Over. [Pause]

speaker: Bean
text: Roger, Houston. We copied the consumables updates, and here are the lift-off times 132:11:35. 134:09:59. 136:08:25. 138:06:50.

speaker: Weitz
text: That's affirmative, Al. [Long Pause] Hello, Intrepid; Houston. I have a couple of words on your rendezvous radar self-test and your tapemeter , if you're interested in them now.

speaker: LM Crew
text: Go.

speaker: Weitz
text: Okay. Your rendezvous radar self-test was good. The checklist had the spec [specification] values, not the actual values, which is the reason for the difference. They ran through them on the ground and it checked out four oh [4.0, meaning perfect]. Your tapemeter perilune checks were also good. MPAD ran a solution through on the ground here using the actual CSM state vectors. They had been slightly perturbed, and they came up with the same values off the chart as you did.

speaker: Bean
text: Fantastic.

speaker: Weitz
text: How about that?

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. Then you think our tapemeter is going to be accurate during the rendezvous then? We can just use that data?

speaker: Weitz
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. [Coughs] How about giving me the word on geology now?

speaker: Weitz
text: He [Ed Gibson]'ll be with you in a minute, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. [Long Pause]

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete and Al, Houston. We're ready to go with the traverse plan.

speaker: Conrad
text: Ho, ho, ho. Good morning.

speaker: Gibson
text: Good morning, good morning. We can pick it up at LSE 7-6G. I think that is the easiest way to follow it on your map.

speaker: Conrad
text: I have it right in my hand. Go.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. First of all, the two prime sites we consider on here are Bench and Sharp craters. We could pretty much follow the traverse which we discussed before. What I'd like to do is give you the additional information that you don't have on your sheet and also, perhaps, to discuss how we'll fit the ALSEP revisit into this. Your first point along the traverse is Head Crater, which we call out 'f' [on the pre-planned traverse]. What we would like to do, in view of the fact that you are going out towards the ALSEP, is to move that site over to the northwest rim of Head Crater; and coordinates there are R-0, 11.0 [drawn at 12.0 on the Houston map]. And then, you will carry out what we already have outlined for Head Crater. That's the two partial pans across Head Crater and document the slumps and ledges. In addition to that, seeing as we have the PSE [Passive Seismic Experiment] so closely located to that, we would like to see if we can get a known signal for the PSE; so, if possible, could you roll a large crater - [correcting himself] a large boulder - the former would have been a little bit harder. Roll a large rock into the crater and take a stereopair of the rock rolling...

speaker: Bean
text: Good recovery. [Pause]

speaker: Gibson
text: Take a stereopair of the rock prior to rolling and a stereopair of the track made by the rock after rolling. Okay; that's point 1. Do you copy?

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes, sir! We'll rock and roll! [Hearty LM laughter]

speaker: Bean
text: [Laughing] Hey, we've had a lot of training for that sort of thing on the geology trips we had.

speaker: Conrad
text: [Still laughing] We're with you all the way. Let's press on from the Head.

speaker: Gibson
text: [Laughing; with a good deal of Houston laughter audible in the background] Roger. We've got some happy looking geologists here. We have Uel Clanton back here, and he's betting that somewhere along the traverse, you'll find some stuff.

speaker: Conrad
text: [Laughing] I think there's stuff all over the place.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. After this first point, then you can go on out to ALSEP. And word on the CCIG is to make sure that it is laying on its back. We would like for you to confirm, however, that you did try to lay it down in the normal mode and that the only way you thought you could make it work is having it lay on its back.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yeah. Look, we are going to go the other way around, I think. Let's go to ALSEP and then to [Station] 1. [Pause] That's the Head crater.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. Fine. Either way you want it. [Pause] Yeah; looking at the geometry...

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, let me tell you another thing while you're standing there. I want to tell you, I do have Bench Crater in view from the window; Sharp Crater, I do not. So it looks to me like it would be relatively easy to go to ALSEP [and then] to the coordinates you gave me on Head Crater. And I am looking at it [Head Crater] right now, and I see several rocks which might do what you want us to do [and] which we might be able to roll down the side of that crater. And followed by one astronaut, probably. But anyhow, we will give that a whirl. And then, is the next point you want us to go Sharp? And, if so, let's press.

speaker: Gibson
text: No, Pete. The next one is Bench Crater and then we'd be moving on to Sharp.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay,...

speaker: Gibson
text: What we would like to do is to move...

speaker: Conrad
text: ...I'd kind of like to do it the other way around and that way I am going around in a circle.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. What we wanted to do was to move your Point b on Bench Crater on over to the northwest edge of that, as opposed to on the southwestern edge.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. I'm with you. Give me the coordinates and we'll do it your way.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. Coordinates on that would be M-0 and 10.0, so you would be up on the north side.

speaker: Conrad
text: Great minds think alike. That is where I was poised [with his pencil].

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. Okay, three things we would like you to do which are in addition to what we already discussed on your plan. Take stereopairs of the features of interest in Bench Crater, especially of the bench; determine whether the bench is bedrock or breccia near the base of the regolith. And, if the bench is bedrock, sample the ejecta representative of the bench or sample the bench itself, if possible. And lastly, look northwest and...

speaker: Bean
text: I understand.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Al. And lastly, in Bench Crater, look northwest and southwest from the rim of Bench Crater to see if Copernican ray material is obviously different from other units.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. Moving on to Sharp Crater, which is coordinate A. First, we call for a full trench site sample in the crest of Sharp Crater; and we want to make sure you also add to that the gas analysis sample. That looks as though it will be pretty much your furthest point out [from the LM]. We'd like a full pan from the rim of Sharp Crater; that, also, is because that is your furthest point out. And, crew option at this point, extend your traverse west into what appears to be Copernicus ray material [if any is visible] and also...

speaker: Bean
text: Hold on for a second, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. [Long Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Go ahead. Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. Last point on Sharp Crater is sample and describe differences across the contact of M-1/M-2 [as is marked in the upper left of the map], if it is apparent when you reach that region. [Pause] On your map, that shows up as a dotted line running northwest-southeast.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yeah. We've got it. [Pause] I can tell you right now, it is going to be pretty darn hard to do that. [If] you're looking cross-Sun, the material looks all the same. Looking down-Sun, it looks all the same, except it's a different color [than the cross-Sun color].

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: It's really weird. I'm sure that you can see the stuff from far out; but down here, it might as well all be the same until you get right up on top of an individual rock.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger; understand. Probably you might not see any color differences, but if you could keep your eye open for differences in rock types [and/or textures]. [Pause] Moving on to the fourth point...

speaker: Conrad
text: We will.

speaker: Gibson
text: ...which is Halo Crater, as we have it called out there. At this point, you can try to join the two core tubes together and core through the thin ejecta of Crater 6, or Halo Crater. When you do that, you'll have to pull the pip pin off the one core tube which you make the bottom tube.

speaker: Gibson
text: We'd like you to avoid the rockiest parts of the crater;...

speaker: Conrad
text: Understand.

speaker: Gibson
text: ...and, if the tubes can't be joined, just take one on the rim and then one about 100 feet west of that location.

speaker: Gibson
text: If you could, give us a pan at that location. And here is a comment which is really applicable to all of the traverse. Document patterned ground and fillets on different slopes and blocks, especially any asymmetric fillets you may run into. We would expect...Well, we would find it most interesting to get this type of information on the youngest material so that's why we call for it here, especially in Halo Crater. The best way to document patterned ground is to photo into the Sun, near-field, and that way the pattern should show up in an optimum way.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Gibson
text: And the last one [that is, the last activity on the proposed traverse] is you go on down the Surveyor Crater, and then in there we have Block Crater. We'd like, there [at Block Crater], to collect the samples of major rock types and a partial pan across the Surveyor Crater. And I think that covers it from our end.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We may have a little trouble getting to Block Crater. I'm not sure whether it is an optical illusion or what; but that wall that the Surveyor is on looks one whale of a lot steeper than 14 degrees. Now, it just may be that we are standing on the other side of the crater ourselves and it just looks a little funny. And we've been discussing the Surveyor a little bit here during the evening. And that crater gets pretty rugged over on that side, especially at the Block [Crater] area, as I remember it from yesterday. But we'll give her a go. Now, when we get in each one of these points, you can remind us of it again. I think we have it fairly well in mind what you want.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay, we'll be talking to you on the way, and one last note of clarification on that CCIG. If it's sitting up so that it's pointing horizontal to the ground [which it is], just leave it alone. If it's flipped over so that it's looking into the ground, then we want you to lay it on its back. If it's already on its back, that's good enough.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Now, the cover should be off; is that right?

speaker: Gibson
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: Conrad
text: If it's not off, should we try and take it off for you?

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by. [Long Pause while Gibson gets an answer from the Principal Investigator]

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, that's negative. If it's on there, leave it as it is.

speaker: Conrad
text: Understand.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 129 hours, 52 minutes. We're presently in the midst of a shift change in Mission Control. Flight Director Jerry Griffin coming on to replace Flight Director Glynn Lunney. The Capsule Communicator on this shift will be Astronaut Ed Gibson. We plan to have a Change Of Shift briefing at approximately 8:30 Central Standard Time in the Houston News Center. We have reacquired the Command Module, Yankee Clipper. We have about 46 minutes remaining before we lose contact with the Command Module, and we plan to continue to allow Dick Gordon to sleep. Pete Conrad advised that the crew will press ahead with preparations for their Extra Vehicular Activity. Beginning that activity as early as 131:30 Ground Elapsed Time or actually between 131:30 and 132...At 129 hours, 54 minutes, this is Apollo Control.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, one quickie. Do you want a core tube at Head Crater, or do you want us to skip that one?

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay, Al; let's look for that third core tube over at Sharp Crater. Take that in doing your trench site sampling. That will allow you to get that biological core tube sample at that point.

speaker: Bean
text: Understand. [Long Pause]

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, Houston. We're having a changeover of sites here and we may be off the line for a short while.

speaker: Bean
text: Thank you, Houston. That's a good way to do it.

speaker: Gibson
text: It'll be in about another 3 minutes that we're handing over.

speaker: Bean
text: Houston, Intrepid.

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Bean
text: A real interesting thing has happened to that solar wind collector. It's been sitting out there since yesterday, of course; and, when I left if yesterday, it was just a flat sheet of foil - you know - restrained at both ends; but as I look out there now, starting maybe a foot from the top, it has sort of folded back around the pole that's holding it. Looks almost like a sail in the wind around the pole. It's sort of bulging in the front and being bent back on the sides. It's real crazy. [Pause: Garbled under Gibson]

speaker: Gibson
text: We've got a fairly strong solar wind, I suspect, Al.

speaker: Bean
text: You may think you're kidding; I don't know.

speaker: Gibson
text: No, Al. I won't think you'd be kidding. It could be, maybe, the front part of that is just thermally expanding a lot more than the back. The back's probably radiating and the front's probably very hot. And just a thermal difference across it could do it. I'm meeting with a lot of approval back here on that idea.

speaker: Bean
text: Yeah, well, it looks like it's wrapped around the pole...That's the funny thing. It looks like the wind is blowing on it.

speaker: Gibson
text: Well, we've got two good ideas, so far. Maybe we can come up with a third.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Intrepid.

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Conrad
text: Rog. The [Primary ECS] LiOH canister was changed out at 130:00:00. EVA Prep is almost complete to PLSS donning. We're just putting the stuff [an anti-fog agent] on our visors.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. We copy.

speaker: Conrad
text: Excuse me; material.

speaker: CapCom
text: Copy.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 130 hours, 35 minutes. The news conference is ready to begin and we'll take down the release line during the conference.

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Go.

speaker: Gibson
text: Will you confirm that you did keep the bracket on the engine cover for TV camera stowage rather than putting it in the jettison bag - that is the ECS LiOH [garbled].

speaker: Bean
text: You better believe it; it's still there.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, one additional word on the CCIG. When you're...When you go out to the CCIG, we will leave the power on to the instrument and we'd like you to tell us what its status is before you touch it. If the status is such that we want it left in that configuration, you'll just move on. If you have to change its configuration, then we'll have to turn the power off and we'd like you to hold off going near it until we give you the clearance. We'll give you a reminder of this when you're on the way out.

speaker: Conrad
text: Understand.

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go.

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, Jane [garbled] sends her congratulations for a job well done. And Al, Sue has followed it all and is thrilled that you've really made it on the money. The children are fine; tired but happy, and they're going to continue following all the way through the second EVA.

speaker: Bean
text: Thank you, Ed.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger; thank you.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston. Intrepid. We'll be coming up on the PLSS Comm in about 3 minutes.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Intrepid. We're standing by.

speaker: Conrad
text: We're at the PLSS comm check, if you want to follow it.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We're with you.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at 130 hours, 57 minutes. There was very little conversation during the News Conference...

speaker: Bean
text: Houston, Intrepid.

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, Houston. We read you loud and clear.

speaker: Bean
text: Roger. I just went to FM and TV and was unable to contact you. Had you all switched over to FM? Over.

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by on that, Al. [Long Pause]

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, Houston. We're configured for the FM. Let's give it another go.

speaker: Bean
text: Coming at you. [static; Long Pause]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: [131:00:xx] Dick Gordon has 30 minutes remaining in his sleep period.

speaker: Bean
text: Houston; Intrepid.

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. How do you read?

speaker: Gibson
text: We read you loud and clear.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. We've got the TV going right now, also.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. [Pause]

speaker: Conrad

speaker: Bean

speaker: Bean
text: Okay.

text: [Garbled] PLSS mode, LMP, to A.

speaker: Bean
text: A.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello there.

speaker: Bean
text: Read you loud and clear, Pete.

speaker: Conrad

speaker: Bean
text: Got them.

speaker: Conrad
text: PLSS O2 Press gauge greater than 75 [percent].

speaker: Bean
text: It is.

speaker: Conrad
text: We have a good Comm check with me. No. I'm sorry, we don't need that. Commander going to PLSS Comm.

speaker: Bean
text: Okey-doke.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hold the [cue] card. [Long Pause]

speaker: Bean
text: [VHF] A and B is Off. Okay. [With] PLSS mode, Commander to B, you get no MSFN reception.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello there. I read you loud and clear. I got a press O flag.

speaker: Bean
text: Read you the same.

speaker: Conrad
text: I got an O2 flag and I've got 80 percent [oxygen].

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. Vent flag P and a Press flag O. Okay, that's what I've got. Usually have an O2 [flag] to begin with, do you?

speaker: Conrad
text: I've got an O2, Press, and a vent.

speaker: Bean
text: O2 will go out in a minute. Okay?

speaker: Conrad
text: Yeah.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. PLSS O2 greater than 75?

speaker: Conrad
text: Yep.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. Perform Comm [check with LMP]...Did that. PLSS mode...I'll go B and you go A. [Pause] How do you hear?

speaker: Conrad
text: Loud and clear.

speaker: Bean
text: Read you the same. Okay. PLSS mode, both of them, AR.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay

speaker: Bean
text: How do you read?

speaker: Conrad
text: Loud and clear.

speaker: Bean
text: Houston, Intrepid. How do you read?

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, we read you both loud and clear.

speaker: Conrad
text: Very good. Very good.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay, Houston, LMP's O2 quantity is 80 percent.

speaker: Gibson
text: 80 Percent. Copied.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. And CDR, 80 percent also.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. We are opening the TV circuit breaker right now.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Bean
text: Final systems Prep. CB [panel] 16 [garbled, probably ECS] Cabin Repress, Close; Verify. [Pause] It's Closed. Suit Fan Delta-P, Open. It's Open. CB [panel] 11 ECS: Suit Fan 1, Open.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay, Verify ECS Caution and H2O Sep[arator] component lights [are] On. Be on in a minute. [Pause] Yeah. Okay. Suit Gas Diverter [Valve] , Pull/Egress.

speaker: Conrad
text: I'll get it.

text: Okay. [Pause]

text: Cabin Gas Return to Egress.

text: Suit Circuit Relief is in Auto.

text: Okay. Connect to the OPSs.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. [Pause] Just a second. [Pause] There is your hose. Let me button your flap.
