speaker: Conrad
text: All right. [Hearty Conrad laugh]

speaker: Bean
text: Man, that really comes out, doesn't it? Gee, that went 50 feet!

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, let's see. Have I forgotten anything? Forgotten anything?

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, you didn't roger the film pack. Do you have all the film packs and the close-up stereo film, as well as the [LM] TV in that ETB?

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Close-up stereo film was in the ETB, two black-and-white magazines and one camera. I threw the other [70 mm] camera away because it was broken. And the TV camera went up, so I believe we've got everything, Ed.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. You got the...Also the one camera which had the third film pack on?

speaker: Conrad
text: The third film pack never got used.

speaker: Bean
text: Yeah, it did too, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Oh, did you?

speaker: Bean
text: Yeah.

speaker: Conrad
text: Oh, I'm sorry. Okay, we got three film packs and one camera up there right now. How's that?

speaker: Bean
text: Did you send the film back up?

speaker: Conrad
text: Yeah.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay, we sent all three film packs back up.

speaker: Conrad
text: Oh, oh, oh, oh. There is something I wanted to...

speaker: Bean
text: That's my low water pressure, Houston. I just turned off my water. That's good.

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by on that, Al. Pete, also how about the tools?

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes, sir. [Long Pause]

speaker: Bean
text: You might want to turn off your water too, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yeah, I knew...I was sitting here thinking there was something I ought to do. [Pause] Mine's off.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. [Pause] [I'm] out of your way.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Houston, I guess you can mark me off the lunar surface; I'm on the footpad.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We got that, Pete, at 3 hours and 50 minutes into the EVA. [Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, up-a [sic] the ladder I come. Heigh-ho, heigh-ho, heigh-ho. Boy, I'll tell you, Al, that LEC really got me dirty.

speaker: Bean
text: Yeah, it flips that dirt all around. [Long Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Heigh-ho. Oh, wait a minute; I know what I want to do. [Getting the map, see comments below] There we go. [Long Pause]

speaker: Bean
text: You want to give me that piece of paper?

speaker: Conrad
text: I couldn't get it up. I dropped it.

speaker: Bean
text: That's too bad.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston, that's my PLSS feedwater [tone because the supply has been turned off], no sweat.

speaker: Bean
text: Head down, come down. That's better. Move to your left slightly.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete.

speaker: Bean
text: That's it; come on in. Come to your left a little bit. Okay, come on up. Little more to the left. Just right.

speaker: Conrad
text: Huh?

speaker: Bean
text: You're just right. Scoot in there. Got to kind of scoot a little bit further in. You got it made! Bump into me, now. Okay. Okay.

speaker: Conrad
text: [Garbled] let me close the hatch.

speaker: Bean
text: Forward hatch , closed and locked as soon as you're out of the way.

speaker: Conrad
text: Say again?

speaker: Bean
text: And I wonder what that's from.

speaker: Conrad
text: What?

speaker: Bean
text: That little...Wait, you need to kick out that piece...

speaker: Conrad
text: I think that came from off of the landing gear. [Pause; Garbled]

speaker: Bean
text: Lock her up, babe. [Joking about how dirty Pete has gotten] You are nice and clean. [Dick] Gordon will be glad to see you.

speaker: Conrad
text: One hatch closed.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay, check that [ dump valve ] for Auto. I think it is, but you can see...

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yeah. I'm flipping. You just...One hatch [dump valve], Auto.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. Okay, let me move out of the way. Both [ dump valves ] to Auto.

speaker: Conrad
text: Tell me when [to start the repressurization].

speaker: Bean
text: Lighting: Annunciator and Numerics, Bright.

speaker: Conrad
text: Wait a minute. [Pause as he turns to change the lighting]

speaker: Bean
text: Okay.  Cabin Repress Valve Auto. [Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: It's Auto.

speaker: Bean
text: Press Regs A and B [to] Cabin. Master Alarm will come on, and CABIN warning light. Okay, here comes the O2. [Repress audible] And the pressure is rising. Looks good right this minute. [Pause] Okay, that's normal. PLSS O2, Off.

speaker: Conrad
text: Say again?

speaker: Bean
text: PLSS O2 Off when you get 3.6 [psi]. [Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: I can't get mine. Can you get it?

speaker: Bean
text: Let me see if I can.

speaker: Conrad
text: I can't get it, Al.

speaker: Bean
text: Just a second. Let me get mine, too. [Pause] Okay.

speaker: Conrad
text: Did you get mine off?

speaker: Bean
text: [Garbled], just a second.

speaker: Conrad
text: I can't hear you. [Long Pause]

speaker: Bean
text: Your O2 is Off. Everything's Off, Pete. [Pause] And the cabin pressure is...

speaker: Conrad
text: Cabin's 4 pounds.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay, going to be taking mine [his PLSS O2] off. [Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: [Sound of repress ends] That's it.

speaker: Bean
text: That's it, babes.

speaker: Conrad
text: What's the rest of the checklist?

speaker: Bean
text: I hope that [hatch] seal is good.

speaker: Conrad
text: Say again?

speaker: Bean
text: I didn't check that seal real closely [for dust].

speaker: Conrad
text: I didn't either.

speaker: Gordon
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. It says here: Verify cabin pressure increasing. [Garbled] PLSS O2, Off. Activate OPS purge valve to depress suit as required. [Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Wow, that's better. [Pause] Hey, don't take your helmet off!

speaker: Bean
text: That's right. Just your gloves.

speaker: Conrad
text: Do we do that?

speaker: Bean
text: Yeah, we do, because we have to put on our other ones. [Pause] Okay.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay, let me read to you.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yeah.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. Cabin Repress valve closes at 4.4. Verify cabin pressure stable at 4.6. Looks good to me, Pete. Post-EVA systems Config[uration]: Verify EV circ... Look over there and make sure Suit Fan 1 [circuit breaker] is closed. And I'll make sure that Suit Fan Delta-P [breaker] is closed.

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, just a second. [Pause as he turns] Suit Fan 1 is closed.

speaker: Bean
text: Suit Fan Delta-P, closed. Okay. We're going to get some ECS caution and H2O SEP component lights out.

speaker: Conrad
text: I can't hear you. What?

speaker: Bean
text: Our ECS Caution and H2O Sep[arator] component lights will go out in a minute. Doff your gloves.

speaker: Conrad
text: Everything's out.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. Descent H2O valve open. Okay, that [getting a drink of water]'s a good idea, boy. [Pause] [Remove] purge valves. [Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Now, we don't have anything left but a little rendezvous. [Sounding like someone about to enter a haunted house] Ha, ha, ha, ha.

speaker: Bean
text: Ascent and rendezvous, babes. [Pete chuckles; Pause]

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Give me your purge valve thing, I'll put it in the TSB [Temporary Storage Bag].

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, your two cohorts are back in. They just finished another 4-hour EVA; accomplished all the objectives and did an excellent job.

speaker: Bean
text: Wait a minute; let me give you my purge valve.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. [Pause]

speaker: Bean
text: You got it. [Pause]

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, thank you very much [garble] right now.

speaker: Conrad
text: [Laughing] This suit stuff has...

speaker: Bean
text: [Finishing the thought]...got all that dirt on it. I think it...Is this mine? [Pause]

speaker: Bean
text: There you go, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: I can't turn it. Can you get it open?

speaker: Bean
text: Sure, sure. [Garbled] purge valve because it has to rotate with the other...Got your...

speaker: Conrad
text: Yeah. If I can find it. [Long Pause] [Garbled]

speaker: Bean
text: I know.

speaker: Conrad
text: It's here somewhere.

speaker: Bean
text: Descent H2O valve open.

speaker: Conrad
text: I'll turn it open. [Pause]

speaker: Bean
text: Purge valve and OPS O2 hose; stow purge valves in TSB [Temporary Stowage Bag.

speaker: Conrad
text: All right, just threw it in there, I'll find the ball.

speaker: Bean
text: Oh, may have thrown it over. [Chuckles] May be behind you. [Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: These things [the OPS oxygen hose or his gloves] won't come undone!

speaker: Bean
text: Bet they've got a lot of that dust on them.

speaker: Conrad
text: Here. Would you turn this, please?

speaker: Bean
text: Yes, I sure will. [Pause] There you go.

speaker: Conrad
text: I don't understand why [garbled]. Here.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. [Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: They're sticking.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. Connect the LM [O2] hoses. Red to red; blue to blue. Suit Isolation [Valve] , both suits. So I'll hand you your hoses, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. [Pause]

speaker: Bean
text: So far, we haven't touched one of those circuit breakers as far as I can tell. [Garbled] around in here. [Pause]

speaker: Bean
text: There's your [LM] hoses, Pete. Got them?

speaker: Conrad
text: Yeah.

speaker: Bean
text: Here's mine. [Long Pause] Okey-dokey. [Long Pause] Red to red; blue to blue; [suit] isolation [valves] both to Suit Flow.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, would you turn mine on? Thank you.

speaker: Bean
text: You've got it.

speaker: Conrad
text: Does that [flow of LM oxygen] feel good!

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. Let's take the PLSS [LCG water] pump, Off; and [PLSS] fan Off; it [the LM O2]'s backpressuring in your fan. [Pause] Okay, that's good. Disconnect PLSS H2O from PGA. Connect LM H2O. I'll get yours and you get mine. [Pause] Lift up your RCU a little bit, Pete [so that he can see the connectors better]. RCU. There you go. [Pause] That did it. [Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay?

speaker: Bean
text: Okay.

speaker: Conrad
text: [LM] LCG Pump [circuit breaker], In [that is, Closed].

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. We're going to get cooler, probably. [Pause] It's in. PLSS mode, both of them O, [that is] Off.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Hello there. [Long Pause]

speaker: Bean
text: Okay, turn your VHF A, Off, and B, Off.

speaker: Conrad
text: A, Off, and B is Off.

speaker: Bean
text: Mode, ICS/Push-to-Talk.

speaker: Conrad
text: ICS/Push-to-Talk.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. Relay, Off.

speaker: Conrad
text: My Relay is Off.

speaker: Bean
text: You're out of VOX, right?

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes, sir.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Houston. How do you read?

speaker: Bean
text: Comm, okay? VHF, Off, Off.

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Intrepid hooked up on the Intrepid system. How do you read?

speaker: Bean
text: They never told us to turn our tape recorder on.

speaker: Gibson
text: We read you loud and clear, Pete, and we're standing by to give you any help on the stowage you may need. And, when you get down to it, we also have some good words for you on how to stow the [LM] TV camera.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, we'll wait for a while. Let us get through our checklist, please.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Houston; Intrepid.

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid; Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Are we a little bit early, or do you want me to go ahead with the checklist and put on my rendezvous radar operate heater circuit breaker [in order to warm up the electronics]?

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by, Pete. [Long Pause] Pete, we show that you are ahead. You can go ahead and complete that step, and we'll be back with you on any items which we would like you to hold on [that is, delay execution].

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Very good. I'll go ahead and put that in, and we're going to go ahead with our jettison here shortly.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston. On the High Gain, would you give us pitch, minus 30; yaw, 175?

speaker: Gordon
text: Hello, Houston; Yankee Clipper.

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger, Houston. Just want to let you know that 158 is going along real great. It's taking pictures every 20 seconds.

speaker: Gibson
text: Real good, Dick.

speaker: Gordon
text: [Garble] just to hear something time line.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. Copy. You're right on the time-line.

speaker: Gordon
text: If you've got Rev 28 update, I'll take that now before we get into the 158 for the next Rev.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Dick. We have the S-158 for Rev 28 when you're ready to copy.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. Go ahead.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. And I put these on T-1 time, 137:28:55, T-2 time is 137:40:55; Canopus, roll 090, pitch 228, yaw 338; T-1 is 137:49:11; Descartes, roll 89, pitch 217, yaw 319; T-1 137:52:42; Fra Mauro, roll 62, pitch 162, yaw 312; T-1 138:03:47. Over.

speaker: Gibson
text: Readback correct, Dick. And we also have map update for Rev 28.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. I copied that. Thank you.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay, Dick. And we also have one extra thing here. You can observe a transient event. You should take photos and observe Alphonsus at a GET of 136:00:02. You need not change film. You can go with the Hasselblad 80-millimeter lens if you want to take photos, and you can go with F:4, 250, at infinity. The transient event, area 7. Your brightening between the central peak and West wall, 110 nautical miles South of track, use window number 1, and it can be performed in the S-158 attitude. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. I copy at 136:00:02, E1 Hasselblad, 80 millimeter, F:4, 1/250th, and it's going to be area 7, window 1, 110 south, and say what it is again, please?

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay, Dick, that's a brightening between the central peak and West wall.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. I've got the camera now. I'll take a look at it.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Dick.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, Clipper.

speaker: Gibson
text: Clipper, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. Is that in the crater Theophilus?

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, say again. Would you...

speaker: Gordon
text: The transient event, is that in the crater Theophilus?

speaker: Gibson
text: That's at Alphonsus, Dick.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Gibson
text: Again, Alphonsus and a brightening between the central peak and west wall.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. I've got it.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, this is Clipper. That first pass is completed.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Clipper. Copy complete. What was the visual on that transient event?

speaker: Gordon
text: I didn't see anything out there. There is a dark area in between the central peak and the West wall, but I can't tell what it is. Looked a little bit darker than the rest of the surrounding area. It's quite a ways away, so - I really can't see much down there.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, how is that charge on battery A coming along?

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We copy.

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, you can terminate the charge on Bat A at 137:00 as in the Flight Plan.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. Let's start on B, I guess, huh?

speaker: Gibson
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay [garble] just be on your toes.

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper.

speaker: Gordon
text: [Garble] want Charlie to go to sleep [garble].

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, say again.

speaker: Gordon
text: [Garble] don't want Charlie to go to sleep?

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, it sounds good, but you're slightly garbled. Maybe you could move the mike a bit away from your mouth.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. I said I didn't want Charlie to go to sleep.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We copy that. Say, Dick, at 140 plus 00, you have a landmark track coming up of 193. It's your option, you can go ahead and do 193 or landmark tracking on the LM. Whichever way you want to go, we'll work you up a PAD.

speaker: Gordon
text: Well, which would you prefer?

speaker: Gibson
text: It's really your option, Dick. We can work up a PAD either way.

speaker: Gordon
text: Let's use the LM, huh?

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. We'll get you a PAD for the LM.

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, well, we need some words on the status of that hatch window in order to help us interpret the data you're getting back from the 158.

speaker: Gordon
text: Well, it's - it's really not too bad. It's got a few drops on the outside yet from that Lox stuff that's on there and I've been trying to keep the inside clean. It's got some smear marks on the inside pane where we've tried to wipe it. It got all wet last night and I tried to dry it off this morning with a towel and some Kleenex. It's still smeared a little, but other than that, it looks pretty good; really not too bad. I'll clean it again right now.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Dick. Thank you.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Houston; Intrepid.

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Commander's feedwater remaining 0.32 kg.

speaker: Gibson
text: 0.32 kilograms.

speaker: Conrad
text: That's right, and we'll have the LMP's for you in just a minute.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, the LMP's water is 0.26.

speaker: Gibson
text: 0.26. [Long Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, as soon as we get through our suit integrity check, we will be depressing the cabin for the jettison.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Intrepid.

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston. One minute - 1½ minutes until LOS.

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, Houston. Comm check.

speaker: Conrad
text: Loud and clear. The equipment's jettisoned. We are just cleaning up the cockpit. Sorry [for not reporting in].

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. We copy two impacts on the PSE during jettison.

speaker: Conrad
text: That's PLSS 1 and PLSS 2.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: As a matter of fact, that may help you calibrate that thing, because I got a clean kick on both of them. In other words, when they left the hatch, they departed the hatch and free-fell all the way to the ground without touching the ladder or anything on the way.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. They pretty much went straight out...

speaker: Conrad
text: [Garbled] roughly did the same thing...

speaker: Gibson
text: ...on a ballistic right on down and hit the ground. Didn't arc up at all?

speaker: Conrad
text: That's right.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. Thank you.

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid; Houston. We're changing over sites in about 10 seconds [means minutes]. We may be losing comm for a minute or two.

speaker: Conrad
text: Thank you.

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid; Houston. We have some words for you on the stowage of the TV and also the equipment which is put on the floor by the [plus] Z-27.

speaker: Bean
text: [Simultaneous with Pete] Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We're right at that point [at the bottom of the left-hand column of Sur-97 ]; we're just ready for you.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay, Pete. And, first, you could fold the TV handle and stow it [the TV] in the LiOH canister bracket on the [back of the] engine cover, lens up. Secure the TV cable end to the camera, pad the camera with utility towels [which are stowed] in the upper boot bay. Replace the knurled knob hold-down, secure the camera with the utility straps. Wrap the straps around the lens and the knurled knobs.

speaker: Bean
text: Understand. [Pause]

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, give me a call when you are ready for some information on the equipment to go by Z-27.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. That'll be 10 [to] 15 minutes.

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, Houston. You can expect lost Comm here for about 1 to 2 minutes. We have a handover.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. Start talking to us about the gear you want us to tie down back of the OPSs.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. [Pause] Okay, first point there is to ensure that the [plus] Z-27 bulkhead is protected [from the gear in the jettison bag]. You can use data books and towels for that purpose. We suggest, also, in tying down the equipment and rocks which you have in the bags there that goes on the floor next to the Z-27 by the OPS, that you use two additional strands of the utility straps. They will go from the top of the jettison bag to the ISA [Interim Stowage Assembly] attach fitting; that's the D ring on the midsection step. This will give you four strands total.

speaker: Bean
text: Say the last part again, Ed.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. We suggest that you use two additional strands of the utility straps. Now, this would go from the top of the jettison bag to the ISA fitting; that's the D ring on the midsection step. This will give you a total of four strands. [Pause] Essentially what we're looking for here, Al, is to tie this thing down with as many strands as you can - at least four - so that in the docking we don't get this thing coming off the floor and busting the straps.

speaker: Bean
text: Understand.

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hello, Houston; Clipper here.

speaker: Gibson
text: Hello, Dick. Pete and Al are just finishing up the post-EVA, and it looks as though they're pretty far ahead. They have a little bit of time to sit back end relax. We have a map update for Rev 29 when you're ready to copy.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, I'm - I'm ready to copy. Tell those guys to sit back and relax. Did a great job.

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, say again. You're broken up.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. I'm ready to copy. Tell those guys they deserve a rest. They can sit back and relax. It's a pretty job.

speaker: Gordon
text: Clipper copies.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Dick.

speaker: Gordon
text: Ed, it sounds like they didn't have any problems down there at all.

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, that's affirmative. They ran into a few things; but, as they did yesterday, they overcame them. No problems. [Pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: I expect most of their problems are human. [Pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Maybe so, Dick, but not many of them errors. Dick, will you go back in your Flight Plan to 131:30? And we missed a crew status report at that point. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. Says here I had 7 hours sleep, PRD [garble] 110 [garble]. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston. How do you read?

speaker: Gordon
text: Loud and clear. How me?

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by, Dick. We still have a lot of garbling, and broken up.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Intrepid. We have everything stowed, secured properly, and we're ready to start the launch countdown at the proper time. And, if you'll give us about 15 or 20 minutes to chow down here, we'll come back with you and have a little chitty chat about the EVA.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. Sounds like a good plan. [Pause] And, Pete, you're still quite a bit ahead.

speaker: Gibson
text: It looks as though the furthest you could go up to in the checklist is on Surface 101 : lift-off minus 2:40. You'll have to hold at that point until we get you the right CSM state vector.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. No problem. I'm not hustling on that. We're just sitting here now; we've got the spacecraft all squared away. I'll say everything's tied down, but man, oh man, is it filthy in here; we must have 20 pounds of dust, dirt, and all kinds of junk.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. That'll be an interesting [return to] zero g.

speaker: Conrad
text: Right. Al and I look just like a couple of bituminous coal miners right at the moment. [Long Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: But we're happy.

speaker: Gibson
text: So are a lot of people down here. [Long Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: Say, let me get a time hack with you on my mission timer. I'm reading 137:40:53, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 137:41; is that about right?

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Intrepid. You're a couple of seconds off; we can give you a more accurate time hack if you like.

speaker: Conrad
text: No, that's all right. I'll bring the computer out of Standby and get the time okay.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: I just happened to think about it; I haven't messed with the mission timer since we landed.

speaker: Conrad
text: Say, Houston, how's the SIDE doing? Did that cold gas jobber-do get running or not?

speaker: Gibson
text: Stand by on that, Pete; we'll get the latest word on it.

speaker: Conrad
text: Also, how are the package temperatures doing? Are they running like they expected? [Pause]

speaker: Gibson
text: Pete, looks good on both counts. The CCIG came up and is looking nominal, and the temperatures are looking nominal.

speaker: Conrad
text: Very good. All equipment's running, huh?

speaker: Gibson
text: That's affirm. And I'll tell you, from watching those plots from down here, that PSE is sure doing the job.

speaker: Conrad
text: Great.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Intrepid.

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, Houston. Go ahead.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. If you'll look at our schedule there, we've been running our tape recorder according to the schedule; and, because the EVAs ran longer, do we have anything left on that for ascent and rendezvous? Can you check that out for us?

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. Will do, Pete. Stand by.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hello, Houston. Clipper and I.

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, we copy.

speaker: Gordon
text: And you're looking for my status report last night. I had 7 hours' sleep.[Pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Had a PRD [garble] 11019.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We copy 7 hours and 11019; and, Dick, we're having a little bit of trouble understanding. You sound...

speaker: Gordon
text: [Garble] Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, you sound slightly garbled. I'm wondering if the microphone is in - the correct position relative to your mouth.

speaker: Gordon
text: How do you hear me now?

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. That's a little better.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. I'm holding it close enough to my mouth.

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, we show a real strong signal down here, but the transmission's still slightly garbled.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, Houston. I'll try to work on it.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.[Long pause.]

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead, Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Dick, would you go ahead and stir the cryos for 3 minutes? We'd like to see where we stand with respect to balancing.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, are you copying those torquing angles?

speaker: Gibson
text: Clipper, that's affirmative. We have the angles.[Long pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, Houston, the cryos have been stirred for 3 minutes.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Dick. We copy that. It looks as though you're almost balanced. About one more Rev ought to do it, and then you'll be going back to Auto.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Gibson
text: Yankee Clipper and Intrepid. We'd like to give you the T-17 and T-18 lift-off PAD's before CSM LOS, coming up in about 8 minutes.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.[Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. [Long Pause while they get the data book out] This is Intrepid ready to copy.

speaker: Conrad
text: This is Intrepid. Ready to copy.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Intrepid. Yankee Clipper, are you ready to copy.?

speaker: Gordon
text: Yankee Clipper ready.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Intrepid copies 140:05:15, 142:03:40.

speaker: Gibson
text: Readback's correct, Intrepid.

speaker: Conrad
text: And, Houston, Intrepid standing by to copy the P22 [radar tracking of the Command Module] Acq[uisition] time and the new octal numbers and we're also ready to debrief with you. Standing by for your questions.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay, Intrepid. We're not planning to do that P22. The job's been done already, so we can forget the P22 coming up at 140 plus 00.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. [Long Pause]

speaker: Gibson
text: And, Intrepid, we have your consumables Pad when you're ready to copy.

speaker: Conrad
text: We're ready to copy.

speaker: Gibson
text: Consumables at GET [Ground Elapsed Time] of 137:00: RCS A, 80 percent; B, 76; O2, and we'll give you first the descent and the ascent. 47, 96; H2O, 39.5, 99.2; amp-hours, 729.7, 572.3.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Copied all that.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay, Intrepid. And on your question on the [Data Storage Electronics Assembly, DSEA] tape recorder. We show that, under the way that we'd normally figure it, that by extending those two EVAs, we come up with 10-1/2 hours, whereas the tape recorder normally goes 10. However, those assumptions are: first, 100-percent activity [that is, the recorder is on all the time] in the descent, ascent, and the rendezvous and 30-percent activity [that is, the recorder is on 30 percent of the time] on the EVA. The 100-percent figure is most likely high and the 30-percent figure is most likely low; so it's pretty difficult for us to come up and tell you exactly when you're going to be cutting off in the ascent or if you will at all.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We'll just go ahead and run it per the schedule.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. [Pause]

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay, Intrepid. And our first comment on the EVA. The Gold Flight Team members back here would like to give you their congratulations for a job well done.

speaker: Conrad
text: Thank you. [Pause]

speaker: Gibson
text: And, Intrepid, we have a few questions. First one of which is on the weigh bags and their cracking. Can you briefly describe the problem that you encountered in cracking and what the reason may be for it?

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, they seem to...When I folded the first big one...Let me think a minute. Oh, I know. The contingency sample one [that is, the contingency sample bag], I believe, has some holes in it, doesn't it, Al? [Pause] I can't remember on that but, anyhow, the first big one [weigh bag] wound up [with] just about an inch-and-a-half-long crack [that] appeared in it when I was folding it. Just like a fatigue failure; and that appears to be pretty much what happened. I noticed a couple of the saddlebags were the same way after we got done rattling around with them. They had some 1- or 2-inch-long cracks which made holes in them.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We copy that. Can you relate it to a given thermal situation? In other words, were they all cold at the time or really couldn't you say that?

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, I really couldn't say. I think you all realize - from the angle that we're at [that is, the LM orientation on the surface]- that the MESA was in the Sun. Did you all know that?

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. No, we didn't know that. At least, I wasn't aware of that one.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. It's not completely in the Sun, but it's almost in the Sun. When I say almost, you know there's some gear struts throwing some shadows and everything, but that area was in sunlight.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. Yankee Clipper, 1 minute to LOS. See you on the other side.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger.

speaker: Gibson
text: Question two, Intrepid. Could you discuss the failure of the camel hander [sic]...[correcting himself] the camera handle?

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes, sir. The knurled knob came off the shaft that it was mounted to, therefore allowing all the pieces to fall apart.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. And how did the hammer fail? Did it fail in some way other than just the chips of the coating coming off?

speaker: Conrad
text: No, no; that's all. Just the coating was coming off.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. [Pause] Okay. What problems did you have with the S-band in terms of [tripping on] the cable; and, also, exactly where did you put it?

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, just the fact that I wasn't looking where I was going. I'd get tangled up in the S-band antenna wire every once in a while. That one's not as bad as the TV [cable], though, because the TV one doesn't lay flat; the S-band one lays flat. We put the S-band out just like we agreed to do it - to minimized running over the wire - which was out the plus-Y direction pretty much.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. And, Pete, when you went back to check the CCIG, could you tell us how close you got to it?

speaker: Conrad
text: I walked up to within about 5 feet of it.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. Thank you. [Pause] Okay, and a question on the third film pack which we used. How much of that was used on the inside, and where in the traverse did you pick it up and change it to one of the existing cameras?

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, I've got some bad news for you and some good news. In the first place, the third magazine was a color magazine, and all it had on it were some shots that were taken of Earthrise and a few things like that coming around on descent. And, unfortunately, Al and I got our signals crossed, and it's outside on the lunar surface right now. Now, what we did was take the black-and-white magazine off of Al's camera when it failed and put it on my camera and used it up so that we have two complete black and whites of the second EVA and two complete colors of the first EVA, and the only thing that's missing is the color magazine that had undocking and a couple other mundane things like that on it at the beginning of the LM operation. And, unfortunately, that's out there in that saddle bag. We didn't catch that one.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay. You did get the Surveyor, though?

speaker: Conrad
text: Oh, yeah. We have all the Surveyor pictures and everything, but they're all black and white.

speaker: Gibson
text: Real good. And lastly, we've been looking at your power consumption profile and notice that you're not using as much as they initially anticipated. They attribute that to the lack of use of the floodlights. Would you confirm that you've not had the floodlights on since the beginning of the first EVA?

speaker: Conrad
text: That's right. We haven't had the floodlights on. And, also, we've used LCG pump very, very little. Every once in a while we give ourselves a squirt. The spacecraft, in contrast to Neil's...We've been very warm. And we've been comfortably warm with just the air in our suits, and I'd say the temperature inside here right now is running in the low 70s somewhere. And it's been that way ever since we got here.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. Okay. That's the last of our questions. We could finish this up if you give us two PRD readings.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Wait one. [Long Pause] Al is 04022, and I'm still 11020. It'd kind of give you the idea mine may have quit running.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay, Pete. We copy a 04022, and say the second [again].

speaker: Conrad
text: 11020, and I think that's what it was the last time I gave it to you.

speaker: Gibson
text: That's correct, Pete. A question on the...

speaker: Conrad
text: Maybe it quit running.

speaker: Gibson
text: Could be. A question on the equipment jettison. Was there anything other than what's already called out for that was jettisoned or not jettisoned?

speaker: Conrad
text: Well, we jettisoned everything according to the checklist.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. Say, Pete, how does the inside of the cabin look about now?

speaker: Conrad
text: Except for...[Stops to listen to Gibson] It's very neat and orderly except for the fact that it's very dirty.

speaker: Gibson
text: Kind of a neat, orderly coal mine.

speaker: Conrad
text: That's about the size of it. The only thing that we do have [that was not jettisoned as per the checklist], of course, is the LiOH canister container which now has the TV camera in it.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. [Pause]

speaker: Conrad
text: EVA antenna is down and stowed.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. And we also understood from Al out there on the surface that only partially deployed; only got up around 60 degrees.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. I was the one that put it up; and, when I put it back down, I discovered that I hadn't turned it the last, about, 20 percent. And, so, it went all the way up, and then I stowed it. So it functioned correctly. It was me. I didn't put it all the way up.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. The comm was beautiful, though. We had probably the best of any Sim we've had.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yeah, I concur; the comm really has been super. [Pause] These PLSSs and suits performed magnificently. These suits are a shambles [that is, dirty] though. [Long Pause]

speaker: Gibson
text: Say, Pete and Al, when you climbed back in, you terminated at 3 plus 55. And, [for] both of you, your reserve was determined by oxygen. In PLSS 1 [Pete's] the reserve was 2 plus 05, which would have given you a 6-hour PLSS; and the PLSS 2 was 1 plus 50, which is pretty close to 6 hours also.

speaker: Conrad
text: That's very good to know, and there's no reason why you can't stay out there and work that long. You don't get tired.

speaker: Gibson
text: Get a little thirsty, though, I bet.

speaker: Conrad
text: We were. We were really thirsty after the second EVA because...I don't know, did you add up how far we went? I think we made a pretty good trip out there.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. We're estimating something over a mile for the full circuit. But that's not counting some of the side jaunts you made.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yeah. We've been trying to follow our tracks [of footprints] out here with the monocular.

speaker: Conrad
text: The other thing that I...Have you got your map book there? Let me talk to you about this big blocky-rimmed crater that's out here.

speaker: Gibson
text: Yeah. Stand by on that. [Pause] Okay. We got the map.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. On the great big map, it's the crater that has got the really big blocks on it, that's just outside the ellipse on map A.

speaker: Gibson
text: Okay, Pete. Which is the great big map?

speaker: Conrad
text: The smaller one [that is, the 1:5,000 map] is...[Answering Gibson] Okay, the one that shows the landing ellipse. It's number 39. Wait a minute. Let me look just a second. [Pause] It's number [LSE 7-] 30 chart. [Long Pause] That crater is on our horizon and we can see it from here. And I can sit here with the map and pick out the really great big boulders and everything. One of the problems up here is there's nothing to break up...or, there's nothing between you and any object that you happen to pick up [visually] out there - like a rock - to judge distance by. And, when we first landed, I really thought that crater was like a thousand feet away, but it's obviously a whale of a lot further than that away. But it looks like it's right next to us, and we can use the monocular and scan those gigantic boulders that are there. That's the only one that's visible to us on the horizon. But I wanted to point out...You can get an idea of the fact - that really looks like it's about a thousand feet away, [and] you know how far it really is [4.5 kilometers or 15 thousand feet] - how difficult it is to judge distance.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Pete. Maybe the use of that LM shadow then was pretty useful. I know in the beginning [at 112:07:13], you doubted that the shadow was really that long, and apparently it was telling you the truth.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yeah. I think you're probably right. The other thing is [that], from the spacecraft here looking at the ALSEP, it looks like it's right under the window. And Al and I's best guess is that it's at least 450 feet away now.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: Say, I got a question for you, Houston. What do the experts think about doing an alignment [of the inertial platform] in orbit now, versus what we got here on the lunar surface yesterday?

speaker: Gibson
text: Copy your question, Pete. Stand by. Also, that crater which you were talking about is, we estimate, 4-1/2 kilometers from your present position.

speaker: Conrad
text: Looks like it's just a hop, skip, and a jump.

speaker: Gibson
text: [Responding to Pete's question about doing an alignment of the inertial platform] Pete, we'd like to go ahead and stick with the procedures we have right now. We can give you an update on it after the two P57's after at insertion. There's a chance that we may not need it.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Well, I wasn't proposing that we didn't do it; we're going to go ahead and do it. I was just curious, after we got a good RLS - which we've never gotten before - out of the P57 yesterday, what everybody thought about that.

speaker: Conrad
text: Say, Houston, one thing that occurred to me...The reason we're not using the floodlights is because that overhead hatch is not rigged right and that microswitch is open all the time - I should say the microswitch isn't rigged right; the hatch is okay. And those floodlights were on all the time, so when we were getting ready to come down over the night side, we had the floods on, just the two lower ones were still always on. So, we pulled that breaker, and we've left it out all the rest of the time. That's the reason.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger. We copy that. [Long Pause]

speaker: Gibson
text: Say, Pete and Al, do you think that if you were out there for say 4-1/2, maybe even 5 hours, you'd get hungry as well as thirsty on an extended traverse?

speaker: Conrad
text: I don't think so, if you chowed down good just before you left.

speaker: Bean
text: I agree with that. You really get thirsty, though. Maybe they can come up with something that you can put on the inside of your helmet, something like - not exactly like - the little valsalva device. Just something where you could maybe reach over and take even a swallow of water. You're only thirsty because your throat is dry, and if you just had something - one swallow - I think that'd fix you up right there.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Al. Say, did either one of you kneel down in order to get anything off the surface, or did you use the newly-developed Bean technique of holding on to the Surveyor parts bag and lowering the Commander to the surface?

speaker: Conrad
text: Yeah. Well, we used all kinds of things like that. You could take the shovel and stick it in the ground and just do a one-arm pushup and lean down and pick up a rock off the ground with the other hand. It's really a ridiculous way to do it. If you had a suit that would bend, why, you'd have the whole program wired. But, you could do that. It's okay. I fell over once out there, and Al picked me back up again. It's no big deal.

speaker: Bean
text: But, in the same sense, you're always fussing around trying to get down there to get these rocks, and we did kneel down a couple of times. I knelt down and picked some stuff up. And it's particularly easy if you got that Hand Tool Carrier with you. But we really do need to come up with some sort of strap or something that would allow you to lean over and grab a rock that won't fit in those tongs.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston. Intrepid, picking up the launch Prep Verb 98 at LO minus 02:50.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Intrepid.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control Houston. We're at 139 hours, 5 minutes into the flight. Meanwhile in Mission Control Center Houston, we are having a shift change. Flight Director, Pete Frank, and members of his Orange Team are now aboard, and a News Conference will be held in the News Center within the next few minutes with Flight Director, Gerry Griffin. We're at 139 hours, 6 minutes into the flight and this is Apollo Control Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay, Houston. You see that 2127. That's the same thing we had before, also.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. You see that 212? That's the same thing we had before, also.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger, Intrepid. Me copy, and we concur. We expect it.

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go.

speaker: Gibson
text: We have a update on the star Ar - Arcturus on page 102 of the Surface Checklist. We'd like you to use Procyon, 16, or Sirius, 15, and that's detent 1. [Pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. [Pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. And we passed self-test all right.

speaker: Gibson
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: Are you ready for E-Mod dump?

speaker: Gibson
text: That's affirmative. We're ready for the E-Mod.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control Houston at 139 hours, 15 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. We're some 2 hours, 50 minutes away from Time Of Ignition and Conrad and Bean start turning their attentions to preparations for liftoff. Both guidance systems, the prime and backup are powered up and systems tests are performed. The 2 guidance systems are aligned, the AGS to the PNGS, the rendezvous radar will be turned on, and the self test is performed, the inertial platform. The inertial platform is aligned for the rendezvous radar tracking of Yankee Clipper on its last overhead pass, this pass prior to lift-off. The radar is turned off following this and remains off during ascent. At this time we will turn the release line over for a News Conference at the News Center. The tape will be turned over directly to transcript. We're at 139 hours, 15 minutes into the flight; and this is Apollo Control Houston.

speaker: Gibson
text: Intrepid, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go.

speaker: Gibson
text: If you will give us P00 and Accept, we'll give you a CSM state vector and RLS update.

speaker: Conrad
text: You have P00 and Accept.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hello, Houston; Yankee Clipper.

speaker: Carr
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston. Loud and clear.

speaker: Gordon
text: Well, hello there, stranger. How are you?

speaker: Carr
text: Morning, Dick. We are fine. How are you?

speaker: Gordon
text: Well, pretty good. I hope you would like to have some company for a change.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Got the house clean?

speaker: Gordon
text: As a matter of fact, I just finished that. I sure do; got everything in order; ready to go towards the LM and bring back [garble] that's quite a chore; keeping this thing clean.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. You got a couple of coal miners coming up to see you.

speaker: Gordon
text: That's okay. I'll be glad to see them.

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. The computer is yours. Break. Yankee Clipper, if you will go P00 and Accept, we have an uplink.

speaker: Gordon
text: All yours.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, you got the lift-off time for me?

speaker: Carr
text: Stand by. [Pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. Your lift-off time is l42:03:47.

speaker: Carr
text: Affirmative.

speaker: Carr
text: Clipper, Houston. Computer's yours.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. And Jerry, will you find out what they want to do about this battery charge, because I'm using the bus ties during the rendezvous?

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.[Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston. Why don't you figure on terminating the battery charge at LOS?

speaker: Gordon
text: All right; I could let it go until I [garble] just before lift-off. That way it might take it all the way up.

speaker: Carr
text: Clipper, Houston. We prefer that you terminate at LOS on this pass.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. That would be one less thing for us to keep track of prior to lift-off.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Conrad
text: Say, Houston; Intrepid.

speaker: Bean
text: Say, Houston; Intrepid.

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. Go.

speaker: Bean
text: Roger. When you look out the AOT in the dark quadrant? You can see these lights - particles of light, flashes of light just seem to come from - in this case, I'm looking in quadrant 1 which is the left one. It's coming from behind me, the left, and they're just sailing off in space. I was thinking they're dropping from my water boiler, but it looks like some of those things are escaping the Moon. They really haul out of here and just press off at the stars.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. [Pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston with a P22 tracking PAD.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Your target is LM; T-1 is 139:57:39; T-2 is 140:02:38; south 05; latitude is minus 3...

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. T 112...

speaker: Carr
text: Latitude, minus 3.036; longitude over 2 is minus 11.709; altitude minus 1.13. If you want to take photos, your DAC settings are 1/60th, 1 over 60, one SP, 1 FPS, and C-EX film. You're - you should be at zero local horizontal rather than 22-degrees pitchdown. Over.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. Understand. T-1, 139:57:39, T-2, 140:02:38, 5 miles South, latitude is minus 3.036, longitude over 2 is minus 11.709; altitude minus 1.13 and [garble] information. I will not use it.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Dick. And I've got a Rev 30 map update when you're ready. [Pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. Yankee Clipper, we copied.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. And, Dick, I've got your consumables update when you are ready.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. At a GET of 139 plus 20, RCS total was 56 percent; Alfa is 58; Bravo, 56; Charlie, 56; Delta, 55; hydrogen tank 1 is 49.9; tank 2 is 49.8; oxygen, 52.7 and 54.4. Over.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. I copy that. And my rendezvous radar transponder self-check is okay.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Gordon
text: Hey, Jerry, I would like to have a DAP update also, please.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Dick. Stand by. We'll get it for you. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. Looking at the DSKY torquing angles?

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. We see them, Pete.

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. How's your drinking water intake then since you got back in? You been replacing quite a bit of it?

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes, sir.

speaker: Carr
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston. If you'll give us P00 and Accept, we have another LM state vector for you.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, Houston. I'm going to stop my roll [garble] here. Okay. Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: All right, Houston. Is there any objection if we track him when he goes by this time? And do you have the OSCIL[?], or don't you want us to do it?

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. We hadn't really planned on doing a P22 on this pass.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. We'll forget it.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. Break. Yankee Clipper, Houston. I've got your DAP update.

speaker: Gordon
text: Sock it to me.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. About the only change you need is you need to go to 0.5-degree deadband, so R1 should read 1110.1.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. Are the weights and trim verified yet?

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Dick. Your weights and your trims are good.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. That's what I was worried about. Thank you. I'll probably go to a half a degree a second during the rendezvous because those maneuvers are pretty long.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Carr
text: Houston, Clipper. Never mind. Forget it.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, Clipper. Never mind. Forget it.

speaker: Carr
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston. We're through with your computer.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. Thank you. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston. On your maneuver, go S-band Omni Charlie. Over.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: And no we're at 139 hours, 49 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12. In Mission Control Center, Houston, we've had a change in the capsule communicators. Jerry Carr, now aboard replacing Ed Gibson at that position. While the line was down Pete Conrad from the Intrepid did call and ask for a lift-off time. Jerry did pass...

speaker: Carr
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston. Omni Delta.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Intrepid.

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. Go.

speaker: Conrad
text: Has Yankee gone overhead yet?

speaker: Carr
text: Not yet, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Give me an overhead time, so I can watch him go by.

speaker: Gordon
text: Take T-2 and add 96, Jerry. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Jerry Carr did pass along an estimated lift-off time. We're 142 hours, 3 minutes, 47 seconds. Our displays in Mission Control show us that Intrepid should enter orbit with an apolune of 46.3 nautical miles, a perilune of 8.8 nautical miles. Delta-V for that ascent burn would be 6,057 feet per second. About 1½ hours before lift-off, Capcom Jerry Carr will be passing the lift-off maneuver pad to Intrepid. Presently we're at 2 hours, 13 minutes prior to ignition; at 139 hours, 56 minutes continuing to monitor. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. Clipper should be overhead at 140:04:10.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Thank you. I'm going to check the plane change and see how good you are. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, Yankee Clipper. Is Intrepid up VHF?

speaker: Carr
text: Stand by, Clipper. Break. Intrepid, this is Houston. Clipper wants to know if you're up VHF.

speaker: Conrad
text: No, but we will come up VHF.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Break. Clipper, Houston. Intrepid says he'll be up.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. Ask him whether he wants us up VHF A or B Simplex.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Ask him whether he wants us up VHF A or B SIMPLEX.

speaker: Carr
text: Clipper, Houston. What would you like, VHF A or B Simplex?

speaker: Gordon
text: [Garble] go on normal VHF ranging.

speaker: Carr
text: Say again, Clipper.

speaker: Gordon
text: How about the normal VHF ranging [garble]?

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. Come up on VHF ranging configuration. Over.

speaker: Conrad
text: Will do.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. We presently show Yankee Clipper in an orbit of 61.7 nautical miles by 58.7 nautical miles. We're now at 139 hours, 53 minutes into the flight. This is Apollo Control, Houston. We're at 139 hours, 58 minutes now in the flight. Our display here in Mission Control shows that the concentric sequence initiate burn...

speaker: Carr
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Dick. Are you going to use the zero-degree pitch or 22-degree pitch down for this pass?

speaker: Gordon
text: Twenty-two degrees.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: The concentric sequence initiate burn is scheduled for 143 hours, 1 minute, 50 seconds with a Delta-V of 49.2 feet per second. This burn done at apolune following lift-off has the effect of raising the perilune a half a revolution later. We would look at numbers at that time for Intrepid of 46.8 by 43.6, some 15 nautical miles below the Yankee Clipper. We're 2 hours, 4 minutes, 18 seconds away from Time Of Ignition. And this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Yankee Clipper; Intrepid on VHF. How do you read?

speaker: Gordon
text: Loud and clear, Pete. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Hello, Houston; Clipper.

speaker: Carr
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston. Go.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. Houston, I don't like those marks at all, that Sun angle was pretty high and the whole area is washed out, and it's the best that I could tell you, I think I was on the Surveyor crater but I can't be sure of that.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Dick.

speaker: Gordon
text: That Sun's a lot too high to define that right now.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Intrepid. We had a visual on him although I couldn't talk to him on VHF.

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. Roger.

speaker: Carr
text: Clipper, this is Houston. Did you read Intrepid on VHF?

speaker: Gordon
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. You sure it wasn't in S-band because, you know, we're in a relay mode.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, Clipper. I think it's VHF, Jerry.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. [Long pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: Hey, Jerry, I sure wouldn't do anything with that P22 data because I'm not sure of it.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Dick. We've copied your data.

speaker: Carr
text: Clipper, Houston. We'll give that data a good evaluation before we do anything with it.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: P22 reference there is the orbital navigational program for the Command Module, Yankee Clipper. We're at 140 hours, and 9 minutes now into the flight and 1 hour and 55 minutes away from Time Of Ignition for Intrepid.

speaker: Bean
text: Houston, Intrepid.

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. Go.

speaker: Bean
text: Got sort of an interesting thing going on AGS right now. I didn't notice earlier, but it may just be because the lights are brighter now. I'm getting an all 8's flash on both the address and the information registers at about one-fifth the brilliance of the normal numbers. And a - it's pulsing every second.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Al.

speaker: Bean
text: If I turn down the illumination level just a little bit, it's not noticeable. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That was Al Bean describing some illumination on his AGS display, the abort guidance system display aboard Intrepid.

speaker: Bean
text: Hello, Houston; Intrepid. You ready for my RCS hot fire?

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Houston; Intrepid. You ready for my RCS hot fire?

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. Roger. Fire away.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Go.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Al. Fredo is here. He and I have both seen that phenomena on your DEDA during testing of most all the spacecrafts up at Bethpage, and it's probably an EMI.

speaker: Conrad
text: That's what we've been talking about, but we thought we'd just touch in on it.

speaker: Bean
text: That's what we've been talking about, but we thought we'd just touch in on it.

speaker: Bean
text: When you go to your roll rate, roll left, pitch up...

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. I think TRW's got a workup on this problem.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay.

speaker: Conrad
text: Here you go, Houston, with roll, pitch, and yaw.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Don't panic. We just blew over our S-band erectable, and we're up on our steerable.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. I was just going to tell you, Pete, we lost some of the data on that fire check.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. You want me to give to you again?

speaker: Carr
text: Stand by. I'll tell you what we need.

speaker: Conrad
text: I never gave you yaw anyway.

speaker: Carr
text: Pete, can you just start over from the beginning?

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Apparently from that last report the erectable S-band antenna outside was felled by that RCS test. We're at 140 hours, 14 minutes.

speaker: Conrad
text: Pitch up is the only one that didn't sound right.

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. I've got a K-factor update for you when you're ready.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. R-1 is 00140; R-2 is all zips, R-3 is 00033.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. 000 - 00140; all zips; three zips 33.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. How'd the hot fire look?

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. That went kind of fast. Give us a chance to take a look at our tapes.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. The passive seismometer just verified that you did do your hot fire.

speaker: Conrad
text: Very good.

speaker: Conrad
text: Does the passive seismometer say my hot fire is Go? [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control Houston. Jerry Carr reported recordings of the panel on the passive seismometer verifying the hot fire on the RCS. This data was received in our Experiment Staff Support Room.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, Clipper.

speaker: Carr
text: Clipper, Houston. Go.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay; have the DSKY.

speaker: Conrad
text: I understand I was Go.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, are you ready for our gyro torquing angles?

speaker: Carr
text: Clipper, Houston. Roger. Go ahead. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. I have a LM ascent PAD and a CSI PAD.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. Just a second. Are you ready for my - the rest of my hot fire?

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. We're ready. Go ahead. Break. Clipper, you can go ahead and torque.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, I did. Thank you.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. I gave you an extra pitchup fire because we were photographing the effects on the ground. It's quite spectacular.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete.

speaker: Bean
text: And we're ready to copy the launch PAD.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. LM ascent PAD follows: T IG 142:03:47.00; Noun 76, 5535.0, 0037.0, plus 000.2; DEDA 47 is plus 37364, plus 05607, plus 58642, plus 56955; DEDA 465 is plus 00370; DEDA 546 is NA; ignition one Rev late is 144:02:09; LM weight, 10789; CSM weight, 35390. Over.

speaker: Carr
text: That's affirmative, Al. P32 CSI PAD follows. Noun 11, 143:01:50.60; Noun 37, 144:38, all zips; Noun 81, 0492, all zips; DEDA 373 is 01818, 275 is 02780; AGS Delta-Vs, plus 0492, all zips, plus 0010. Over.

speaker: Bean
text: Roger. 143:01:50.60; 144:38, all zero's, 0492, all zero's, 01818, 02780, plus 0492, All zeros, plus 0010.

speaker: Carr
text: Affirmative, Al.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, Houston. I'm standing by for your up-data link and the LGC gyro compensation.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, this is Clipper. I copied those Pads.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Clipper. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston. Over.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Dick. You can terminate your battery Bravo charge now, and we'd like to have you put your O 2 tank 1 heaters and your hydrogen tank 2 heaters back to Auto. And dump your waste water to between 5...

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger Roger. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Yankee Clipper. Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: I have - got the H 2 and O 2 heaters, and dump the water to 52 percent.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. That's it, Dick. Thank you.

speaker: Gordon
text: And I'll do a purge next.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Gordon
text: I'll do a purge on the oxygen and hydrogen fuel cell.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control Houston. We are about 5 minutes away now from Loss Of Signal with Yankee Clipper. Next time around, Yankee Clipper will be on his 30th revolution and Intrepid will lift-off on the 30th revolution. We're at 140 hours, 26 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 12.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: In the ascent maneuver pad data pass up to Intrepid, which Al Bean copied, a lift-off time was given of 142 hours, 3 minutes, 47 seconds.

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Pete, we'll be setting your gyro compensation uplink to you after you've done your second P57.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay, must be a mistake in the checklist.

speaker: Carr
text: Yes, that's right. It's not - it's poorly placed in the checklist.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. How'd the hot fire look all the way around? Everything okay?

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: PAD data shows a horizontal velocity for Intrepid of 5,535 feet per second. We're at 140 hours and 28 minutes now into the flight.

speaker: Conrad
text: Got another question for you, too, Houston. What did Yankee Clipper's orbit finally decay down to? How well did you hit 60?

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Pete. It's 61.9 by 58.4 at CDH. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: Yes, that's pretty good, and we're targeted for zero CDH here on this thing, right?

speaker: Carr
text: That's affirmative.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: CDH standing for Constant Delta Height. It's the second maneuver in the rendezvous sequence. Given a normal or nominal situation it could very well turn out to be zero. It's designed to fine tune the orbit and with the numbers we're looking at it might very well turn out not to be necessary.

speaker: Carr
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston. We're about 35 seconds from LOS. You're looking good, and we're looking for an AOS at 141:17.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay, Jerry. Thank you.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: We've had Loss Of Signal with Yankee Clipper. We're at 140 hours, 32 minutes into the flight.

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. How do you read?

speaker: Conrad
text: Loud and clear.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. Read you the same.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 140 hours, 46 minutes now in the flight. We're 1 hour and 17 minutes away from Time Of Ignition, away from Intrepid's lunar lift-off from the Ocean of Storms. Intrepid will ignite running almost 5,000 pounds of propellant through the upper stage ascent engine. Ignition will occur with Yankee Clipper passing just overhead about 80 nautical miles ahead of Intrepid. Intrepid goes through a short vertical rise and pitches over to climb to altitude horizontally inserting into orbit with a velocity of nearly 6,000 feet per second at an altitude of some 60,000 feet. It's been a period of quite between Capcom Jerry Carr and Intrepid. We've been watching data on the displays at - the crew aboard Intrepid has completed loading their abort guidance system ascent targeting data. We're at 140 hours, 48 minutes now into the flight, and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control Houston now 140 hours, 52 minutes into the flight. We are still looking at a lift-off time of 142 hours, 03 minutes, 47 seconds. This ascent from the lunar surface is designed to put Intrepid in an initial orbit of 46.3 nautical miles by 8.8 nautical miles. For the burn we're looking for a Delta-V of 6,057 feet per second. The first maneuver following ascent, the concentric sequence initiate, is scheduled at 143 hours, 1 minute, 50 seconds with a Delta-V of 49.2 feet per second. The burn is scheduled to be done at apolune following lift-off and has the affect of raising the perilune. We're 1 hour, 10 minutes away now from scheduled Time Of Ignition. This is Apollo Control Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, Intrepid.

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. Go.

speaker: Conrad
text: Any objections to us starting P57 now?

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. We prefer that you wait until 45 in order to maximize the Delta-T there.

speaker: Conrad
text: You mean 15, I hope.

speaker: Carr
text: Yes. That's right - 15. We were thinking in terms of lift-off minus 45.

speaker: Conrad
text: I'm with you.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control Houston. Program 57 reference there is the lunar surface alignment program for the LM guidance computer. We are at 141 hours, 2 minutes into the flight, and 1 hour, 2 minutes away from Time Of Ignition. This is Apollo Control Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston.

speaker: Bean
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Al. Would you put battery 5 on the line now? Before, it wasn't really carrying it's load as well as it should have, and we'd like to pre-precondition that one, get it a little warmer and get it started early.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay. I noticed that; we'll do it.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: That's exactly what it did prior to descent - not much.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control at Houston at 141 hours, 9 minutes into the flight. We are 55 minutes away from ignition at this time. And some 8 minutes away from reacquiring the Command Module Yankee Clipper. In the Mission Control Center, a period of relatively quiet preparation, no large contention of persons have arrived yet into the viewing room, however in the control center proper certain key NASA management officials as well as fellow astronauts have arrived on the scene. Rocco Petrone, Apollo Director of the Apollo Program, as is George Low, Chris Kraft, Director of Flight Operations for the Manned Spacecraft Center, Jim McDivitt, Manager of the Apollo Spacecraft Program at MSC, Jim Lovell, the Commander for Apollo 13, Al Worden is here; Donald K. Slayton, Director of Flight Crew Operations, and Tom Stafford, Chief of the Astronaut Office. We are at 141 hours, 10 minutes into the flight and this is Apollo Control Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 141 hours, 16 minutes now into the flight. We're less than a minute away now from reacquiring the Command Module, Yankee Clipper, now on its thirtieth revolution.

speaker: Carr
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston. How do you read?

speaker: Conrad
text: Loud and clear. We're standing by...

speaker: Gordon
text: Clipper, read you loud and clear.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston, Yankee Clipper. Read you loud and clear.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Clipper. Reading you the same.

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay. Looks Go here, Jer.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Dick. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Clipper, Houston. Your state vectors are all good, so there'll be no uplink to you this time. Your map update PAD is scratched, and I've got a landmark tracking PAD if you're ready to copy?

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. Do you want us to do this one, or can we skip it?

speaker: Carr
text: Stand by. [Pause.]

speaker: Gordon
text: The reason I say that, Jerry; since I can't see them at these high Sun angles, it's pretty academic to do this one. I'd just as soon save the gas and skip it.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Dick. We're talking about it.

speaker: Carr
text: Clipper, Houston. The data is only in the event you want to try to watch lift-off.

speaker: Gordon
text: Yes. I know that. I don't think I can see them, Jerry, so let's skip it. The sun angle's too high.

speaker: Carr
text: Okay, Dick.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. You heard that exchange between Dick Gordon and Capsule Communicator Jerry Carr. What the discussion evolved about, Dick Gordon, aboard the Yankee Clipper, had the option of tracking Intrepid with his sextant on lift-off. As you heard, he indicated that the sun angle appeared too high to acquiring a sighting so that will probably be deleted from the actual Flight Plan. We're at 141 hours, 21 hours into the flight, 42 and a half minutes away from Time Of Ignition, and this is Apollo Control Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid. Houston. Your gravity angle difference looks good and, there'll be no uplinks to you this time.

speaker: Conrad
text: Very good, very good.

speaker: Carr
text: Yankee Clipper, Houston.

speaker: Gordon
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Dick. Here's the Comm plan. About the time - When you get VHF communications established with Intrepid, we're going to dump the MSFN relay. If for some reason you lose it and you want to - you want to hear the - the Intrepid lift-off, let us know, and we can reconfigure in about 20 seconds; but we would prefer to leave the relay out as long az you've got VHF.

speaker: Gordon
text: Roger. I think that'll be fine. Thank you. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Conrad
text: Boy, this place is fascinating, absolutely fascinating.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That was Al Bean aboard the Intrepid. We're at 141 hours, 23 minutes now into the flight.

speaker: Carr
text: Pretty nice looking torquing angles, Intrepid.

speaker: Bean
text: Yes, sir. I like them.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control Houston 141 hours, 30 minutes now into the flight. Conrad and Bean are now going through the final phases of verifying navigational alignments. You heard that car up from Jerry Carr committing the torquing angles onboard as they are going through Program 57, lunar alignment. At this time, Flight Director Pete Frank is checking status, pulsing all of his flight control team as to our status Go or No-Go, and we're standing by.

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. You're Go to East off on this Rev.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control Houston, You heard that call from Jerry Carr giving them a Go for lift-off this Rev. At T minus 10 seconds, one of the two, probably Conrad, pushes the abort stage button and the 2 stages, although still mates are no longer mechanically secured to each other. The ascent engine is armed at minus 5 seconds. Conrad pushes a Proceed button on his computer display telling it to continue on in program 12 for lift-off. At T zero he pushes the Engine Start after verifying that the engine is indeed On. We're at 32 minutes now away from ignition, and this is Apollo Control Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger - Roger.

speaker: Bean
text: Houston, did you copy the values [garble]?

speaker: Carr
text: That's affirmative, Al, and they're Go.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control Houston at 141 hours, 42 minutes now into the flight. We're 22 minutes away from Time Of Ignition. After ignition, Conrad confirms that the LM is stable and the altitude is increasing. Visual cues are prime for the first fifteen seconds. After pitchover is completed, the crew will be able to make their first solid checks on the primary guidance and navigation systems' performance. At lift-off plus 4 minutes, Conrad yaws Intrepid 20 degrees right to insure a continuing S-band lock. When time from ignition reaches approximately 6 minutes, 15 seconds, the onboard displays are changed from a velocity and altitude numbers to velocity to be gained. You'll probably hear Al Bean calling out some of these numbers. Engine shutdown monitoring is performed onboard simply by observing the velocity to be gained displayed. We're at 21 minutes now away from Time Of Ignition.

speaker: Conrad
text: Houston, we're firing ascent 1.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Intrepid. [Long pause.]

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. Looks good.

speaker: Carr
text: [Houston having looked over the tank pressure telemetry] Intrepid, Houston. Looks good. [Long Pause] Tank 2 looks good.

speaker: Carr
text: Tank 2 looks good.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That was Capcom Jerry Carr telling Intrepid that their tank pressures look good. Meanwhile in the Control Center, our upfront displays have switched over from the Flight Dynamics Trajectory Displays, the lunar map being taken down for this ascent phase of the mission. We're at 141 hours, 44 minutes and 19 minutes, 45 seconds away from ignition.

speaker: Bean
text: Bat's 2 and 4 coming off, Houston.

speaker: Conrad
text: [As per Sur-113 ] Batts 2 and 4 coming off, Houston.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Intrepid.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control Houston at 141 hours, 49 minutes.

speaker: Bean
text: Houston, Intrepid. Are you recommending VHF A Receiver On or Off for launch? Over.

speaker: Carr
text: Stand by, Intrepid. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: We are 14 minutes away from time of ignition now - the...

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. Need to have your VHF A Transmitter to Voice Range and Receiver, Off.

speaker: Bean
text: That's where she's at. Thanks.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Intrepid presently has Program 12 entered on their onboard computer; this is the guidance program for lunar lift-off. We are 141 hours, 50 minutes into the flight, and a little more than 13 minutes from Time Of Ignition.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control Houston, 141 hours, 52 minutes till the flight. Flight Director Pete Frank making a final check around the room as to the - our status for lift-off. We are 11 minutes, 48 seconds from scheduled Time Of Ignition. This is Apollo Control Houston.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: This is Apollo Control Houston. We are 10 minutes now away from Time Of Ignition. 141 hours, 54 minutes into the flight of Apollo 12. FIDO reports we have high speed data coming in from all 3 sites; we are at 141 hours, 56 minutes - 7 minutes, 54 seconds away from liftoff at this time. Mark - 5 minutes from scheduled Time Of Ignition. We are at 141 hours, 59 minutes now into the flight. We are 4 minutes away now; this is Apollo Control Houston standing by.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Mark 3 minutes from lift-off.

speaker: Conrad
text: Hello, Houston; Intrepid is on Vox. How do you read?

speaker: Carr
text: Loud and clear, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger. Checklist is complete; standing by for T IG minus 2.

speaker: Carr
text: Roger. [Long pause.]

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: That was Pete Conrad reporting they had completed their checklist. We're at 142 hours, 1 minute...Mark 2 minutes.

speaker: Conrad
text: T IG minus 2, 400 plus 10. Set your watch.

speaker: Bean
text: I set that at 1 minute.

speaker: Gordon
text: Houston Clipper. I have the LM.

speaker: Conrad
text: And start camera.

speaker: LM crew
text: [Garble].

speaker: LM Crew
text: Start [garbled under Gordon]

speaker: Carr
text: Roger, Clipper. Intrepid, Clipper's watching you.

speaker: Conrad
text: Howdy, Yankee Clipper. Okay. Very good. [Long pause.]

speaker: Conrad
text: On my mark, Yankee Clipper, it will be 1 minute.

speaker: Conrad
text: Mark. One minute. Master Arm is On [garble]...

speaker: Gordon
text: Okay.

speaker: Bean
text: Okay.

speaker: Conrad
text: 367, Read.

speaker: Bean
text: I've got it. First stage push in 30 seconds, Pete.

speaker: Conrad
text: Roger [Pause.]. Watch the ALSEP, and I'll fly the bird.

speaker: Bean
text: Sounds good to me.

speaker: Bean
text: Thirty-five?

speaker: Conrad
text: DSKY's blank. Average g; abort stage...

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: 30 seconds.

speaker: Bean
text: Abort stage, push.

speaker: LM Crew
text: Abort stage, push. Engine arm, ascent.

speaker: LM crew
text: Engine arm, ascent.

speaker: Bean
text: All we lack is Pro and, then after, we get engine, start.

speaker: Conrad
text: Okay.

speaker: Conrad
text: Twenty seconds.

speaker: Carr
text: Looking good, Pete.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: 10 seconds.

speaker: Conrad
text: Arm.

speaker: Bean
text: Go.

speaker: Conrad
text: Lift-Off.

speaker: Conrad
text: And away we go.

speaker: Bean
text: Boy, did it fire.

speaker: Conrad
text: Yawing? Looks pretty good

speaker: Bean
text: [Garble] our descent stage - holding on.

speaker: Conrad
text: Looks good. ALSEP looks good.

speaker: Bean
text: [Garble] It didn't get the ALSEP.

speaker: Public Affairs Officer
text: Looking good.

speaker: Carr
text: Intrepid, Houston. Copy ignition; guidance looks good.

speaker: Conrad
text: Pitchover's looking good. Okay. Boy, you sure do [garble].
